Because iPhone 3GS has been the best selling smartphone in history. It's the gold standard. So in the early days of iPhone 3GS a year ago, AT&T's return rates were 6%, which is below the smartphone average. And everybody was pretty happy about that. What are they for the iPhone 4? Again, you go online and you read all these articles about it, and you'd think it must be, jeez, at least half the people must be returning their phones, right? It's pretty serious. Well, we've got the data now. And the hard data says, it's 1.7%. It is less than a third of the return rates for the iPhone 3GS. Hard data, just a few days old. So smartphones have weak spots, about a half of 1% of all iPhone owners have called Apple Care about anything related to antennas and reception. And the returns at our largest iPhone 4 reseller, are a third of what they were for a phone that was regarded as spectacular a year ago. Okay? Pretty interesting. One more data point. AT&T has given us the early call drop rates information, just three days ago. They obviously run the, a very sophisticated network, they do a great job. And uh, they log call drops. That helps them improve their network. And so, we can't give out the absolute call drop data, that's very confidential and proprietary to them. For competitive reasons, they don't want to give it out, and I totally agree with them. But they're going to let us release the delta to the iPhone 3GS. So how is the call drops, how have iPhone called, how do call drops on iPhone 4 compare to call drops on iPhone 3GS during its early period, a year ago? How many additional calls are dropped per every 100 calls you make, on an iPhone 4 compared to an iPhone 3GS? And I can tell you, since we are being totally transparent, that even though we believe the iPhone 4's antenna is superior to that of the iPhone 3GS, I must report to you that the iPhone 4 drops more calls per 100 than the iPhone 3GS. That's what the data says. We got it three days ago. So how many more calls per 100,


---

## Part 2

**[Steve Jobs]**: Does the iPhone 4 drop than the iPhone 3GS?
Again, listening to Antennagate on the web, you would think, it must be dropping half the calls.
It must be dropping at least 50 more calls per hundred or 25 more calls per hundred, right?
Wouldn't you expect that?
This is the hard data.
The iPhone 4 drops less than one additional call per hundred more than the iPhone 3GS.
Less than one additional call per hundred.
Now, even less than one is too much for us.
We, we're trying to find out why.
We want to drive this lower than the 3GS.
But this does put it in perspective.
So, I have my own pet theory on this, which we have no proof of, but I'll give it to you anyway.
When the iPhone 3GS came out, we did not change the design from the iPhone 3.
And there was a healthy market of cases for the iPhone 3G that were already in stores that fit the 3GS perfectly since the design didn't change.
And in our stores, 80% of the iPhone 3GS users walked out with a case.
iPhone 4 has a radically new design.
None of the old cases fit.
Since we didn't show it to anybody, none of the new cases are ready.
And we can't make enough of our bumper cases.
And so in our stores, about 20% of the people are going out with a case.
And I think that has something to do with this disparity.
But who knows?
We're going to track it down.
But again, zooming out, less than one additional call drop per hundred calls over the iPhone 3GS.
So if you put these four things together, smartphones have weak spots.
Most every smartphone we've tested exhibits the identical behavior if grabbed in a reasonable way as the videos you've all seen on the web of the iPhone 4.
Around a half of 1% of iPhone owners have called AppleCare in relation to reception and antenna issues.
Only 0.55% of all iPhone owners have called.
An extremely low number.
The return rates for iPhone 4 are running 1/3 of those for the iPhone 3GS a year ago.
And the iPhone 4 drops less than one more call per hundred than the iPhone 3GS.
Now, when we look at this data, when our engineers and scientists look at this data, it's very hard to escape the conclusion that there is a problem, but that that problem is affecting a very small percentage of users.
I myself have gotten somewhere over 5,000 emails from users telling me how their iPhone 4 works perfectly and they can't figure out what all of this is about.
So we think there is a problem, but we think it's affecting a small percentage of users.
And we think some of that problem is inherent in most every smartphone.
But having said this, we care about every user.
And we're not going to stop until every one of those is happy.
But I think it's important to understand the scope of this problem because what the data says leads you to the conclusion that this has been blown so out of proportion that it's, it's incredible.
I, I know it's fun to have a story, but, uh, it's less fun when you're on the other end of it.
So, we care about every user.
So let me tell you what we're going to do.
The first thing we did yesterday, we released iOS version 4.0.1.
That is now out.
People are updating it.
It fixes the, uh, wrong formula that we used to calculate how many bars to put up for a given signal strength.
And there was a nasty exchange bug in there that a lot of our corporate customers are hitting and that's fixed as well.
So those bugs are fixed.
iOS 4 is out.
Uh, 4.0.1 is out and we recommend that every iPhone owner, uh, update to it.
Secondly, a lot of people have told us the bumper solves the signal strength problem.
Consumer Reports is the latest one this week.
We've heard it from a lot of people.
Why don't you just give everybody a case?
Okay, great.
Let's give everybody a case.
We've got our bumper case here.
We want to give everybody a free case.
Every iPhone user is going to get a free case.
One for every iPhone 4.
If you've already bought one, we'll give you a full refund for a bumper.
And we're going to do this for every iPhone 4 purchased through September 30th.
We'll reexamine this in September and decide whether to keep going or maybe we'll have a better idea.
Uh, but, uh, at least through September 30th, a free case for every iPhone 4.
And if you bought a bumper, we'll give you a full refund.
Now, everything in life is more complicated than it seems on the surface.
We're going to send you a free case.
We can't make enough bumpers, right?
We were planning on selling them and making a certain percentage and we have the tooling done.
If we're going to try to give a bumper to everyone, we, no way we can make enough in the quarter.
So what we're going to do is source some other cases and give users a choice of cases.
And they'll be able to pick one.
And you can apply on our website starting late next week.
It'll take us about a week to get this all up.
Pick a case, zoom, we'll send it off to you.
That's simple.
So, a free case for every iPhone 4 user.
Simple.
And if you're still not happy, before or after you get a free case, as we've said, you can bring your iPhone 4 back undamaged within 30 days for a full refund.
We've waived any restocking fees, anything, full refund.
So we are going to take care of everyone.
We want every user to be happy.
And if we can't make them happy, we'll give them a full refund.
Does that make sense?
So, I've got some other updates for you.
Um, just some other things going on relative to the iPhone 4.
And then we'll get into Q&A.
Again, iOS 4 version 4.0.1 was released yesterday.
We're tracking some problems with the proximity sensor and we're working on some solutions and hopefully we'll get those into the next software update.
This seems to affect again a fairly small number of users, but it's uh probably a pesky problem for those users, so we're going to try to get it fixed as fast as we can.
White iPhone, a lot of people waiting for the white iPhone.
We're going to start shipping it end of this month.
And our quantities will be limited at first and we're ramping up as fast as we can.
But white iPhones will start shipping at the end of July.
And also, on July 30th, we are going to bring the iPhone to 17 more countries.
And uh these are the same 17 we talked about before, uh with the omission of just South Korea because it's going to take us a little longer to get government approval there.
Uh, but um 17 countries, July 30th.
So that's the update on the iPhone 4.
In ending, and I'd like to just kind of give you a feel of what we care about and how we operate and how we make decisions.
We love our users.
We really love them.
And we try very hard to surprise and delight them.
We work our asses off for them.
And it's great.
And we have a blast doing it.
And we make some pretty interesting products for them.
Macs and iPods and iPhones and iPads and Apple TV, the App Store, the iTunes store, Mac OS 10, iOS, iLife, iWork, Final Cut.
We make some pretty great products for them.
And what motivates us is to just have them love them.
So we love our users.
And we work really hard to surprise and delight and delight them with these products.
We also connect them with great apps and developers through our App Stores and great content through iTunes and really bring the world of content creation and app creation and our users together in some extremely innovative ways, even if we don't make a lot of money from it.
We love our users so much that we've built 300 Apple retail stores for them to give them the best buying experience in the world and more importantly the best ownership experience in the world with genius bars that cost nothing to come in and talk to people and get your products fixed and get advice.
We have one-to-one seminars to teach people how to use our products.
We had over 60 million people through our stores last quarter.
60 million.
So we do all this because we love our users.
And when we fall short, which we do sometimes, we try harder.
We try harder.
We pick ourselves up, we figure out what's wrong and we try harder.
And when we succeed, they reward us by staying our users.
And that makes it all worth it.
So that's what drives us.
And when we have problems like this and when people are criticizing us, we take it really personally.
Maybe we shouldn't.
You know, maybe we should have a wall of PR people keeping us away from all that, but we don't.
We all read these stories.
We all take it really personally.
And if a user's having a problem, it's our problem.
So we've been working really, really hard for the last 22 days to try to understand what the real problem is so that when we solve it, we actually solve it rather than just putting a band-aid on it or giving a certain press person what they think they want us to do.
And we think we've gotten to the heart of the problem here.
And the heart of the problem is smartphones have weak spots.
We made ours extremely visible.
Some took advantage of that to demonstrate it.
It was very easily demonstrable.
We screwed up on displaying too many bars and we made that demonstration more theatrical than it needed to be.
And so for those small number of customers that are having problems, we're going to give them cases, which we think will take care of most of those problems.
And for those that still are unhappy, we're going to give them a full refund.
And that's everything we can do to try to make every customer happy.
But the data supports the fact that the iPhone 4 is the best smartphone in the world.
And that there is no Antennagate.
There is a challenge for the entire smartphone industry to be able to improve its antenna performance someday to where there are no weak spots on any smartphone.
And we're dedicated to doing that.
But unfortunately, that's a day in the future.
So for today, we love our customers and we're going to try to take care of every single one.
And that's what I had.

# Apple Computer_ The Macintosh Portable (1989)

**Source**: /Volumes/NvME-Satechi/steve-jobs.ai/Database_Steve_Jobs/1980s/Apple Computer_ The Macintosh Portable (1989).mp4

**Transcribed**: 2025-12-31 10:03

---

**[Narrator]**: I would take a portable computer with me on the road all the time, whether it be in the middle of a rainforest or on top of a mountain, on a plane, anywhere we might find ourselves doing a story.

**[Narrator]**: Mike Sarraille has traveled the globe, producing stories from Niger salt caravans to Bali water guides to Quebec ice boat racing. His international business is organized around a Macintosh network. Now with the Macintosh portable, his office can go with him around the world.

**[Mike Sarraille]**: Because we're in the television business and because we're a small business, the Macs have made us look like a big business. It makes us look like a big network. It makes us move and react and operate like a network. And that's essential to our operation.

**[Mike Sarraille]**: Because we depend on foreign networks for much of our material, it's very important that we're linked up with them. And my French counterpart at TF1 in Paris has a Mac. We were doing a story with them on the Niger salt caravans. It was important that we had a copy of their script that we could put into our system that had much of the research and all the facts. The Mac allowed me to stay in touch with my French counterpart at all times during the evolution of the story. And so it's important that we hook up our systems and become somewhat of a mini global network.

**[Mike Sarraille]**: ScanMan has allowed us to copy in maps, copy in contracts, family trees, historical documents, things of that nature that we can keep and have access to. What we can do with the scanners, we could scan in a local map, a map that relates specifically to our story. And so it allows us to be kind of a duplication service with modifications. And the modifications are the things that we need to keep us all getting to the right point at the right place at the right time.

**[Mike Sarraille]**: We have a habit of taking some very sophisticated electronic equipment into some very odd places. We were doing a story in Monte La Selva, the rainforest reserve in Costa Rica, where we literally had to climb 90 feet up into the jungle canopy to do the story. So in addition to bringing up very expensive camera equipment, it would be just as easy to bring up the portable Mac and still operate from a treehouse or a tree platform 90 feet above the jungle in Costa Rica. So the portable Mac, it goes where we go.

**[Mike Sarraille]**: Logging tapes after a shoot every night is probably the most tedious but one of the most essential things we do on the road. So if I can log into the computer what I have on videotape, I can write a script and give specific time code cues to our editor and get send back by modem a script that he can actually start working with. And I've already picked out most of the shots. I've identified the key players. I've been able to highlight the the main sound bites. So anything that helps us logging tapes, which is so key to our job, is incredible for us.

**[Mike Sarraille]**: The portable Mac allows us to keep moving. If someone needs something, we've got it. That's key to my business.

**[Narrator]**: Collecting details is crucial to solving crime in today's world. Accuracy is the key. Now with the Macintosh portable, the investigative team can be organized and use their time efficiently.

**[Law Enforcement Officer]**: Using the forms on the computer, we have the ability to save a lot of time, a lot of manpower, and again money, which is really what we're after. We want to solve crimes, save money, be efficient.

**[Law Enforcement Officer]**: As evidence is collected on scene, it's bagged, it's annotated or initialed as to who's collected it and what it was. But there is an evidence collection form that again in the computer can be immediately filled out, printed out, connected right to that bag of evidence. So it helps maintain a very strong chain of custody.

**[Narrator]**: Also on the premises with the Macintosh portable and a measuring tape is the illustrator. Gathering specific dimensions, he'll generate a detailed floor plan which can be used to help reconstruct the crime scene.

**[Law Enforcement Officer]**: The illustrators here have been working on Macs can now go out to the field and feel very comfortable with the machine that they're using. They have the same benefits that they have here at headquarters. They have the same applications. They're running the same kind of software and they're doing the exact same work on that portable as they do here at headquarters.

**[Narrator]**: The floor plan provided by the illustrators can now be used as a reference diagram to help with the questioning of the witnesses.

**[Law Enforcement Officer]**: People who previously had to go out on scene, interview witnesses, etc., would come back to the office and we would have pages and pages of notes and then it would only have to be completely regenerated all over again. We're going to start by entering it into the computer.

**[Law Enforcement Officer]**: The Mac portable is going to be great because it can one go right on the network or when it's out in the field can be modem in. At that point, that information then can be taken to the next step. It can be colorized, it can be animated. So if we have a large case and we have say five to seven illustrators working on that case, we can work on that case all at once. It's a shared workload then.

**[Law Enforcement Officer]**: What we would really like to see courtroom presentation go is to be able to take the technology of a portable Macintosh, be able to print the hard copies for use in court, but then go to a package of some computer animation where we walk into court with not an armload of charts, but a videotape.

**[Law Enforcement Officer]**: If you're sitting in a jury or you're the judge, you want to see it. You don't want to conceptualize it in your mind. So if they can see that incident actually reoccur, the power of that is great.

**[Narrator]**: In today's environment with all the technology that's out there, people want immediate answers. With the portable, we can give them those immediate answers.

**[Insurance Agent]**: When we're meeting with a client and we bring something like this in and are able to answer a question more quickly or more effectively, that is going to give us an edge over our competition.

**[Narrator]**: Edna Insurance Corporation conducts mid-year reviews to update client policy information. Tony Parker and Margo Johnson carry everything they need in the Macintosh portable.

**[Insurance Agent]**: Right now when we go to visit policy holders, depending on what we'll be covering, sometimes it's necessary to bring volumes of books. We won't have to do that anymore because we'll be networked with our home office and have that same information on the computer.

**[Narrator]**: Any additional information the sales team needs for the mid-year review can be easily accessed by connecting to the home office.

**[Insurance Agent]**: With the modem, my manuals are there, my home office people are there, everybody's there at the client's office with me. And that way I can get most of my answers immediately.

**[Software Developer]**: To make the machines really contribute to the work of the office, they had to be connected to each other. And so we we chose the Macintosh because that connectivity was so easy to do.

**[Narrator]**: After locating the additional information, the service rep adds the adjusted data to the client's file. This makes it possible for Tony and Margo to create an updated graph on site.

**[Insurance Agent]**: There it is.

**[Insurance Agent]**: All right.

**[Insurance Agent]**: That's great. That's great. I can't believe you got them that fast.

**[Insurance Agent]**: The communications aspect of it is going to be terrific. It's just going to prove that we're more efficient and uh that we really know what we're talking about. We've got the data there. We can develop it for them. It's helped us uh do our job better.

**[Narrator]**: One week later, Tony and Margo present the revised policy information to the client and her staff. By projecting the graphics from the Macintosh portable, they are able to make a powerful large screen presentation.

**[Insurance Agent]**: We're able to put out something that looks uh very professional and and uh puts on a good image. We are a company that is taking all the technology that we can handle and put it to good use and to their advantage.

**[Insurance Agent]**: It has become a part of our office. I don't think we can function as effectively without them.

**[Insurance Agent]**: I doubt the portable will be away from me at all.

**[Narrator]**: Firefighters face a serious challenge in the complex environment of today's cities. Each fire is a venture into the unknown with dangerous building structures and electrical and chemical hazards. The Macintosh portable is a powerful new tool that allows firefighters to battle the biggest enemy of all, time.

**[Firefighter]**: The greatest advantage of being able to have a portable with us in the vehicle en route to the scene is a lot of times we have long response times, six or seven or eight minutes, and we can be making decisions by using the computer while we're en route. The captain can bring up a data card about that building and it will tell him all the essential information he's going to need to know. And then from that he can access particular information about the water system so he'll know what hydrant he wants to hook up to, what other engines are going to go to which hydrants when they arrive. With the new Macintosh portable, you'll be able to actually run the computer while you're en route to the scene and make better use of that time. And by having a rugged dependable piece of equipment that can be operated while you're moving, it's going to be a great advantage for all of us.

**[Firefighter]**: The worst situation is going to be a warehouse or a large structure fire where you have smoke banking almost to the floor, very poor visibility, and you're basically going into the building blind. And it's it's really important us to know something about the inside of that building. We don't just want to walk into something that we know nothing about.

**[Firefighter]**: Okay, we have very poor visibility. Can you give me any information on the floor plan?

**[Firefighter]**: Stand by, we'll bring it up now.

**[Firefighter]**: That's clear.

**[Firefighter]**: By using the portable, they can bring up the floor plans for the particular area of the building that's involved. Anything else that we might need to know about that building can be brought up and graphically shown on the screen so that the command post can give their orders as far as what they want the companies to do.

**[Firefighter]**: 136, advise we do have the floor plan up on this now. We have two hazardous materials locations. We have carbo insecticide in 20 lb bags stored on the left side of the building. And on your right side, you've got some propane cylinders uh should be stored near the garage door, approximately six to eight cylinders. Copy?

**[Firefighter]**: That's clear.

**[Narrator]**: The hazardous materials program shows two immediate dangers at the scene. The pesticide can form a poison gas and the propane is a powerful explosive. The propane must be removed before it overheats and explodes.

**[Firefighter]**: We looked at a lot of other portables before we even talked about changing from the Macintosh just so we could use a field portable. But a problem with many of the portables is the battery life. And we need a portable that's going to go out and do the job for six or eight hours during the day or at a at a fire scene or at a hazardous material scene. We need a portable that's going to work for long hours and the Macintosh will do that.

**[Narrator]**: The Macintosh portable has given the Winterville firefighters information and time. Two crucial elements for staying alive in a dangerous occupation.

**[Narrator]**: 7,000 years ago, a volcanic eruption collapsed Mount Mazama. The explosion was 42 times the power of Mount St. Helens. Springs, snow, and rain began to fill the depression with water and in time formed the deepest body of water in the United States, Crater Lake.

**[Narrator]**: This summer we'll complete a five-year investigation into the mysteries of Crater Lake. The team is headed by Oregon State oceanographers Bob Collier and Jack Diamond. They hope to prove that hydrothermal springs are venting up from the floor of the lake and are responsible for its unique chemistry.

**[Narrator]**: The Deep Rover will take the scientist into the darkest regions of the crater. Traveling with them to depths that will exceed 1900 feet is the Macintosh portable.

**[Oceanographer]**: We have a a whole variety of essentially state-of-the-art instruments which make measurements during our dives. Eventually all of this data has to flow together and be merged into one data set. We found in previous years that this whole operation is so intensive that we we would never get the time to do that synthesis until after the program was over with. Now that we have the portable Mac, we could essentially acquire data in real time and display it in real time.

**[Oceanographer]**: We're stuck down here in the field in an operation that's costing us many, many, many thousands of dollars a day and we can't afford to make the wrong decisions. And so the more computing power we have, the more effective the research will be in the end.

**[Oceanographer]**: The portable now can be the driving force in the field for our instrumentation controls. Attached to the submarine are a whole bunch of different sensors. At any given moment, the pilot is looking at at readings from those sensors, temperature, depth, direction. He also is looking at a stream of character readout. So as he sits there, he's got to instantaneously make literally hundreds of decisions. So what the Macintosh portable now allows us to do is interface into those sensors and give a visual representation of where we're going.

**[Oceanographer]**: The way we've designed our team is to uh have one of our research assistants, Bobby Connard, work on moving that data into a form where we can create plots, contour diagrams of the track of the vehicle and and superimpose all of these data sets and be able to bring them out, look at them, print them, take them out on the next day's dive and make decisions based on that right away.

**[Oceanographer]**: The ultimate goal is to get something out that the rest of the world can see. What we're able to do now with the introduction of the portable is complete the circle. We can now take come right in off the field, not worry about having to go through a million different types of translations, manipulate the data very transparently and literally desktop publish the end result.

**[Narrator]**: During the final weeks of their investigation, the team discovered a source of hot water that appears to indicate the existence of a hydrothermal vent. Five years of intensive research and the onsite data analysis now made possible by the Macintosh portable seems to have paid off.

**[Law Enforcement Officer]**: What we would really like to see courtroom presentation go is to be able to take the technology of a portable Macintosh, be able to print the hard copies for use in court, but then go to a package of some computer animation where we walk into court with not an armload of charts, but a videotape.

**[Law Enforcement Officer]**: If you're sitting in a jury or you're the judge, you want to see it. You don't want to conceptualize it in your mind. So if they can see that incident actually reoccur, the power of that is great.

**[Narrator]**: In today's environment with all the technology that's out there, people want immediate answers. With the portable, we can give them those immediate answers.

**[Insurance Agent]**: When we're meeting with a client and we bring something like this in and are able to answer a question more quickly or more effectively, that is going to give us an edge over our competition.

**[Narrator]**: Edna Insurance Corporation conducts mid-year reviews to update client policy information. Tony Parker and Margo Johnson carry everything they need in the Macintosh portable.

**[Insurance Agent]**: Right now when we go to visit policy holders, depending on what we'll be covering, sometimes it's necessary to bring volumes of books. We won't have to do that anymore because we'll be networked with our home office and have that same information on the computer.

**[Narrator]**: Any additional information the sales team needs for the mid-year review can be easily accessed by connecting to the home office.

**[Insurance Agent]**: With the modem, my manuals are there, my home office people are there, everybody's there at the client's office with me. And that way I can get most of my answers immediately.

**[Software Developer]**: To make the machines really contribute to the work of the office, they had to be connected to each other. And so we we chose the Macintosh because that connectivity was so easy to do.

**[Narrator]**: After locating the additional information, the service rep adds the adjusted data to the client's file. This makes it possible for Tony and Margo to create an updated graph on site.

**[Insurance Agent]**: There it is.

**[Insurance Agent]**: All right.

**[Insurance Agent]**: That's great. That's great. I can't believe you got them that fast.

**[Insurance Agent]**: The communications aspect of it is going to be terrific. It's just going to prove that we're more efficient and uh that we really know what we're talking about. We've got the data there. We can develop it for them. It's helped us uh do our job better.

**[Narrator]**: One week later, Tony and Margo present the revised policy information to the client and her staff. By projecting the graphics from the Macintosh portable, they are able to make a powerful large screen presentation.

**[Insurance Agent]**: We're able to put out something that looks uh very professional and and uh puts on a good image. We are a company that is taking all the technology that we can handle and put it to good use and to their advantage.

**[Insurance Agent]**: It has become a part of our office. I don't think we can function as effectively without them.

**[Insurance Agent]**: I doubt the portable will be away from me at all.

**[Narrator]**: Firefighters face a serious challenge in the complex environment of today's cities. Each fire is a venture into the unknown with dangerous building structures and electrical and chemical hazards. The Macintosh portable is a powerful new tool that allows firefighters to battle the biggest enemy of all, time.

**[Firefighter]**: The greatest advantage of being able to have a portable with us in the vehicle en route to the scene is a lot of times we have long response times, six or seven or eight minutes, and we can be making decisions by using the computer while we're en route. The captain can bring up a data card about that building and it will tell him all the essential information he's going to need to know. And then from that he can access particular information about the water system so he'll know what hydrant he wants to hook up to, what other engines are going to go to which hydrants when they arrive. With the new Macintosh portable, you'll be able to actually run the computer while you're en route to the scene and make better use of that time. And by having a rugged dependable piece of equipment that can be operated while you're moving, it's going to be a great advantage for all of us.

**[Firefighter]**: The worst situation is going to be a warehouse or a large structure fire where you have smoke banking almost to the floor, very poor visibility, and you're basically going into the building blind. And it's it's really important us to know something about the inside of that building. We don't just want to walk into something that we know nothing about.

**[Firefighter]**: Okay, we have very poor visibility. Can you give me any information on the floor plan?

**[Firefighter]**: Stand by, we'll bring it up now.

**[Firefighter]**: That's clear.

**[Firefighter]**: By using the portable, they can bring up the floor plans for the particular area of the building that's involved. Anything else that we might need to know about that building can be brought up and graphically shown on the screen so that the command post can give their orders as far as what they want the companies to do.

**[Firefighter]**: 136, advise we do have the floor plan up on this now. We have two hazardous materials locations. We have carbo insecticide in 20 lb bags stored on the left side of the building. And on your right side, you've got some propane cylinders uh should be stored near the garage door, approximately six to eight cylinders. Copy?

**[Firefighter]**: That's clear.

**[Narrator]**: The hazardous materials program shows two immediate dangers at the scene. The pesticide can form a poison gas and the propane is a powerful explosive. The propane must be removed before it overheats and explodes.

**[Firefighter]**: We looked at a lot of other portables before we even talked about changing from the Macintosh just so we could use a field portable. But a problem with many of the portables is the battery life. And we need a portable that's going to go out and do the job for six or eight hours during the day or at a at a fire scene or at a hazardous material scene. We need a portable that's going to work for long hours and the Macintosh will do that.

**[Narrator]**: The Macintosh portable has given the Winterville firefighters information and time. Two crucial elements for staying alive in a dangerous occupation.

**[Narrator]**: 7,000 years ago, a volcanic eruption collapsed Mount Mazama. The explosion was 42 times the power of Mount St. Helens. Springs, snow, and rain began to fill the depression with water and in time formed the deepest body of water in the United States, Crater Lake.

**[Narrator]**: This summer we'll complete a five-year investigation into the mysteries of Crater Lake. The team is headed by Oregon State oceanographers Bob Collier and Jack Diamond. They hope to prove that hydrothermal springs are venting up from the floor of the lake and are responsible for its unique chemistry.

**[Narrator]**: The Deep Rover will take the scientist into the darkest regions of the crater. Traveling with them to depths that will exceed 1900 feet is the Macintosh portable.

**[Oceanographer]**: We have a a whole variety of essentially state-of-the-art instruments which make measurements during our dives. Eventually all of this data has to flow together and be merged into one data set. We found in previous years that this whole operation is so intensive that we we would never get the time to do that synthesis until after the program was over with. Now that we have the portable Mac, we could essentially acquire data in real time and display it in real time.

**[Oceanographer]**: We're stuck down here in the field in an operation that's costing us many, many, many thousands of dollars a day and we can't afford to make the wrong decisions. And so the more computing power we have, the more effective the research will be in the end.

**[Oceanographer]**: The portable now can be the driving force in the field for our instrumentation controls. Attached to the submarine are a whole bunch of different sensors. At any given moment, the pilot is looking at at readings from those sensors, temperature, depth, direction. He also is looking at a stream of character readout. So as he sits there, he's got to instantaneously make literally hundreds of decisions. So what the Macintosh portable now allows us to do is interface into those sensors and give a visual representation of where we're going.

**[Oceanographer]**: The way we've designed our team is to uh have one of our research assistants, Bobby Connard, work on moving that data into a form where we can create plots, contour diagrams of the track of the vehicle and and superimpose all of these data sets and be able to bring them out, look at them, print them, take them out on the next day's dive and make decisions based on that right away.

**[Oceanographer]**: The ultimate goal is to get something out that the rest of the world can see. What we're able to do now with the introduction of the portable is complete the circle. We can now take come right in off the field, not worry about having to go through a million different types of translations, manipulate the data very transparently and literally desktop publish the end result.

**[Narrator]**: During the final weeks of their investigation, the team discovered a source of hot water that appears to indicate the existence of a hydrothermal vent. Five years of intensive research and the onsite data analysis now made possible by the Macintosh portable seems to have paid off.

# Apple Computer,   Chapter One 1989

**Source**: /Volumes/NvME-Satechi/steve-jobs.ai/Database_Steve_Jobs/1980s/Apple Computer,   Chapter One 1989.mp4

**Transcribed**: 2025-12-31 10:02

---

**[Narrator]**: In 1923, Lon Chaney's brilliant characterization of Quasimodo in the Hunchback of Notre Dame played on the audience's tendency to stereotype, to prejudge individuals according to their appearance, rather than understand them for who they really were.

**[Narrator]**: It's been nearly a century since the Hunchback of Notre Dame horrified audiences in the silent movie houses. But have attitudes changed much in 95 years? Or do we still judge far too quickly the content by the cover?

**[Narrator]**: Oh, where do we go from here?

**[Computer Voice]**: Show me writer's block. The current project is untitled. To continue, you may wish to review your outline, explore the suggestion box, or view great writers' methods. Sometimes a short break helps to stimulate ideas. Perhaps you'd enjoy a pleasant walk.

**[Narrator]**: Oh, it's not that bad yet. Um, show me the outline.

**[Computer Voice]**: Your next heading is Technology's impact on attitudes toward people with disabilities. The subheading is the catalyst for change.

**[Narrator]**: Okay, I need some examples. Um, where can we go for information about how attitudes and expectations have changed toward people with disability in the last, say, 15 or 20 years?

**[Computer Voice]**: I have a list of consultants who provide data excerpts in related areas. There is also a media index called Capabilities Enhancement.

**[Narrator]**: Good, show me the index, hold the list.

**[Child 1]**: Did you guys just finish an entire box of cookies?

**[Child 2]**: Mom, the science said makes you hungry. Besides, it wasn't entire box. You had some too.

**[Narrator]**: One, I had one. Well, maybe two. Honey, it's too early for dinner. I'm working against a deadline. Can you wait about an hour?

**[Child 2]**: Maybe.

**[Narrator]**: The lonely, unappreciated scientific genius forges on, despite enormous odds.

**[Narrator]**: Right. Happy forging. Bye.

**[Scientist]**: Okay, so much for the hydrogen iodide. One more unit and we're done. Now, wait a second. What did they think would happen if we used chlorine with this? Zach, don't do this to me, please. Come on, one last sense of adventure. Frustrate me.

**[Narrator]**: Show me this one.

**[Man]**: Hi, Cindy.

**[Computer Voice]**: Well, hi there, Cindy. What's cooking today?

**[Cindy]**: I'm cooking some strawberry cake for Mom's birthday.

**[Computer Voice]**: A strawberry cake for Mom's birthday? Okay. First, let's get our equipment. A big spoon, a mixing bowl, and your special measuring cup.

**[Cindy]**: Okay.

**[Computer Voice]**: The first thing to do is to put the measuring cup on the scale.

**[Computer Voice]**: Good. Now, pour in three-quarters cup of milk.

**[Computer Voice]**: That's it. Keep pouring.

**[Computer Voice]**: Cindy, you stopped. You need one-quarter cup more. Here, I'll show you. Fill it up to the yellow line.

**[Cindy]**: Okay, because of the crack.

**[Computer Voice]**: That's it. Keep pouring. All the way up to the yellow line.

**[Cindy]**: That's it.

**[Computer Voice]**: Good. Now, make sure you stir the batter until it is smooth and creamy.

**[Computer Voice]**: Cindy, are you finished yet?

**[Cindy]**: Yep.

**[Computer Voice]**: Did you get all of the lumps out?

**[Cindy]**: Mhm.

**[Computer Voice]**: Okay. Now, put the baking bowl into the microwave and I'll take care of the rest. I'll call you when it's ready, then we can put on the strawberries.

**[Cindy]**: [Laughter]

**[Computer Voice]**: Well, Cindy, that should just about do it. I hope you had fun making Mom's birthday cake. I think she'll really be surprised.

**[Narrator]**: Good. Save this in the presentation folder. Show me the main index again.

**[Scientist 1]**: It's not doing anything.

**[Scientist 2]**: Good. We'll just submit the results and move to the next one.

**[Scientist 1]**: No, wait, maybe we should try heating it up.

**[Scientist 2]**: I can't believe this.

**[Narrator]**: Show me this one.

**[Woman]**: Sorry, I said, if you'll let my advertising deficit ride through this quarter, I promise to make it up to you in the fall.

**[Man]**: Steph, that's what you said last year.

**[Woman]**: I know, but this year I'm planning a huge promotion to get ready for the holidays. I think we can at least double our normal business for the season. How much stock would you need?

**[Man]**: I'm estimating about 10,000 pieces. And I want to run four weeks of full-page ads in the mailer.

**[Man]**: Four weeks, really?

**[Man]**: I think we can work something out.

**[Man]**: Well, I'll have to talk with my sales manager, but yes, I think we can.

**[Waiter]**: Bonjour, Madame. Bonjour, Monsieur.

**[Woman]**: Bonjour, Pierre. Nice to be back.

**[Waiter]**: Monsieur, vous désirez un apéritif?

**[Woman]**: Non, merci. Thanks. Would you like a drink?

**[Man]**: No, no, thank you.

**[Woman]**: I think we'll just see the menu, thank you.

**[Waiter]**: Très bien, Madame. Tout de suite.

**[Man]**: Impressive. I didn't know you spoke French.

**[Woman]**: Well, I don't really, but I understand a little.

**[Scientist 1]**: Wow, I think we just discovered hydrochloric acid, partner. Now let's add the fluorine.

**[Scientist 2]**: Zach, I just realized something. And now for the hydrogen. Zach, don't these halogens, as you go up the periodic table, don't they get smaller too?

**[Scientist 1]**: You were saying?

**[Scientist 2]**: Never mind.

**[Professor]**: Gentlemen, we can discuss this particular reaction tomorrow in lab. In the meantime, please review the program on halogens before it means the end of civilization as we know it.

**[Scientist 1]**: I'll review it right away, sir. Good luck.

**[Scientist 2]**: Some partner.

**[Narrator]**: As we move into the 20s, we begin an era of discovery where doing even simple things can bring great power. Each new year brings the hope that even our bravest dreams may yet come true. Quasimodo is a symbol of the last century's sometimes backward ways. Then people like Stephanie and Cindy are symbols of the future. Technology is not the only answer, but it can be and is a catalyst for change.

**[Narrator]**: Stop. Let's shut down.

**[Computer Voice]**: This document is unnamed. What is your title?

**[Narrator]**: Good question.

**[Narrator]**: Hey Einstein, you got any good ideas what I should call this thing?

**[Child]**: Call what?

**[Narrator]**: The project I'm working on.

**[Child]**: I don't know. Is it finished?

**[Narrator]**: No, I just got started really.

**[Narrator]**: Chapter One, that's not a bad idea. Okay, you guys, let's see.

documents.title: Apple II Forever - Apple IIc Apple II-GS 1988
documents.speaker: Steve Jobs
documents.content:
# Apple II Forever - Apple IIc Apple II-GS 1988

**Source**: /Volumes/NvME-Satechi/steve-jobs.ai/Database_Steve_Jobs/1980s/Apple II Forever - Apple IIc Apple II-GS 1988.mp4

**Transcribed**: 2025-12-31 10:05

---

## Part 1

**Narrator**: If I say the word Apple, you say the word Macintosh. But if I played the same game just a few years ago and said Apple, you would probably say two or two E or two plus, for it was the Apple II that started this company. But with the recent success of the Macintosh and the Mac II in particular, there have been rumors that the old Apple II was headed for the orphanage. Not so, for there's a new Apple II C and a new Apple II GS. Today, we take a look at the new generation of Apple II computers on this edition of the Computer Chronicles.

**Narrator**: The Computer Chronicles is made possible in part by McGraw Hill, publishers of Byte Magazine and BIX, the Byte Information Exchange. In print and online, Byte and BIX serve computer professionals worldwide with detailed information on new hardware, software, and technologies.

**Narrator**: Welcome to the Computer Chronicles. I'm Stewart Cheifet, and this is Gary Kildall. Gary, what I've got over here in this little briefcase is an original Apple I computer before they thought about cases for computers. This guy put it into his briefcase. Uh, this is literally a museum piece, but it's only about 10 years old, and of course, it represents state-of-the-art technology, uh, at the time for personal computers. Knowing what we know about technology and PCs today, what is the point in coming out with a new eight-bit computer like the 2C Plus?
**Gary Kildall**: Well, Stewart, it's important to understand what the Apple really, where it came from. Uh, Steve Wozniak is the guy that engineered this thing, and he was a video person as well as a computer person. He realized you could put these two things together. Great for playing games, uh, real low cost because you could hook it to your TV set. As a result, they got a head start in a lot of the other PC, uh, computer manufacturers. A lot of software was produced, good customer basis. It's a sufficient machine for a lot of people to use in education and the home and so forth. And Apple said, "Well, why not service that customer base and give them a new machine?"
**Narrator**: Well, we're going to take a look at that new machine today. It's the Apple 2C Plus, and we'll see how it has improved on its ancestors. We'll also take a look at GSOS, the new operating system for the Apple II GS, and its new ability to work with a CD-ROM drive. Now, Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak were the architects of this early generation of Apple II computer. John Sculley is the driving force behind Apple now, and we're going to start out this program by visiting John Sculley in his office at Apple to find out about the company's real commitment to the future of the Apple II.
**Reporter**: Since its introduction over 10 years ago, the Apple II has proven to be a sturdy and persistent computer with a loyal following of devoted fans. There are now about 4.5 million of them scattered around the world. But company support for the Apple II line, at least in the eyes of its owners, hasn't always been evident, as Apple President John Sculley admits.
**John Sculley**: Well, I think in many ways that Apple II users have felt abandoned by Apple because they haven't heard many messages from the top people in our organization to give them encouragement that the Apple II was important. And to be perfectly honest, this was a very conscious, uh, direction on our part as we were trying to convince business users that Apple wasn't in the home computer business only, that we were also, uh, able to provide very powerful business workstations. Without the success of the Macintosh in business, we couldn't afford the huge investment we have in research and development and the supportive proprietary technologies for Macintosh and the Apple II.
**Reporter**: Today, the Apple II has become three machines, including the little changed IIe, the colorful II GS, and the portable II C Plus. But increasingly, the Apple II series appears to be headed in a different direction from the company's most powerful and expensive computer, the Macintosh.
**John Sculley**: The best way to, uh, really understand the two products is to look at the software bases that they have. The software base for the Apple II, uh, is largely educational software and enthusiast software. And it continues to have a tremendous, uh, amount of new software as well as many popular titles from the past. Uh, the Macintosh, on the other hand, from the start was a computer that was aimed at higher education, colleges, universities, as well as business.
**Reporter**: Apple Computer has other reasons, beside owner loyalty, to keep the Apple II line moving forward. For one, it's a billion-dollar industry all by itself, and the machine has captured over 60% of the educational market. Moreover, the installed base is enough to keep users and suppliers busy for many more years.
**John Sculley**: There are a lot of businesses that adopted the Apple II a long time ago, that already had made the investment in Apple IIs, don't want to give up that investment. They have their files on, on Apple II computers, and so the Apple II GS has found its way into many small businesses.
**Reporter**: As with any other kind of computer product, the marketplace determines whether a computer will live or die. And John Sculley believes that customers for the Apple II will be around for some time to come.
**John Sculley**: We'll do everything we can to make the Macintosh, uh, as powerful as we can, but it doesn't mean that there aren't people out there who like a stick shift, uh, who want to have the, the real feel of the, of the chips. And that's the experience that you get with an Apple II. You're close to the technology.

**Narrator**: Joining us in the studio now is Laura Coraharo, product manager for the Apple II C Plus, and next to Laura is Bill Cleary, formerly with Apple, formerly with the Apple division of Activision, and now out on your own with Bill Cleary Communications. Gary?
**Gary Kildall**: Laura, I'd say it's quite an improvement over the, uh, Apple that was in the briefcase.
**Laura Coraharo**: Apple I, huh?
**Gary Kildall**: Um, what is, uh, what are you really, what are the new features of the Plus?
**Laura Coraharo**: Okay, um, just to start off with, you, we used to have in the 2C a 5 1/4-in disc drive, and now we have a 3 1/2-in disc drive. So what that offers is five times the storage capacity and three times faster than 5 1/4 accessing your, um, programs. We used to have a power supply that was external on the 2C.
**Gary Kildall**: We all remember the power supply.
**Laura Coraharo**: Yes, brick on the leash. What we've done is internalized the power supply, and it resides right here inside the case. So we've done the obvious changes to the C, to the C Plus, so that they're, um, they're obvious, but they were important features that we needed to do to improve the C.
