documents.content:
Good morning. Thank thank you for allowing us to be here today.

Um, we've made a lot of progress in the last six months and I'd like to give you some updates, tell you about some new stuff and then we got some fun stuff to demo for you if that's okay. So, let's start off. We started thinking different about six months ago. And the first uh sign of that that people could buy, we announced on November 10th, which was a very different chip, a very different store and a very different factory. And I'd like to give you some updates on those things now. It's been it was 51 days before the end of the quarter on November 10th when we announced those. 57 days ago today. And uh so I'd like to go through each one and tell you where we're at. First of all, for those of you who were not at November 10th, we introduced a very different chip and of course that chip was the G the Power PC G3. Uh developed by Motorola and IBM. The thing's a screamer. And it's just wonderful. Matter of fact the Power PC the Power PC is in an incredibly sweet part of its life cycle now for the next few years. And the chips are they're coming out I think are going to are going to toast Pentiums every step of the way. So, when we look when we look at the Power PC G3 and we compare it against uh Intel's fastest uh processor class, the Pentium 2s, uh they're much faster on integer performance and on floating point. As a matter of fact on integer they're 44% faster and on floating point, uh they're 15% faster. This is really good. And when you actually do real world stuff, we took uh I think uh approximately uh 16 Photoshop tasks and uh ran through them one by one in an automated fashion on each of the machines. And so on a on a Pentium 266, Pentium 2 266, this thing took uh over 800 seconds. On a Pentium 2 300, uh it took over 700 seconds. And of course on a G3 266, it took a little over 600 seconds. So, this gives you a feeling for how fast these chips are. And we built these, we built three systems around these chips that could really deliver the performance of the raw chip. The first one was our desktop system. Second was the mini tower and the third was our G3 portable, which is, you know, twice as fast as the fastest Pentium portable you can buy. And so we also priced these things pretty aggressively. Uh, we still want to make a little bit of margin, but we really need to be matching the prices of the PC industry much more closely and we've got that message. And the response has been phenomenal to these products. Uh, the review response has been great. I mean everybody understands that these products are wickedly fast. And um that's the primary message. Now, when we went into the quarter, we were forecasting that we would sell 80,000 of the combined G3 product line. And uh we were wrong. We were wrong. The the reaction was so great that we actually shipped over 130,000 of these machines. Now, what's really also great is that we did it uh in a matter of 51 days in the quarter. And that was due to a lot of work by the engineering teams to make this a rock solid product that was incredibly easy to build and by the operations team that worked very long hours to build these products, did a fantastic job and to the sales teams. And everybody at Apple worked really hard to make this possible including a lot of our partners outside Apple. Now what's what's really neat is if you annualize this, that's a rate of a million computers a year. A million G3s a year in our first 60 days. And that means that although it wasn't a third of our unit shipments in the last quarter because we only shipped them for 51 days, at this rate, they've already climbed to over a third of our unit shipments in terms of an annualized rate. And I think you're going to see that continue to climb this coming quarter. So we we could not be happier. I'm I'm told that there were some problems with new product introductions from Apple in the past. And having been through a lot of new product intros myself, I can tell you that I have not seen any that are any have been any smoother. This went really, really well. Which brings us to a very different store. We distribute our products in a lot of ways. We're a large company. We have national resellers. We have regional resellers like Fries and Micro Center and Comp USA is terrific. Distributors Ingram Micro Wage and we have about 3,000 VARs. We debuted the Apple store on November 10th and we sell direct to education. We have about 7,000 education accounts in North America. And this type of a system is paralleled in Asia and in Europe. Now, we have been doing a very significant tune up to this distribution channel. We went out and shopped all of the channels and we found that in some they were great and in many the buying experience couldn't be worse. It was worse than your worst nightmare. And so we went out to a lot of these folks and said we've got to clean up the buying experience here. And we had some partners say this is awesome and we had some partners say well, we have other things to do. And so we've really focused on our channel and I want to tell you give you two updates here. The first is Comp USA. Comp USA said we want to be partners with you guys. We were with Apple in the beginning and uh we we know you guys are coming back. So, we put together a program with Comp USA uh to put an Apple store within a store in each of their 140, 150 locations in the US. And rather than waiting, rather than waiting a year to plan this out in the typical Apple fashion so everything would be perfect, we said let's just go. Everything's not going to be perfect at day one. Let's build these stores, let's get them done as fast as we can. Everybody won't be trained on day one, but we have a very significant training program going on right now. Let's go. And we built 57 of these stores already and the rest are going to be built by February. And let me give you a tour of one right now. Um we've got uh Quick Time VR over here if we could switch over to that and uh let me uh drive here. So, here we are. Uh here's the parking lot as you can see. So, we can swing around from the parking lot and uh let's just go on in there. Go right on in there. Boom. And here's the inside of the store. There's the Apple store within a store in the corner as you can see. Let me just uh turn around and take a look. There's the rest of the store right here. And there's the Apple store. As you can see, you can see it very easily. So, let's just wander over there. And let's go on in. And there's the Apple store within a store in Comp USA right here. And uh as you can see, there's some software right here. Of course the brand advertising, we can walk on in. And here we are and there's all these kiosks around the store. This one's for design and publishing, there's for education, etc. And again, here's we've just come in here, the store right here. There's the band, the backs of the banners as you can see. Here's some uh accessories here. You know, scanners, printers, all sorts of things like that. And um every single system we make is displayed here. And you can see, as you can see up above, see all these boxes up there, all the Apple boxes and you can see this wall of software right here. So, let's go back and see the systems right now. Here's all the portables that we make. And uh you swing around, you can see uh here's the CPUs. And here is that wall of software. It's terrific actually. Let's go ahead and just walk a little closer. You can see System 8 and a bunch of other software here. Bunch of boxes up there. Again, all of the branding. And that gives you an idea for the store.

So, it looks really great. How's it working? In October, before any of these stores went live, our sales of CPUs, the ratio of Mac CPU sales to the total Comp USA CPU sales was 3%. We were 3% of their CPU sales. We got 57 stores installed. In those 57 stores in the month of December, we were 14% of their CPU sales. And the rest of the stores will be in by the end of February and we're just beginning. And this represents a tremendous opportunity for our software partners, software developers as well to get their software back in these stores. We could not be happier with how this is going. Another thing we couldn't be happier about is the Apple store. The Apple store debuted uh on November 10th. As you know, we have a good, better, best paradigm in the store and you can completely customize the products any way you want them. We have hundreds of configurations for our G3 products as you see here. And of course you can buy over the store and you can have stuff shipped to you. And what's really great about this is not only have we set a new standard out there for sophistication and simplicity for online commerce, but the Apple store has become one of the top selling e-commerce sites on the web in its first 30 days and even beyond that, we are getting millions of hits a day and people are using this as the ultimate online configurator to figure out what they want to buy and then they're buying some are buying it on the store and most are going back out to the dealers and the resellers out there to buy their products, which is great too. So we we could not be happier about this. And build to order. Build to order was designed to give our customers a lot more choice. So they didn't have to buy what they didn't need and so they could configure their systems exactly as they wanted to. It was also designed to dramatically simplify inventory at the dealers and the distributors and at Apple and to provide instant availability of new components and configurations. So we don't have to wait a few months to see these things slowly move through the channel to the end customer. And everybody's told us Apple can never ever execute this. And you know what? It all worked. It worked great. We took thousands of orders, we shipped thousands of systems on time and it's worked like a champ. And I think our operations team has done a phenomenal job on this. Everything we do in the future is moving in this direction. It is a fundamental paradigm shift not just for these products but for our company and we intend to continue to offer more and more choice. Our resellers and our education customers will be buying from us this way as well by the end of this current quarter. Think different. We needed to get back on the air. We promise we will be continuing to develop great software for the Macintosh, built for the Macintosh from the ground up for our Macintosh customers and we're really looking forward to uh doing that and delivering you great products and working with Apple to do that.
Thank you very, very much.

**[Steve Jobs]**: Thank you Ben and to the whole Microsoft team.


---

## Part 4

**[Steve Jobs]**: I've heard a few boos turn to Yahoo's out there.
Um, we're we're starting to see two phrases come back to the Macintosh software market.
First on Macintosh and only on Macintosh.

Now, Macintosh has always been the preferred solution for users.
But we have a lot of customers who have to manage enterprises, be they corporate or academic enterprises.
And they need industrial strength applications in finance, to human resources to be able to do that.
And we have today, we're today announcing that we have partnered with Oracle to do this.
And Oracle is bringing their, I think 40 enterprise applications to the Mac.
Everything they've got.
Larry Ellison, the CEO and chairman of Oracle is on Apple's board of directors as you know.
We have a very close working relationship with Oracle.
And to demo some of these applications right now is John Wookey, VP of financial applications of Oracle.

**[John Wookey]**: Thank you.
Um, good morning.
I'd like to uh thank Steve and and thanks folks at Apple for uh including Oracle applications in this uh enormous event.
Um, Oracle is a pretty well-known company to most people in the audience uh but primarily as a technology company as a database company.
Um, what's less well-known is the fact that Oracle is a very large supplier of what are called enterprise applications products.
Um, these are the financial accounting products and manufacturing products that run a lot of the companies that we all work for.

Now, Oracle applications is actually uh a billion dollar company within Oracle.
We're the second largest provider of enterprise applications in the world.
We've got something like 5,000 customers working in about 70 countries around the world on our applications.
Now, ERP systems like all other components of the software industry have evolved rapidly over the last five or six years and and five or six years ago, what everybody ran were character-based products running on something like a, you know, host terminal configuration.
Um, at that time what evolved was something called client server computing.
Client server computing for the first time starting leveraging the capabilities of the desktop for these ERP systems.
And what they really were trying to leverage was the great graphical user interface and the great access to information that those systems enjoyed.

Um, one of the interesting uh things about client server products is when everyone started building them, they had an idea that they'd build them for many different client platforms.
So they started off building a system that they thought they could deploy to Windows, to Macs, to, you know, workstations and X terminals running motif.
Now, the reality was that didn't happen.
Um, it was much more complex to deliver these applications in a client server model than anyone thought.
And so guess which ones got dropped.
Um, guess which clients we ended up deploying on.
Obviously it was Windows.
It was just a sort of a market size decision.
So everybody in the ERP space basically delivered applications, these client server products that only ran in a Windows environment.
Now, it turned out there were some other problems with these client server applications.
Um, they were a lot more expensive than people thought.
Um, they didn't have quite the performance that people had hoped for.
And in the end it turned out that deploying these very complex enterprise systems into a client server model was extremely difficult, extremely complex and much more expensive than people thought.
Um, well a couple years ago, uh kind of a strange guy came up with a new idea.
Something that Oracle we started calling network computing.
The idea that changing the model of computing really was something that was important.
And from an applications perspective, what was important to understand was we want to keep the capabilities of client server computing that were good, the user interface, the access to information.
We wanted to keep those things.
We wanted to address some of the other problems that actually that had come up in client server computing.
One of the most important ones we wanted to be sure we addressed was support for a heterogeneous client environment.
We want to be able to start delivering applications that work in a Windows environment, in a workstation environment and absolutely in a Mac environment.
And that's what we started doing a couple of years ago.
We started building a series of applications that we called web deployed applications.
Um, David Flexo who's joined me here on stage from our fabulous event support group, um, is going to bring is going to show a few applications here.
On the very right you see basically a number of the applications shown, general ledger AR, fixed assets, bunch of accounting applications as Steve said, about 40 enterprise applications that we can now support in this model.
If you bring up the GL application real quickly.
And this is a journal entry product, okay?
This is the the the product that you use for enter manual journal entries and I promised the people at Apple I would not start demoing accounting products at this conference.
Um, and I'll keep my promise.
Uh, but this is basically a simple Java applet that's running on a Macintosh, right?
This is the same enterprise applications that, you know, a couple years ago if you were running you had to run client server meaning you had to go out and buy a Windows desktop to run these applications, you can now run these on a Macintosh and that's what's important.
And as I said, there's 40 of these applications representing every business function from finance to manufacturing to human resources, payroll to salesforce automation.
Now, given that no one wants to see me enter a manual journal entry, I thought I would demo very quickly something else, something that may be uh more uh easy for everybody to grasp because it's a very common business function that everybody wants to see and it's something called an employee expense system.
Now, this is actually a new category of application that we developed started starting a couple years ago called self-service applications.
What we were trying to do was change the model for some of the business functions that people had.
Rather than having your accounting department enter all your requisitions and your expenses, why not let employees do that directly?
And that's what we've done and start building a series of applications called self-service.
So let's go ahead and enter an expense for Mac World in this case.
Very simple screen.
Okay.
We'll start entering receipts for and as you can see up in the right there's a little icon that has a wizard function that again, these are occasional users.
So you have to be able to guide them.
Also understand that this entire application is customizable for so any enterprise can actually change how it looks to their operation.
It's also a multi-currency system.
It supports all the different tax processing.
It's a multilingual application.
So you can install this on a central server server in Brussels and have uh you know, your employees across Europe actually access it in their own language.
So let's go ahead and enter a few expenses.
We probably all came here on a plane.
Um, go ahead, you click on the calendar which shows you the date, the expense type which is the air looks like we flew in Southwest, okay, new receipt.
Um, go ahead and enter some nice accommodation here in San Francisco.
Well, maybe not in San Francisco, okay.
Uh, new receipt and we probably ate a meal yesterday or today, so click down a little uh meal icon.
There you go.
And uh say we had it McDonald's so it was a happy meal.
Great.
We can look at our receipts now.
You can go through all your receipts and look at them again.
The idea here it's very simple to use.
You can remove receipts if you like, go to the expense summary.
And this is probably what most people look like.
This is what your normal paper form looks like that you submit.
So now when you finish this, you go ahead and you can submit it off to your boss and through workflow rules that Oracle's built that you customize for your own uh enterprise, you can now route it to your supervisor then automatically goes in your accounting function and so on and so on.
And this is all running on a Mac.
And just for a change today we actually decided to run this under Netscape.
Um, thank you David.
So the message here, the message here is very short, very simple.
Um, in the past enterprise applications decisions meant we dictated the desktop.
In the future that's no longer true.
This new deployment model and we have a new version coming out, a new major functional version coming out in the second quarter of this year called release 11.
It will support Windows, it will support workstations and it will absolutely support Macintosh.
Thank you very much.
Have a great Mac.

**[Steve Jobs]**: Thank you John and thank you Oracle.
We're working very closely with Oracle to bring these apps out.
We hope in April and we think they're going to be pretty strong.
And again, you get all the other benefits of working with a Macintosh which basically uh you know.
Next up, you know, more websites are created on Macs than any other computer.
And there's a reason for that because that's where all the incredibly cool tools are and the best versions of those tools.
And Apple wants to stay in this position.
And so we've been working with some of our key developers uh to help them bring some of their very advanced products on the web to market and we are thrilled today to be able to have Macromedia demo their new visual web creation product Dream Weaver.
We think this is a breakthrough product in terms of the creating the visual uh websites and we are working with them uh going to be helping them co-market this product and we think it's really terrific.
So I'd like to welcome Kevin Lynch from Macromedia up on stage now.

**[Kevin Lynch]**: Thanks Steve.
We're really happy to be here today to show Dream Weaver.
Dream Weaver is the most practical, most powerful web authoring tool in the world.
And when we were designing Dream Weaver, we talked to a lot of web authors uh who largely are on the Macintosh as Steve says.
And we learned that one of the biggest issues with current web authoring tools was that they mess up your HTML.
So you go back and edit it, it's very confusing.
So we've worked really hard on that and Dream Weaver doesn't hose your code.
So it leaves your HTML stuff exactly as you wrote it.
So I'll take a look here at uh using Dream Weaver and we've blended visual HTML source editing uh with both visual mode and a text mode.
And you can use them simultaneously.
We have here a page from the White House.
I copied this off the White House site.
This is uh their actual actual page.
We put some stuff in layers here.
And when you're editing a page in Dream Weaver, you can edit things visually, but you can also show an HTML inspector here.
And as you're editing things in a visual mode, you can see it tracks live in the HTML.
Even as you're making edits, you can type in this top level thing here, it's like this and it will update in the HTML as you're typing character by character.
So you can watch the quality of the HTML that's being generated by Dream Weaver and if you'd like to change it, you can just click into this inspector window here and type directly in the HTML yourself.
Now, sometimes you'd like to make a lot of changes to HTML and you'll notice here that we have uh in the HTML inspector a button that's labeled BB edit.
And I can press this button and it will actually launch BB edit with the HTML that I'm currently editing.
So uh we've actually included a full copy of BB edit with Dream Weaver.
So when you purchase Dream Weaver, we've got a partnership with Bare Bones and you get a copy of BB edit.
And you can edit things here in BB edit.
For example, I can make this a larger font size.
And I'll close that here.
So I'm able to go back and forth between uh BB edit source editing and Dream Weaver and I can just pick Dream Weaver here.
I don't have to even save the document.
They know how to talk to each other and it will send the update automatically and create the larger font size inside of Dream Weaver.
So this allows you to to do really great designs with the productivity of a visual tool and still retain the control over the HTML that you need.
So in addition to the HTML editing we've seen here, we also have support for some powerful features including dynamic HTML.
Dynamic HTML is a new new uh technology built into the 4.0 web browsers and you can do things with dynamic HTML such as position items anywhere you like on the page.
So now I can actually drag and drop things anywhere I like and set the position to pixel level accuracy on my web pages.
In addition to dragging them around, you can also because this is a Macromedia product, we've built in a timeline.
And so you can do animations on your web pages now.
And it's as easy as dragging an item from your page onto a timeline, drop it right there.
I've just added it to my timeline.
And if I'd like that flag to fly say over the White House, all I have to do is drag it to the right side and drop it and what will happen is it will create the starting and end points for my animation.
And I can preview that inside of Dream Weaver live like this.
If I'd say like it to curve a little bit, I can drag it over to the top here.
It'll create a a smooth curve for me.
So now I've done some animation in HTML.
Now you might want to look at this inside of a browser.
We've got a keyboard shortcut here that'll preview your web page in any browser that you choose.
We're running IE4 here and it will load the page and automatically do the motion that we've built with dynamic HTML.
So now it's possible to use a visual editing tool to create dynamic HTML without needing to write any of the JavaScript yourself.
This is all pure HTML and JavaScript underneath and it works across browsers.
Dynamic HTML is different in both Netscape and and Internet Explorer, but we've written dynamic HTML in a way that a single file will work in both browsers uh seamlessly.
So in addition to the single page editing that we've been looking at here in Dream Weaver, we also support sitewide editing.
And with Dream Weaver, you can do things for example like repeating headers and footers or navigation bars and we've got a library palette here that lets you build a collection of items that you might want to use across your whole site.
And to add them to your site, it's easy as dragging them onto the bottom of the page and drop them onto your page like this.
And I've just added this to my page.
Now I've got some other documents in my site here.
For example, the briefing room page and you can see at the bottom of this page, we also have that same footer at the bottom of the page.
So later say I wanted to update my footers.
Let's imagine um like Apple were to acquire the White House.
So we might want to um update the footers in that case.
And I can do that very easily just by double clicking on this element in the palette and it opens up the repeating element in its own window and I can select an item here and I can change its image.
I'll make it be the Apple logo.
Now when I close this window, it'll ask me if I'd like to go and update my entire site.
You can see the the palette here has been updated but these pages still need to be updated.
I'll say yes.
Now we can go through thousands of pages in your site and automatically update all of the footers across all of your pages.
So we can see here it's updated the icons.
So with Dream Weaver, it's possible to do visual editing in a high level view like this and HTML source editing with a full control and not no loss of fidelity as well as sitewide changes like these uh headers and footers navigation bar changes.
Dream Weaver is available now at Mac World if you'd like to uh purchase it.
Uh you can come by the Macromedia booth and it's $2.99 through February.
And we're also announcing uh today at Mac World that we're shipping Freehand 8.
Freehand 8 supports um vector-based transparencies that also can print, which is a first uh on the Macintosh and we'd love you to come by and take a look at that as well.
Appreciate your time.
This is uh Dream Weaver.

**[Steve Jobs]**: Thank you Kevin and thanks to all the team at Macromedia.
They've given us an incredibly warm welcome and we are interacting with them quite a lot and really, really enjoying it.
Lastly, today, Riven.
You know, I guess some of the prior management didn't like games.
Uh, because I heard this from so many developers that that that they got no support from Apple on games and the the current management team really likes games.
So we are uh we are dedicated to get some great games back on the Mac.
And uh we are working on that very hard and I think we're starting to see some great results.
And it's my great pleasure today uh to welcome Rand Miller on stage, the creator of Riven.

**[Rand Miller]**: Thank you.
I've got to uh start this off by telling you guys I feel a little out of place here for a couple reasons.
First off, I usually sit home in Spokane, Washington in the snow with my family and I don't speak to like groups of 10 million people.
Um, so if you guys will just consider this like a chat, it'll kind of help me.
The naked thing doesn't work for me.
So just, you know, just have a little chat for me.
Um, the other reason I feel a little out of place is because um um the people who preceded me, um Microsoft and Oracle and Macromedia, Apple, um there's a lot of productivity software in there and in case you don't know what we do, it's stuff to waste time.
So uh um actually, the way I figure it is with all the time you'll save using the other products that have just been introduced.
You get my picture there.
Uh, it's actually pretty appropriate that that uh I'm here aside from the fact that I don't usually do this because um um well, let me start on a little Riven walk through and I'll explain why.
Uh I'm also a Mac fanatic.
We use Macs at the office.
Um, Apple has provided the tools that we need to basically build our worlds.
Um, they've been the enabling technology from the beginning uh that we've used.
Uh with things like the Mac itself, things like Hypercard and uh even CD ROM stuff, Quick Time.
Um, those things have been the tools that enabled us to build worlds.
Now that Apple has announced support for DVD, um, we've got additional tools to build uh our worlds even better.
Yeah, I'm tempted to stand right in the middle and like raise my hands at that part.
I don't get to play it on this big of a screen usually.
Um, now those of you who have played Riven will notice something really intriguing right here.
Uh, no nasty dialogue box comes up uh telling you to uh swap CDs because this is uh the DVD version of Riven.
Um, that's the first obvious advantage we have with this new new tools that Apple's providing us with.
Um, Riven comes on five CDs.
Um, how many of you used to think that CDs had a lot of storage space on them?
Uh,


---

## Part 5

**[Speaker 1]**: Uh now we can fit those five CDs onto one DVD ROM. Um obviously giving us a nice a nice advantage there. Uh Riven is basically graphics and sound and animation movement. Those are things that that Apple has always led the way with. Uh the Mac has always been there doing those things better. DVD at this point serves those things up just a little bit faster.

Excuse my pregnant pauses here. I'd just like to watch. The actually Riven Riven does a better job of talking than I do, I think. The uh let me just say at this point, the pictures, go go into some of the some of the thing ways we use Macs. I know a lot of you've heard that we used SGI workstations for the images and we did. We modeled and rendered the images on SGI workstations. What you may not know is that every artist had next to his SGI workstation a Macintosh uh at Cyan. We we uh it was an integral tool. In fact, the textures that you see here, whether it's the dirt, the trees, the uh beetle climbing up the fence post, the wood, the gates, those were all manipulated on the Mac before going over to the SGIs. Um and they were post-processed on the Mac as well. Uh all the compositing, all the retouching, um all that stuff was done on the Macs. In fact, I think sometimes the artists couldn't wait to get onto the SGI and back off the SGI. That whole Unix thing kind of confused them. Um the sounds that you hear uh were all sampled on the Mac. They were compiled on the Mac. Uh the music that Robin wrote in many of the locations, he had two Macs, one monitor that had either the the uh visual or the or the movies and another one hooked to the MIDI workstation to uh to actually compose on the keyboards. Um and of course, what would we do without QuickTime? Um all the motion, whether it's from that beetle that was walking up the wall to the live action, to the CG uh built things that were composited, layered, and compressed um in QuickTime. Um in fact, the compression that you're actually seeing here on the on some of the movies is QuickTime uh based, but it's for the CD ROM. DVD version will allow us to improve that uh even more.

It's kind of a little 60s flashback there or something. I don't know. Um I've got to say at this point, you know, we started over 10 years ago building our worlds, using Macs, using uh HyperCard, black and white world called The Manhole. And uh it it's uh of all the crazy things, we built that world on five floppy discs that later will be able to be combined onto a CD ROM. Well, it's a little bit of déjà vu now at this point to be combining five Riven CDs onto one DVD. Um at this point, I'm going to stop the exploration.

I decided I better let leave a leave leave some for you guys to explore if you haven't already. Um let me end by saying that it uh we're excited about the tools we get from Apple and from the people who support Apple. Um it's it's what's kept us in business. As long as we get those tools, we'll continue to provide you uh bigger, better, more immersive worlds to make you much less productive. Thank you.

Thank you, Rand. It's a little like the journey we've been on the last six months. So, we have been working a lot with our developers and we're going to do even more uh the coming quarter and every quarter thereafter. Uh we went out and we just made a very short video of some of these developers and I'd just like to show it to you now for those of show you give you a feeling for the other 50 products that are being announced today out there.

Apple and Broderbund together. Gambate! You won't find a product like this on Windows. You want software for the Mac? We've got it. The Mac kicks ass! 100,000 registered developers. We've never left. Number one selling game for the Macintosh. Thank you, Apple. Apple is back and Connectix is right there with them. Go Apple, we're behind you. These things are selling like hotcakes.

First and best on Macintosh. Apple dominates education. Microsoft Office 98 for the Macintosh. Real Player for Macintosh. Cool. Welcome. You've got mail. Statistics for everyone. Ha! Upgrade. Dozens of Adobe products for the Macintosh. Reader Rabbit's with you all the way. The number one educational product of all time. Here's looking to another 10 great years together. Insanely great software for an insanely great computer. Only available on Macintosh. Microsoft has innovated on the Macintosh from the beginning and there's a lot more to come.

So, we've been really hard at work over the last six months. The whole Apple team has just performed wonderfully. And uh I really appreciate the opportunity to give you some updates today. There's a lot of great stuff being introduced at the show. So, thank you very much. I forgot something. I forgot something. There's one last thing I got to tell you. I'm uh I'm really pleased to report something today. We're going to officially report our financial results on January 14th. Uh we had our finance team working over the holidays and I really want to thank them for that to allow me to report this to you today. Every group at Apple has been burning the midnight oil over the last six months. The product groups, hardware and software have been doing great. Our sales and marketing groups all around the world, our manufacturing, our distribution, and we're starting to really see the results. I hope you saw some here today. But when it all comes together, it's really nice. And it's all starting to come together for Apple. Last Maybe after. Thanks. So, it's all come together for us in our fiscal Q1 which just ended. We had revenues of $1.575 billion. And Apple Computer last quarter made a $45 million profit.

So, words words cannot express how proud I am of the team at Apple. I think they've done an incredibly great job and a lot of our partners out there are really supporting us. And I can tell you, I think for sure that that Apple is coming back. Now, we are in right now Apple's fiscal second quarter, which is historically for some reason the last few years been the worst quarter of Apple's fiscal year. I'm not sure why. So, who knows what's going to happen this quarter, but we're going to be burning the midnight oil again and uh we're going to work our best to to deliver a result you'll be proud of us for again. So, thank you very much. We really appreciate your coming. Have a great show.

**[Speaker 2]**: Lady, ladies and gentlemen, please stand by for our following session featuring Kai Kraus and friends. Our session will begin shortly.

documents.content:
Here's to the crazy ones.
The misfits, the rebels, the troublemakers.
The round pegs in the square holes.
The ones who see things differently.
They're not fond of rules and they have no respect for the status quo.
You can quote them, disagree with them, glorify or vilify them.
About the only thing you can't do is ignore them.
Because they change things.
They push the human race forward.
And while some may see them as the crazy ones, we see genius.
Because the people who are crazy enough to think they can change the world are the ones who do.
Thank you.
Thank you very much.
Thank you.
This is good.
I I just got off a red eye to get here.
I didn't think I could be here today and I managed to to make it.
So this is this is good.
We got some great stuff to talk about today.
So let's get into it.
Um an American named Abraham Maslow came up with a theory that he called the human hierarchy of needs.
And this theory was very simple one in concept, somewhat profound in its implications that humans have needs that must be met.
And these needs can be stratified into certain levels and they need the bottom needs to be met first and then they progress to the next level and when those are met, they progress to the next level.
So you start off with the physiological needs, food, clothing and shelter, let's say.
If those are met or once those are met, you then be can start to be concerned more with the safety of your environment.
Eventually with love, with esteem, with self self-actualization.
I don't know if this is true or not, but this is what Abraham believed.
And um I thought this was good was a good model.
So I borrowed it today uh to construct um Steve Jobs's uh version of this, which which I call the Apple hierarchy of skepticism.
And uh and let me explain this to you.
When I when I uh came to Apple a year ago, um all I heard was uh, you know, that Apple is dying, Apple can't survive.
And the it turns out that every time we convince people that we've accomplished something at one level, they they come up with something new.
And and I used to think this was a bad thing.
I oh Jesus, when are they ever going to believe that we're going to going to be uh able to turn this thing around.
But actually now, I think it's great.
Because what it means is they we've now convinced them that we've taken care of last month's question.
And they're on to the next one.
So I thought, well, let's get ahead of the game.
Let's try to figure out what all the questions are going to be and map out where we are.
So that's what that's what the Apple hierarchy of skepticism is and it it borrows from uh from Dr. Maslow.
So, the first level, what we encountered a year ago was survival.
And a lot of people thought Apple was in this some sort of death spiral, which I think there was some truth to.
Uh what did we do?
We did many, many things, but the three things that stood out in people's minds was we brought in a new management team to run the company, a new board of directors that's got some phenomenally experienced uh people on it.
And we did a deal with Microsoft.
The the largest software company in the world wanted to help Apple was a fact that didn't didn't escape very many people.
And it added a lot of credibility to what we were doing.
And the combination of these three things and a lot of other medium-sized things, I think convinced people fairly rapidly that survival, at least in the short term, was not an issue.
And it gave us some time to demonstrate that we could accomplish some other things.
So immediately, once we did these things, then everybody moved up a level.
And uh, you know, I I I can't see when you do that.
Thanks.
So maybe later could we do some more?
That would really help me.
Thanks.
So they moved up a level.
So if it wasn't about survival, it was, well, but there's no stable business in the Mac markets.
That was the next level of the hierarchy.
So we had to start demonstrating that we had a stable business and that one could be made from the Macintosh market because it's a great market.
So what did we do?
Well, the most important thing was profits.
In the end, that's what a lot of people look at.
And so the first full full quarter of the new management team, Apple delivered profits of $47 million, right?
For the quarter ending the end of December.
And in the next fiscal quarter, the second fiscal quarter ending the end of March, Apple delivered a quarter with $55 million worth of profits.
This went this went a long way to convincing a lot of the skeptics.
And we will be announcing the results of our third fiscal quarter, the one that just ended at the end of uh June, a week from today, and I'm very pleased uh to tell you that it will be our third consecutively profitable quarter.
Fred Anderson, our really great CFO would cut my head off if I told you the results.
I'm dying to, but I I can't.
So um I think you'll be pleased.
In addition to that, we're seeing the resources of Apple rise in terms of cash, in terms of people, our retention has gone uh way up.
We're losing hardly any people from the company now and we're hiring incredibly good people into the company.
We also realigned our distribution channels and of course, the most visible part of that was Comp USA.
There have been many other parts of it as well.
Uh but Comp USA is is is a very important part and sort of the symbol for the whole realignment of distribution and it's working great.
And we began an advertising campaign for brand around think different and for some very specific product advertising.
So for for the first time in a long time, people saw Apple on television and in outdoor and in print.
And we also invested in an online store.
And we went from nothing online to I think the gold standard of e-commerce now in terms of ease of use and clarity and it's been we've won every award in the book.
Uh we are one of the largest e-commerce sites now on the internet.
And if you take all of Apple's websites together, this is a pretty good indication about the interest level in the company.
It went from a million hits per day a year ago to 10 million hits per day today.
And that's terrific.
So the the aggregate of all of these things was that the market value of Apple's risen from about $1.8 billion uh a year ago to about $4 billion yesterday.
I don't know what it is today.
Uh and what this means is that people are seeing a stable business, which is good and that a business that is in under control, which is also good.
So what do they do then?
Well, they they don't send us a a card or anything.
They just go on to the next one.
So what's the next one?
Well, if you've survived and you got a stable business, well, what's your product strategy?
You know, your product driven company, you better have a dog on good product strategy.
And we did not talk about that much for many months.
And the reason we didn't talk about it for many months was because we wanted to keep ourselves and the outside world focused on what we were doing at each moment in time, our results, not some vision out in the future.
So we didn't talk about it, but we were working our tails off on it.

documents.content:
Good morning.
Welcome to uh Thank you.
Thank you very much for coming to Webmania.
We got this really great theater and uh we're going to try to tell you about some products we're incredibly excited about and uh see what you think of them.
We've got a whole day planned.
I know some of you can't stay for the whole day, but we're hoping most of you can.
We've got I think uh four more talks uh starting about a half an hour after this one ends.
So I'm going to go into a lot more detail a little bit later if you can stay.
Um we've changed our name, as some of you may have known, from Next Computer to Next Software.
We've been a software company for two years and we finally got around to changing the name.
Um and uh I am Steve Jobs, the chairman and CEO.
What we'd like to do today is uh introduce our Web Objects product family.
Uh this is I think one of the most significant product introductions we've ever had in our 10-year history.
And uh we've been working on this stuff in many ways literally for 10 years because approximately two-thirds of the product content is stuff that we have been perfecting over those years and has fit perfectly in the web.
And about a third of it is extending some of that to specifically address the web.
So these are very, very mature products hitting the ground very early on in the in the web's life cycle.
As we look at the web, everything that's been done to date, sort of from the beginning up till now, we sort of look at as Act One of the web.
And Act One has clearly focused uh on the browser.
Um we we have pages that get served over the web and and we can look at them miraculously from from anywhere on the internet with a web browser.
And what people have been doing with this is is what we call static publishing.
They have been looking at pages and navigating to other pages, but the quantum unit is a page.
And these pages need to have been made up by somebody, a person or several persons, using one of many tools you can do to construct these pages.
But once they're made, they're as they are until some human being changes them.
And so when you're looking at a page, there's probably 300,000 other people who could be looking at that same page.
It's not different for each person.
It doesn't change as the world changes until a human being gets in there and changes it.
And this very simple model has brought us a long way.
Here's an example of a static web page that some of you might have learned about Webmania from.
This is on our was our homepage until uh yesterday.
Uh here's another one.
Uh guy named Rick Smolan who did the a day in the life books is doing a day in the life of cyberspace on the web and he's published a website.
Uh here's Intel's homepage if you want to read about Pentiums.
Uh you can go there and and learn all about that stuff.
Here's another example of you know, educational one, a college.
Um here's one of my favorites.
And uh So you can go to just, you know, now hundreds of thousands of of of pages, probably millions by now and and uh see them just as everyone else can see them.
And this is very, very powerful and it's all focused on the browser.
Now, when you're consuming this information on the browser, um what you find is you want more.
And especially if you have a PC and you use the PC for other things, you find that the PC can do things that the web can't.
And that has to do with the user interface.
So let's say you're using Windows and um you like animation in Windows.
Well, you can't do that on the web today as an example.
Now, when you look at user interfaces, they all have capabilities.
They all have capabilities with limitations.
In the case of Windows, let's say that this square represents its user interface capabilities.
If that was the case, then proportionally, this is what a web browser can do user interface wise.
A small fraction of what you can do on Windows today.
And naturally, people want to enhance the user interface of the web browser so it can be more like their PC.
And that's been what's happening.
Most of what you read about in the news today concerning the web has to do with enhancing the user interface of the browser.
So as an example, we have plugins.
The Netscape browser has plugins and the most popular one is probably the the Macromedia Shockwave where you can download it and see some animation in your browser.
Play your director files in your browser just like you of course can on the PC.
Another big one we've heard about is Java.
Again, Java is an interpreted language that runs on the browser uh that will, you know, is is pretty close to being real out there and it will let you do some things like animations and run little applets to do things on the browser, primarily to enhance its user interface to try to make the surface area of that red square as close as possible to the surface area of the blue square.
And that's where most of the action has been in Act One of the web.
It has been to enhance the user interface.
Now, all that's well and good, but we're starting to move into Act Two of the web.
Because what people are finding is is that being limited to these static pages that people build by hand, they can't do some incredibly important stuff that they want to do on the web, especially if they're businesses.
And people want to now focus on the server, which is becoming the limit of what can be done and focus on how to provide what we call dynamic services instead of just static publishing on the web.
So again, the focus of Act Two is going to be on the server.
And what are what are the the essential issues on the server?
Let's take a look.
Let's go back to static publishing and kind of recreate that symbolically.
When you're going to do static publishing, you can think of it as taking a book or a brochure, in this case a brochure about Dodge cars and like tearing out or cutting out the pages very carefully and putting them on an HTTP server.
Now you probably recreate them another way, but metaphorically this is what you do and you could you could look at them all.
And this works great for some things, but what happens if the page that the customer wants doesn't exist?
What do you do then?
Now, how could that be?
How could it not exist?
Well, let me give you a few examples.
You can go to the Federal Express.
Matter of fact, how many people have used the Federal Express package tracking website?
Few.
Okay, let me explain it to those of you haven't seen it.
You go to the Federal Express's website, the www.fedex.com and you can get into package tracking.
And if you've just sent a package or if somebody's just sent one to you, you can type in the air the package tracking number and this application will go to, I believe it's four databases, find out where in the heck your package is and then it will need to build a web page to send back to you so you can see it.
How does it do that?
They they thought about hiring 10,000 gnomes to do this probably, but what they did instead was they have the computer build the web page dynamically.
It didn't exist one second and the next second it exists because the computer built it from all this data, sends it back to you and you can see exactly where your package is.
It's very cool.
We have over 10,000 people a day tracking their packages this way now.
Another example of course is is one of the many um web navigation products.
You want to type in, you know, web objects and find all the pages that on the web that have web objects.
You can use web crawler as an example.
It's a very good one.
Well, obviously your request needs to be answered in a custom way.
They're not going to have a web page with every answer for every question.
They'd have millions of web pages they'd have to build and they'd have to update them each day.
That's crazy.
So what they do is they take your request, they search their index database and then they build your response on the fly and send it back out to you.
Now, it turns out to do this, these are very, very trivial examples of dynamic services and yet they're very hard to build on the web today.
They take months and months and months to build.
So how can we make this a lot easier?
Well, this is precisely what Web Objects does.
Web Objects takes responses from customers, gets the information and dynamically builds web pages on the fly, hands them back to the HTTP server so that they can be served out to the customer making the request.
Where does it get the information to build those web pages?
It gets it from a library or a database not of pages, but of components to pages.
Pictures of cars, descriptions of cars, prices coming out of a flat file or SQL or some kind of a database.
It it gets the information from components and data sources to build these pages on the fly.
And what I'd like to do and oh and and in addition to that, there's a scripting language involved so that you can define how you want inputs from the customer treated.
You can define how all these components go together to build that page.
Let me give you a demonstration now of something we've built using this exact technology, which we call a virtual showroom.
We happen to use the Dodge car showroom as an example.
So let me show you what a dynamic website looks like.
Okay.
So I'm by the way using Windows 95 here and uh this is a Netscape browser running on Windows 95.
And what I've done is I've gone to the Dodge virtual showroom example site here that we have up on a server somewhere.
And what this allows me to do is this shows me all the cars that Dodge makes.
And so I'm going to select all of them for now.
And here's all the price points from $8,000 to $90,000.
And I'm going to select them all.
And here's all the models, two-door, four-door, van and truck.
I'm going to select them all.
And I'm going to sort by uh model type and I'm just going to say display cars.
Now, this information is going to be sent back to the HTTP server, which is going to pass it off to Web Objects, which is going to parse it all and it's going to look up in its database all this information and then sort it by model type, build a dynamic web page and send it back.
And here we go.
Here's the Avengers first because they begin with an A, the Caravans because they begin with a C.
And we can get down here.
There's a lot of Caravans.
Then there's Neons and then there's Ram trucks, right?
And then here's Vipers.
Okay, well let's go back and let's say I want to take all this information again and sort it by price and display the cars.
Well, obviously that's a completely different web page using the same data.
And so Web Objects is building that web page now and sending it back to me.
So now the Neons are at the at the front because they're the cheapest, you know, and here's uh here's a cheap Ram truck and the cheapest Avenger and you know, they're all kind of all mixed up just sorted by prices and probably if we go down here to the end, you know, we'll see that Viper.
There it is.
Okay?
Now, I'm going to go back up to the beginning.
Uh okay, and I'm going to pick Oh, come on.
There we go.
I'm going to pick that Neon.
Uh and uh let's take a look and see what we can learn about this Neon.
So we click on it and again, Web Objects builds this page on the fly.
And I can say, well, that's interesting.
I'd like to see what this car looks like in uh in, you know, in white.
So I'll click on the white paint chip.
Again, Web Objects is just going to go grab the white picture, rebuild the white page and send it out to me.
Or let's take a look at lime green.
Again, let's rebuild the page and send it back to me.
Now, you notice that we have op we have the base price of $9,500 here and we have options.
So I haven't picked any.
So let's go pick an option.
And again, these prices were gotten right out of out of the the uh the the database that's used to create this.
And let's pick package B. Uh and now what it's done is it's come back and built a page with a check mark on package B.
It's added it to the option price.
Somebody's done a calculation in the scripting language to add it to the option price and total it up.
Uh it's grayed out package 25B on the bottom because that's a subset I guess of package B.
Let me pick package package 25A too here.
And um so it'll build that web page and add it again with the total added.
And so now I've got a $14,000 car.

I can put a down payment maybe of uh you know, $5,000 here.
Maybe I want to lease it over 60 months and I can say calculate it and it'll calculate my my lease payments.
So again, every one of these pages is being built on the fly because it it couldn't possibly be built beforehand.
There's too many permutations, too much data and too much input from the user.
