Uh the definition is not final and we are working closely with Netscape on that definition and we will have JavaScript as our scripting language as soon as it's ready, which we hope is going to be sometime uh this fall or early winter.
Compiled Java also doesn't exist.
The Java that we've all heard about is interpreted Java that runs on the cl on the browser.
But we for the server need compiled Java for the speed because if we're serving all these browsers, we have to run a lot faster than any single browser.
So we need compiled Java and again, we're working very closely with Sun on that and we will have that later on this year as well.
And so what we have done is today we have a very elegant script, a very simple scripting language called Web Script and as soon as we can get JavaScript, we are going to move to that, which we believe will be certainly by Q4 of '96.
And today when you write objects to move in to Web Objects Pro, the compiled language is C and we will move to compiled Java as fast as that is ready, working with Sun, which we also believe will be by Q4 of this year.
You can download beta versions of Web Objects today.
You can download the code and the virtual showroom demo also today.
And we want people to take that if you will as the example program for Web Objects and build your own virtual showroom out of it or cut and paste out of it to build whatever dynamic website you want.
And production versions are available the end of March.
Here's the website.
Uh you can simply choose your platform, Windows NT, Solaris or Next Step and be guided through a very simple download script.
Uh unfortunately, the traffic or I guess fortunately, the traffic at our website yesterday went through the roof.
Uh we maxed out our T1s.
There's been over a thousand downloads already and uh we are now moving the software out to alternate websites so that hopefully the traffic will be will be uh acceptable.
And so if you have a little trouble downloading it, try a few more times.
It'll it might take you a few minutes to get through, but but you will get through.
And we're doing everything we can to get a T3 as fast as possible.
Now, we've decided to take a new approach to pricing at Next.
Um We we have decided to give away uh Web Objects.
And uh this was a long and hard decision uh but we think it is the right one because we really believe that every website should have this software.
It is that good, it is that important.
And so uh when the production versions of Web Objects are ready, you'll be able to download them for free as well as the beta versions uh at the end of this month or end of this quarter right off our website.
Now, how are we going to make money on this?
Uh we we have thought of a way.
And here's the way.
Um the version of Web Objects that is free is the base version.
It's an incredibly powerful version.
We've often debated whether we're giving way too much away, but we've decided to go for it.
But we have the other two versions and the other the the base version has full dynamic services and the scripting language in it.
Web Objects Pro adds the ability to add custom objects.


---

## Part 2

**[Steve Jobs]**: with compiled code and we're going to charge $2,999 for that.
That also includes full support and also it includes full distributed objects.
So if you want to distribute your computational logics over several machines, you can do that with Web Objects Pro.
And the final high-end version for the enterprises, which includes our very sophisticated database technology, enterprise database technology is about $25,000 and up.
So we hope that Web Objects is going to really turn everyone on to dynamic websites and then a lot of people will buy Web Objects Pro and some in the enterprise will buy Web Objects Enterprise.

And again, what we believe is is that every website is going to go dynamic and every website needs Web Objects.
And so what we want to do by providing Web Objects for free is encourage everybody after they download their server from Netscape to go right to the next website and download Web Objects to layer on top of it and turbo charge that website free.
To help people get started, uh we have formed a consulting group called Web Architects and we do advanced website consulting.
We have over 40 consultants on board now.
We are one-stop shopping for advanced websites.
We will do consulting on technology all the way up to completely building websites for customers.
Uh creatively, artistically as well as the technology.
We are fluent in major enterprise issues, getting data off of main frames, etc.
We really understand this stuff because that's what we've been doing for the last many years.
We have six web engagements today with Fortune 50 companies.
So this is this group is up and running and we are doing some pretty sophisticated stuff and we are ready to help you.
If you have any needs, please get a hold of us.
We have, you know, people we can get available very quickly.

And now I'd like to focus on customers.
Uh our goal is to build a series of highly visible wins, both external websites and internal custom applications using web technology in large accounts to build our reference accounts base.
And we're pleased to announce that we already have several customers.
A lot of them won't let us talk about them at this stage uh for competitive advantage reasons, but four of them have graciously allowed us to uh discuss a little of what we're doing with them today.
Uh the first one is Mary Lynch.
Uh Mary Lynch is building major internal custom applications uh using Web Objects today.
And we have a whole team working with them and I think uh some of those applications may get rolled out to consumers uh during the course of 1996.
Another one that we can't say too much about is Motorola.
They are building major internal custom web applications again using Web Objects.

Next one is Dreamworks.
Dreamworks uh is building uh again some very sophisticated internal custom applications and they've chosen to build them on the web for the reasons that we have discussed, the multi-platform issues, etc.
And we're very pleased to have uh Dylan Kohler, who is in the Animation Technology division of Dreamworks up here with us today and what I'd like to do now is invite Dylan to come out and spend a few minutes telling us what they're doing with Web Objects.
Thank you, Dylan.

**[Dylan Kohler]**: I'm not as good at speaking on the fly as Steve is, so I'm actually have to consult my notes.
Um our task in technology at Dreamworks is to set up, starting with feature animation.
What we see is the digital studio for the 21st century.
To us, this means that we here adhere to the strategy that we are in the business of making movies, games and music and that we aren't in the business primarily of writing software.
To fit that strategy, we use whatever tools already exist and we can buy off the shelf.
Where they don't exist, we're working with our partners, Silicon Studio, IBM and Cambridge Animation Systems to build them.
The one exception we have made to this strategy has been for our production management system.
This is the one subsystem we are developing in-house because we felt we alone were best qualified to translate our production experience into code.
We still wanted to adhere as much as possible to the tenant that we write as little custom code as possible.
To make this task even harder, our production schedule for the first film Prince of Egypt was moved up, so we needed to get the system up and going even sooner than before.
We had proceeded a ways down the road of designing a traditional client server system and we were kind of slogging through the evaluation of what cross-platform development tools are out there to help us with that.
That's when we came across Web Web Objects and we were delighted because uh we feel it fits our strategy very well indeed.
By deciding to use the Web Objects framework as our delivery mechanism, we benefit from having the client side of our production management system already written for us.
It's Netscape, Mosaic and so on.
That part just fell off of our schedule.
It was a relief.
What's left is the custom server side of things, the kind of production management guts and that's what we had intended on writing ourselves anyway.
And now we're in a position to be able to draw upon EOF to tap into our database in a very clean and object-oriented manner.
So Web Objects is enabling us to build a production management system elegantly and efficiently.
We know the interface works uh given that the numbers that there are out on the web already uh using it.
Um and our our users are able to benefit from changes to the system as soon as they're put up on the server.
We like that.
With our new plan drawing on Web Objects, we'll be up and running much sooner than we than before and with quite frankly a design that we're much more comfortable with that that's going to orient us much better for the future.
Thanks.

**[Steve Jobs]**: Thank you, Dylan.
Uh another customer that is a a long time customer of Next that has uh spawned a whole new area of relationship with us is Fannie May.
Uh we've been working with Fannie May for years.
Uh these guys are terrific.
As you know, uh Fannie May, if you will, coagulates home loans from the lending institutions, packages them up and sells them uh to the financial markets and has enabled millions of people to own homes that would not normally be able to.
In the process, they've become one of the most profitable corporations in the world.
And we're very pleased uh that Marty uh Colburn, the vice president of Technology integration could uh uh come out and be with us today from Washington DC and tell us uh for a few minutes what they are also doing with Web Objects.

Marty, thank you.
**[Marty Colburn]**: Fannie May is a congressionally chartered shareholder owned corporation and our mission is very simple is to provide low and moderate income Americans with housing.
And we've been successful at that and along the way have made a few dollars.
We're we're extremely excited about this technology and about Next technology.
As Steve mentioned, we've been a long time partner of Next.
We began developing technology using their software and services in 1992.
And just last year we committed to a strategic relationship with Web Objects being just one aspect of that.
Uh where we see the true benefit with the technology is looking at how we would uh develop a new paradigm at Fannie May where we could put applications out into lender shops as well as internally and we expect to be able to do that with the Web Objects framework.
Additionally, this shows a commitment to us from Next to continually change the development paradigm.
The thing that initially excited us about Next technology was the robust nature of the technology and the ability to develop applications very quickly.
This is just an evolution along that paradigm.
So again, we feel like they're affecting the development environment in a positive way.
It aligns very well with Fannie May's commitment to developing programs that continue to take cost out of home ownership and in 1996 you'll see several applications coming out from Fannie May that take advantage of web technology.
Thank you.

**[Steve Jobs]**: Thanks, Marty.
Thank you very much uh Marty and Dylan.
We've got other customers as well for this even though we're not yet shipping the products uh that we've been working with using the beta software and I think you're going to hear about a lot of them uh over the coming next few months.
What I'd like to do now is demonstrate Web Objects Enterprise for you uh and uh show you a real world application using um legacy enterprise data.
So what we're going to do again is use Web Objects Enterprise all the way up uh at the enterprise level into major uh corporate data in this case on a main frame in England.
And the company is OAG, the online airline guide.
I'm sure a lot of you've seen the book uh that looking up airline flights.
They have it on a CD ROM as well.
Uh they actually again get all of the airline flight information from all the airlines and then actually send it back out to the systems like Saber and the other airline reservation systems.
So they're kind of at the hub of this airline reservation uh wheel.
And they actually offer the ability to look up flights and book flights now uh on 3270 terminals.
Um and what they want to do is move that in you know, into this century from a UI point of view and move it on the web so that everybody has access to this and they have chosen Web Objects to do that.
So what I'd like to do now is is show you that demo.

So here we are.
Um let me go ahead and uh You can get the lights down on me so that's as visible as possible, please.
So let's take a look at this.
Um the first thing is it's going to ask me where I want to fly from and to.
So I'm going to say well we're near San Francisco, so it's it's going to pick all the airports going to the main frame database and picking all the airports.
I'll pick San Francisco International.
And um where I want to go, I'm going to say Chicago.
And I'll pick O'Hare and you see that it's rebuilt web pages now putting these things at the top, right?
So that's my my source and my destination.
Now what Web Objects has done is it's built a page and downloaded a Java applet onto that page and you're now seeing Java running on my Windows 95 with Netscape that was downloaded from Web Objects on a server somewhere over the net because of course Web Objects can download Java applets today on the browser.
Okay, um so let's go ahead and uh continue ordering my tickets here.
I probably have to pick now the day I want to fly and um so let's book it a little further ahead here so I can cancel this later on.
Uh February 29th, let's say.
And um I'm going to go ahead and maybe maybe take an evening flight here and again it's rebuilding the page with evening or maybe I'll go back to a morning flight.
Okay, and uh let's go ahead for flights now.
And it's going to go query the database and here's all the flights that fly from San Francisco to Chicago on Thursday February 29th uh in the morning.
And uh I'm going to pick maybe this one here leaving at 8:30.
I pick that one and uh hopefully it will come back and show me all the fairs.
Um I'm going to pick the cheapest one uh although I don't want to pick the one I can't cancel, so I'll pick this one here.
Um and so now it's confirming that flight.
Uh it's got my information here and I will say purchase the ticket.
So now it's it's going to to London to this main frame, so it might take a few minutes here, a few seconds.
And there we go.
There is my confirmation number.
I've actually booked this ticket now.
Every screen you saw was built on the fly based on my requesting more and more information or specifying more and more information.
Now, uh what I'd like to do now is we've got a phone hook up here.
Um could we get United Airlines on the phone, please?

Turn up the volume.
You can tell that this is real, can't you?
**[United Premier Desk]**: United Premier Desk, Paula Greenhow may help you?
**[Steve Jobs]**: Hi, I would like to check a reservation, please.
I have a confirmation number.
**[United Premier Desk]**: Okay.
**[Steve Jobs]**: Uh confirmation number is 6R1734.
**[United Premier Desk]**: For Job?
**[Steve Jobs]**: Yeah.
Jobs, good job.
Mr. Jobs, uh-huh.
**[United Premier Desk]**: Okay.
**[Steve Jobs]**: And what flight is that and what what day and where is it going?
**[United Premier Desk]**: Okay, and what's your premier number?
It's not on here.
**[Steve Jobs]**: I I don't have one.
**[United Premier Desk]**: That's flight 144 out of San Francisco at 8:35 in the morning.
**[Steve Jobs]**: And where's it going?
**[United Premier Desk]**: To Chicago at 2:43.
**[Steve Jobs]**: Thank you very much.
**[United Premier Desk]**: Thank you.

**[Steve Jobs]**: So again, I I hope that gives you a feel for the power of this.
Um and I hope you agree that that the website you just saw is orders of magnitude more dynamic than anything that exists on the web today.
Every single one of those pages could not have been pre-created because it was based on information I was putting in or information in the database.
If one of those flights was canceled, it would have been yanked and the page would have had to have changed.
There was no with with 10,000 gnomes, you couldn't build every permutation of pages that you would need.
They've got to be built on the fly.
And again, this app was complete this app's it's taken us about two weeks to write this.
Most of it frankly was interfacing with the main frame.
The actual app took only a few days to write with Web Objects.
So what I'd like to do now is is is ask you if you would to remember five things uh from today's presentation.
Uh the first one is that the second act of the web, the web act two is going to focus on the server because we have to now pay attention to the server to move from simple static publishing to really dynamic services like you just saw, which is what customers really want and which is what businesses really want so that they can provide information and services and products over the web.
So act two of the web is going to focus on the server.
Web second message is Web Objects works with all web browsers and all HTTP servers, including of course Netscape browsers and Netscape servers and we work very closely with Netscape to make sure that's all the case and we're all standards based.
So it works with all web browsers and all web servers.
Third, Java.
We are 100% behind JavaScript and compiled Java on the servers.
We are helping to enable those products to become real and we will have them as soon as anyone does on the server side.
And we believe that bringing those products to the server is going to be a major step forward.
Next, we are providing Web Objects for free.
Uh we believe this uh this is going to expose everyone to Web Objects and so there's no reason for not taking a look at this revolutionary new technology.
And lastly, we hope that it becomes a standard out in the marketplace and that everyone decides that they want to simply turbo charge their web server by coming to Next's website and downloading Web Objects for free on top of their web server and having the ability to now to create truly dynamic websites very, very easily.
And we hope that you're going to see our Web Objects powered by Web Objects logo popping up in a lot of websites in the next few months as people build websites even with the beta software, which is in quite good shape that you can download today and of course with the production software that you'll be able to download at the end of this quarter.
Now there are three additional presentations that will follow this one um by approximately uh I think 45 minutes or so and I'd encourage you to stay around to hear them.
Avi Tevanian, our vice president of engineering is going to take us through more technical details of Web Objects.
Jean-Marie Hulot uh is going to take us through in depth how simple Web Objects is to use and Chris Shoven is going to take us through really how to get started using Web Objects.
So I'd I'd encourage you uh even though it's uh raining today to to stay around for those other presentations.
Thank you very much for coming this morning.
Thanks.

documents.title: Steve Jobs NeXT Computer Expo Keynote May 25 1993 NeXTSTEP 3 1 Intel Intro Amazing Demos.
documents.speaker: Steve Jobs
documents.content:
Good morning, I'm Steve Jobs.
Thanks for coming.
The first thing I wanted to talk about today was our transition.
We've got six things we want to cover.
Six challenges that we've had.
Completing the transition, communicating our strategy, shipping Nextstep for Intel today on May 25th, signing up key PC partners, completing the enterprise solution, and getting developers to try Nextstep.
Like to spend a few minutes on each of these.
Start with the transition.
Now, we set ourselves a 100-day transition to move from a hardware systems company to a software company.
We've succeeded in transitioning to a software company.
And this 100 days, our factory's been closed, the inventory's been sold.
We've seen the last of black hardware.
I know.
We've really wanted to take care of our customers, though.
And in addition to coming out with future releases on black hardware, we've sold our service business to Bell Atlantic so that service is going to be seamlessly carried forward.
Our hardware designs are being sold to Canon.
We've got a new senior team that's I think in a in fit and fighting shape.
In addition to that, we've added some new members to our board of directors, two really fine people.
Daniel Case, who's the president and co-CEO of Hambrecht & Quist.
Hambrecht & Quist is one of the most respected investment banks in high technology.
They've had a lot to do with Adobe and Sybase.
And Larry Ellison, the president and CEO of Oracle Corporation, the third largest software company in the world behind Microsoft and Computer Associates.
We think these folks can really help us as we form our strategies and execute them to be successful as a software company.
And the one one thing I'd like to leave the transition with is thanks.
You guys have really hung in there with us when the going was tough, our third-party developers, our employees, our customers.
And we really, really have noticed it and appreciated it.
Thank you very, very much.
The transition as of today, the transition as of today is officially over.
It's behind us and we are now as of today a software company.
So communicating our strategy, what is our strategy to win?
Our strategy in a word is based on objects.
We intend we believe that there is a revolution happening of large proportions around object-oriented technology.
And if we execute well, we can ride this revolution to some serious success.
In the 1980s, we focused our computing technology on improving individual productivity.
But in the 1990s, our customers are telling us unanimously that what they have to focus on is improving organizational productivity, operational productivity, automating the heart of the business.
Now, we could help individual productivity with shrink-wrap software, spreadsheets, word processors, the like.
But we can't do that with operational productivity.
Why not?
Because you can't go buy an application to automate your hospital at Egghead.
You can't go buy an application to do derivative commodity trading at the software store.
You've got to write these things custom.
That's the only way to get them.
And the solutions we've had in the '80s just don't work.
Let's take a look at some conventional wisdom.
People absolutely want to get off their mainframes, right?
Client-server computing is really hot.
People want to get onto client-server computing.
But there are some real dynamics changing in the marketplace.
The first one is the demand for these custom apps is going through the roof and people cannot keep up with them.
In addition to that, the the users are demanding faster and faster time to market.
They need these applications in weeks and months, not years because they're at the core of their competitive engines.
We think Nextstep is a breakthrough answer to this challenge.
It is widely now agreed, even by our competitors, that you can build apps in Nextstep five to 10 times faster than any other environment known to people.
And when you build these apps, they are usable by mere mortals.
These are not something that you need rocket scientists to use.
They have a fit and finish that users have come to expect by their use of shrink-wrap software.
The maintenance costs are dramatically reduced because of object-oriented technology, which is a very, very important part for IS departments.
And there's an ability to unify the desktop.
The goal used to be, as you know, to get a computer on every desk.
Now the goal is to get only one computer on every desk and to have that one computer execute the custom applications, the shrink-wrap productivity applications, and the legacy applications.
And Nextstep does all of that.
Now, as I said earlier, this is catching a wave.
Uh, Byte thinks pretty highly of Nextstep.
We're starting to get some recognition for the technology.
There's going to be a lot of fud about objects over the next year because they're going to get really hot.
Everybody's going to have objects, object-oriented vacuum cleaners.
But be assured, Microsoft does not have objects.
This is a quote from Business Week.
And we we agree with that quote.
Now, where does this all fit in?
The strategy of this object-oriented revolution.
Where does it all fit into the rest of the industry?
Well, as you know, we have client-server computing.
So let's take a look at the operating systems that come to bear to make this a reality.
They're different.
On the server side, we have Netware, we have Unix, and we have a contender in NT.
They'd very much like to become a server operating system.
On the client side, we have five, right?
We have Nextstep, we have OS2, Solaris, Unixware, and of course, Windows NT.
Now, let's take a look at some of these folks.
OS2's premise, their entire premise is based on better windows than Windows.
And the problem is that most folks don't believe that premise is sustainable when their source code license runs out next year and most importantly when Microsoft comes on much stronger with NT Windows.
And so most people are very concerned that OS2's differentiation can continue.
The next thing to note is that three of the five client operating systems are based on Unix.
Nextstep is one of them.
Let's take a look at the other Unix contenders, Solaris and Unixware.
There's another fundamental problem here and it's very simple.
Windows NT is going to be as good as X Motif Unix.
Maybe not this year, but certainly next year.
And in this marketplace, if you're 25 or 50% better or even twice as good, that's not good enough.
The Microsoft monopoly will squash you.
You've got to be five to 10 times better and most people don't see enough differentiation here for that to work.
And so we believe that those folks don't have the differentiation to sustain themselves against Windows NT and will therefore fade.
We don't consider this good news.
We don't.
But we do believe that Nextstep is one of the few hopes to create an alternative standard.
And this is what we're up against.
Microsoft owns the standalone shrink-wrap operating system business.
They're in high volume with it.
They have almost 100% market share.
But they don't have objects and they don't know how to deal with an enterprise-wide solution.
We've got that stuff today.
We've got to get it into high volume before Microsoft gets the technology.
And we're running as hard as we can to do that to create this alternative so that we all have a choice.
And I think we've got a real shot at it because it's going to take them a long time to get there.
And this this is why we're all here.
Okay.
That's our strategy.
It hasn't changed a lot since we've become a software company.
But what's changed is is that we have liberated Nextstep from the black box.
We have eliminated the need to run it on proprietary hardware and we have reduced its effective price from a computer system costing $10,000 list to a software package costing $795.
We got to ship it on May 25th.
We made it.
The products are shipping today.
You can buy them on the show floor.
They're in distribution.
They're at some of our OEM partners.
They're shipping today.
They're very real.
$795 for the user system, $1995 for the developer system.
Included in these boxes is a third-party product CD-ROM which has 46 demo applications all running on Nextstep for Intel.
In addition, we are supporting the standard six languages that we have for the last 18 months, English, French, German, Spanish, Swedish, and Italian, all off the one CD-ROM drive.
And we have documentation in English, French, or German.
Let's take a look at some of the new features about Nextstep 3.1.
The most important one, of course, is it runs on Intel.
And here's the system that you need to run it.
A 486 of at least 25 MHz.
You do need an FPU.
8 megabytes for black and white minimum, 16 megabytes color.
At least 120 megabyte disk.
We run in 8-bit, 2-bit, or 8-bit grayscale on VGA and the 8-bit grayscale is gorgeous.
In color, we run with local bus, VL bus, ISA, and PCI.
We work with ATI chipsets, S3 chipsets, Winjins, Qvisions, and a whole bunch of other stuff that's being done now.
So this stuff works with almost every new color system that's been shipped.
And it screams on the Pentium right out of the box.
You can take this stuff out of the box, load it on a 486 or a Pentium and it screams on a 486 and it screams squared on a Pentium.
The second thing is we've added support for portables and notebooks.
There's half a dozen portables on the show floor you can see today and they're remarkable.
Driver kit.
Driver kit is a real breakthrough for us, especially as we enter the PC market with its myriad number of required drivers.
We want to be able to write drivers really fast and we want to be able to link them in dynamically.
So we have come up with a whole new way of writing drivers.
What we've done is we've said our object-oriented technology at the top of our system lets us write applications five to 10 times faster.
What if we use that same technology to write drivers with?
And so we've put object-oriented technology at the bottom of our system and we've created a kit for writing drivers that allows you to write drivers literally five to 10 times faster, dynamically link them in, and work with Nextstep for Intel.
And we brought in a really great partner of ours, Pencom, and taught them how to write these driver kit drivers a few months ago.
And this is a quote by Frank King, their president.
They were blown away.
These were extremely seasoned Unix driver writers.
And they looked at writing drivers a whole new way, subclassing a disk driver, changing 10% of it and having a new driver.
And it all works and it's all in Nextstep 3.1.
Fat binaries.
Our marketing department calls these multiple architecture binaries.
Um, fat binaries are also pretty remarkable.
First of all, our developers have been able to simply recompile their applications and run them on Nextstep for Intel usually with zero source code changes.
We went to Word Perfect as an example and said, please recompile for Intel.
And they said, that's great.
It'll take us about four months.
We said, four months?
It should take you about a day.
And they said, no, no.
Everybody tells us that, but it takes four months.
Three hours later, they were running their product on Nextstep for Intel with zero source code changes.
McCaw Cellular recompiled all their custom apps in an afternoon, no source code changes.
Will Tell, same thing.
Customer after customer, developer after developer.
Now, let's look at the developers.
They didn't want to have to put out a separate box, one to service the installed base of Motorola hardware and a new one for Intel.
Let's look at system administrators.
They didn't want to have two folders on the file server, one with the versions for the Motorola products, one with the versions for the Intel products, maybe another with the versions of the apps for a new architecture.
So what we did was we looked at Nextstep and realized that Nextstep factors out most of the code into a machine-independent format anyway.
And in a typical app has only about 25% of the bits on its disk or in its file are machine-dependent.
So we created a way that from any Nextstep platform, you can cross-compile that 20% for any other platform and stack as many of them as you want in one file.
Therefore, by increasing the size of the app typically only about 25%, you can have a version of the app on a floppy in one SKU that you stick it in either a Motorola or an Intel Nextstep computer.
It figures it out, launches and goes and does the right thing.
You can have one icon on a server, you double-click it from any Nextstep workstation, it figures out what the architecture is, loads the right binary and goes.
And we can add future binaries.
So in one SKU, one box, a software developer can by simply pushing a few buttons on the compiler, generate versions of Nextstep applications for an endless variety of architectures.
The next one is Photo CD.
We have worked with Kodak.
Uh, a lot of our developers came to us and said this Photo CD stuff is revolutionary, but we all don't want to go license it ourselves.
Could you please do it and put it in the system?
We did just that and the results are stunning.
Okay.
Fast Windows with Insignia Soft PC.
Microsoft needs emulation technology.
So they go to Insignia, the best guys on the block.
And Insignia says, great, we'll help you out, but we want source code to the Windows so that we can make great emulation products for other people.
Microsoft cuts the deal.
We've been working with Insignia for over a year now.
We've made a lot of enhancements to our kernel so that we actually can run Windows really fast in Nextstep Windows.
And the product is going to be offered by Insignia for $249, I think.
It's going to ship right on the CD-ROM this fall and you're going to be able to run it for 60 days for free and then you get to call them up and pay them if you want to keep running it.
But we finally figured out how to run Windows really fast, much faster than any prior emulation technology and you'll be able to see this very shortly.

There's going to be a test on that last stuff after this keynote.
Can we Okay, great.
Um I'm really uh privileged to be here this morning and my colleagues and I feel uh really special to be able to talk to you today um about some really exciting stuff.
I want to talk about three things today.
Uh the first one is the Centenary.
Second one is scale and complexity.
And the third is a place in history.
Let's start with the first one.
As I was doing some research uh for today, I discovered a really startling fact that is all the more relevant since computer graphics is making major contributions to the motion picture industry and seems quite appropriate since we are in Los Angeles, which is the worldwide center for motion pictures.
And that fact was that this year is the hundredth anniversary, the centenary year of the first motion picture.
The first motion picture was shown in 1895.
It was uh created by two brothers, Antoine and Louis Lumiere and it was projected below the Grand Cafe in Paris, France.
100 years ago, December 28th, 1980 1895.
So we are at the Centenary of this incredible invention.

Now, what I'd like to do is examine how technology has influenced the motion picture since that time.
How has the incorporation of technology progressed and how has it changed the way we view motion pictures?
Well, the invention of the motion picture was an amazing feat of technology.
The Lumiere brothers invented their own cameras, their own projectors.
We went along for almost 40 years before we saw the next major technological innovation, which was sound.
In 1927, the Jazz Singer premiered, starring Al Jolson.
It was mostly a silent picture with a few songs, but in it Al Jolson spoke several lines and with those lines ended the era of silent pictures forever.
As a measure of how revolutionary this was, US movie attendance went from 60 million persons in 1927 when the Jazz Singer premiered to 110 million persons in 1929.
Incidentally, um the Jazz Singer was immensely popular and saved the studio that produced it, which was on the verge of bankruptcy and that studio was Warner Brothers.
If Warner Brothers had not taken a major gamble on new technology, there would be no Time Warner today.

The next major incorporation of technology was in 1932.
In 1932, Technicolor had perfected their three-strip color film process after having had many problems with some earlier technology.
Unfortunately, they could not interest any major studio at that time in making a color film.
Can you believe that?
Uh the studios treated it as a outrageously risky expense and refused to pony up the money to make color films.
There was only one studio at the time that decided to go for it and that was Walt Disney.
And Walt Disney trained their animators in color theory and produced the first color films, the Silly Symphony cartoons, which won several Academy Awards and ushered in the age of color.
The next major breakthrough was in 1937 with Snow White, the world's first animated feature film produced by Walt Disney.
It incorporated many innovations including the multi-plane camera and really was the first new form of motion picture entertainment since the invention of the motion picture itself some 42 years earlier.
Animation would never be the same again and Disney's led the way since then.
The next innovation was two years later.
While there were a half a dozen live action films which incorporated Technicolor before the Wizard of Oz, none of them were either commercially successful nor did they ignite the public's demand for color.
The Wizard of Oz changed all that and became the icon of bringing color into live action films.
We then progress almost 40 years before the next major incorporation of new technology, which was Star Wars in 1977.
Star Wars not only totally redefined the science fiction motion picture film genre, but it also elevated special effects to become an equal partner to live action in storytelling and motion pictures.
Now, although Star Wars's effects were produced pre-computer graphics, they really opened the door for everything that followed and we are still living in their shadow today.
We then progress a little over a decade to Terminator 2.
Although Terminator 2 was the first film to bring computer graphic special effects into the mainstream.
Although there were a few films to incorporate computer graphic special effects like Alien and the Abyss before Terminator 2, Terminator 2 was what captured the public and elevated special computer graphic special effects to the mainstream.
This was followed two years later by Jurassic Park, which carried the art a little further and created the most commercially successful film of all time because of the computer graphic special effects.
And that brings us to 1995.
In 1995, the centenary year of the invention of the motion picture itself, we have another major milestone.
Something I think will go down as a landmark in motion picture history.
And that is the first completely computer generated feature length motion picture.
Completely computer synthetic on the hundredth anniversary of the motion picture itself and that of course is Toy Story.

Toy Story represents the computer graphics community contributing not just special effects to a motion picture but the entire motion picture itself.
It's a breakthrough on the scale of Technicolor, Snow White and Star Wars.
It is way beyond what we've seen in computer graphic special effects.
Without diminishing Jurassic Park in any way, let me illustrate.
If you take Jurassic Park and stack all of the frames that contain any computer synthetic element back to back, you get about five and a half minutes.
Of course, these frames do not include background sets or anything, usually just a one computer synthetic element.
Toy Story is 79 minutes in length and every frame is totally synthetic.
Major minor characters, background sets, etc. an order of magnitude leap.
And again, most importantly, we see computer graphics not just playing a supporting role to live action, but actually providing the entire vision for the motion picture.
Now, I know a lot of you have seen Toy Story, a clip in the film show.
I have that clip here today on film if you'd like to see it again.
Would you like to see it or would you like to skip it?
Okay, great.
Well, I'd love to show it.
So could we get the lights down and show the first clip?

As you know, Woody is played by Tom Hanks and Buzz, the spaceman is played by Tim Allen.
Uh Toy Story's been written, directed and produced by Pixar in a partnership with the Walt Disney Company.
And uh we can see how it turns out at Thanksgiving.
Next, I uh we've come a long way in 100 years.

documents.content:
# Steve Jobs Talks About The Powermac G5 Not Making 3ghz WWDC 2004

**Source**: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ObO3co4qttw

**Transcribed**: 2025-12-26 12:13

---

**[Speaker 1]**: Um, now I'd like to talk about the Power Mac.
We just introduced a new line of Power Macs a few weeks ago as well.
2 1/2 GHz.
So we've got dual processors in every single model of Power Mac now, up to 2 1/2 GHz G5 processors, up to 1.25 GHz front side bus.
This is super important because this is how you move information in and out of the processor, which is oftentimes far more important than the actual processing speed of the processor itself.
And, you know, the fastest our competitors offer is 800 MHz.
We're at 1.25 GHz and it's it's incredible, plus you have two of them.
8x SuperDrive starting at 1999 for dual processor system.
So these are the new Power Macs.
Now, I want to talk about 2 1/2 GHz because I stood up here a year ago and said we'd have 3 GHz within a year.
What happened?
What happened was the G5, as you know, is a very complex chip.
And in the semiconductor industry, to make things run faster, they've traditionally shrank the geometries.
And so the Power PC was being made in 130 nanometer geometries, and in the last year, the semiconductor industry has gone from 130 nanometer to 90 nanometer, expecting everything would just get faster, no problem.
It hit the wall.
The whole industry hit the wall at 90 nanometer, and it's been a lot harder than people thought.
And so the speed increases have been very small compared with what we've been used to for the last five years.
And IBM's done really well relative to the rest of the industry, but less than we all hoped.
So let's take a look.
Two biggest two biggest technologists in 90 nanometer, Intel and IBM.
A year ago, when we stood here and you sat here, 3.2 GHz was the fastest Intel processor money could buy, and we just introduced 2 GHz on our Power PC G5.
Intel had a 3.4 GHz release during the course of the year, and just this last week, they introduced 3.6 GHz, and just a few weeks ago, we introduced 2.5.
So everybody's showing their cards within the last week or two, and here's what they are.
And take a look at this.
Intel's gone up 12 1/2% in a year, and IBM's going up 25.
So we're not thrilled about missing 3 GHz.
But we are pleased that the Power PC has increased its performance twice as fast as Intel, as the entire semiconductor industry has had a tough time with 90 nanometer.
Now, in addition to going up twice as twice the level of performance that Intel has over the last year, we give you two of them.
And so we think the Power Mac is an incredibly high performance system, the highest performance system that you can buy.
And we'll keep striving for that 3 GHz, one of these days we'll make it, but we're doing pretty well relative to the rest of the industry.

documents.title: Steve Jobs' closing statement at MacWorld 1997 after his return to Apple
documents.speaker: Steve Jobs
documents.content:
Lastly, I want to just talk a little about about Apple and the brand and uh and what it means I think to a lot of us.

You know, I think you always had to be a little different to buy an Apple computer. Uh when we shipped uh the Apple 2, you had to think different about computers. When computers were these things you saw in movies, they occupied giant rooms. Uh they weren't these things you had on your desktop.

You had to think differently because there wasn't any software at the beginning. You had to think differently when the first computer arrived at a school where there had never been one before and it was an Apple 2. I think you had to think really differently when you bought a Mac. It was a totally different computer, worked in a totally different way, used a totally different part of your brain. And it opened up a computer world for a lot of people who thought differently.

You were buying a computer with an installed base of one.
You had to think differently to do that.
And I think you still have to think differently to buy an Apple computer.
Uh and I think the people that do buy them do think differently and they are the creative spirits in this world.
They are the people that are not just out to get a job done, they're out to change the world.
And they're out to change the world using whatever great tools they can get.
And we make tools for those kinds of people.

So hopefully, what you've seen here today are some beginning steps that give you some confidence that we too are going to think differently and serve the people that have been buying our products since the beginning.
Because a lot of times people think they're crazy.
But in that craziness we see genius and those are the people we're making tools for.
Thank you very much.

documents.content:
Good morning.
Good morning. Thank you.
Isn't it great to be in San Francisco?
So, we have so much great stuff for you today that we may even have to take a stretch break in the middle here.
A lot of good stuff. I hope you love it as much as we do.
So, there are about 3,800 of us here today.
Uh, we're a little over 1% of the registered Apple developers. There's over 300,000 now, and that number has tripled since the since the introduction of Mac OS 10.
Uh, not only carbon and cocoa developers, but a ton of Unix developers have joined us, a lot of Java developers as well. So, we're really excited about this.
I want to start with some updates and then we'll get into the meat of today's presentation.
First, I want to talk about Airport Extreme.
Uh, Airport Extreme is our 54 megabit per second airport product that's based on the industry standard 802.11g.
And the standard was not yet ratified when we started shipping in January. We were the first to ship this, but it was ratified a little over a week ago.
And one week after it was ratified, we had an airport soft software update on the net for base stations and cards to bring them totally in compliance with the final ratified spec.
We are 1,000% sure that 802.11g is the successor to 802.11b. It's totally backwards compatible.
And as I mentioned, Apple was the first to ship 802.11g in our industry, just as we were the first to ship uh 802.11 wireless networking in computers years ago. And I'm pleased to report that since we started shipping 802.11g in January, we've shipped over 300,000 802.11g products.
So, that's an update on Airport Extreme.
We couldn't be happier with the progress.
Next, I want to give you an update on our retail stores.
Uh, this is off the charts. Uh, it's been 25 months since we opened our first store. We now have 58 stores open.
Since we've opened them, we've had over 17 million visitors to our stores.
17 million. This is our store in New York.
It's one of the coolest stores in New York. If you've ever been there, I'd worth a visit if you're in the city. It's wonderful. This is our largest store in Los Angeles in the Grove Shopping Center and again shows how much software we carry in our stores. We love to carry your software.
And among the many stores we're going to be opening in the next year, we're opening three really great stores, one in Chicago, one in San Francisco, and one in Tokyo. We're opening Chicago this coming weekend.
And this is a photo from last week.
This is right on Michigan Avenue, which is the uh best shopping street in America outside of 5th Avenue in New York. It's phenomenal. That big Apple logo in the middle is actually a window uh that you can see right in, get some natural light in the second floor. In San Francisco, we don't have anything constructed yet. We'll open San Francisco uh next spring. But uh this is a rendering. I wish it was as easy to build them. Uh,
And uh this is at the end of Stockton Street, viewed from Market Street. This is what it will look like, only a few blocks from where we are sitting here right now. And in Tokyo, we are opening a store.
It's going to be great. In Tokyo, we are opening a store on the Ginza, uh, which is the number one shopping street in the world, and we're opening it early next year, and again, this is a rendering of what it will be.
So, we've had 17 million visitors and counting. We love to sell your software and hardware accessory products. So, keep keep feeding them to us and we can't wait to put them in our stores. So, that's an update on our retail stores. Next, iPod.
iPod, again, we couldn't be happier with. We just introduced our third generation iPod. Our competitors haven't even caught up with our first generation yet. We're in our third and it is amazing. Uh, it is as light as two CDs in their jewel cases. It is as thin as two CD jewel cases back to back. It has a dock so that charging and sinking is even more convenient than before. And I've got a great milestone today. Today's an auspicious day because later on today, we will ship our 1 millionth iPod.
So, another great product for music, of course, iTunes 4. And the greatest feature of iTunes 4 is of course the iTunes Music Store. Being an auspicious day today, it was eight weeks ago today that we launched the iTunes Music Store, only eight weeks ago, and I'm pleased to report that in the first eight weeks, we've sold over 5 million songs online.
We crossed the 5 million mark this last Saturday and we again are thrilled. Now, we ran an ad campaign about uh about the iTunes Music Store and you know when you run an ad campaign if it's really working, if it if it resonates with the culture, if people start to parody it. And uh it wasn't very long before that happened and uh when I saw this on on TV. they found another tape Osama bin Laden found it was released. you know they were playing this thing over and over again on Al Jazeera network. You know I get the premium cable package so I get Al Jazeera. Well well well show the latest Osama bin Laden tape. I like big butts and I cannot lie. You other guys can't deny. When a girl walks in with an itty bitty waist and a round thing in your face you get sprung. I want to get with you and take your picture. You say you want to get in my Benz? Well use me.
So, doesn't get any better than that. Okay, so that's the iTunes Music Store. Next, I want to give you an update on Safari. documents.content:
So, you're a developer and you've just spent two weeks or maybe a little bit longer writing this amazing app and what is your dream? Your dream is to get it in front of every iPhone user and hopefully they love it and buy it, right?

That's not possible today. Developers don't, most developers don't have those kinds of resources. Even the big developers would have a hard time getting their app in front of every iPhone user.

Well, we're going to solve that problem for every developer, big to small. And the way we're going to do it is what we call the App Store. This is an application we've written to deliver apps to the iPhone. And we're going to put it on every single iPhone with the next release of the software.

And so our developers are going to be able to reach every iPhone user through the App Store. This is the way we're going to distribute apps to the iPhone. So let's take a look inside the App Store. Uh, it's got the five buttons across the bottom. So we have a featured section, which is the ones we're featuring. Just added, staff favorites. We've got categories here. If you want to find a game, if you want to find a business application, you want to find an application about finances, an example, easy to find stuff and browse the different categories.

Of course, we've got our top lists, our top downloads, top 50 in this case, where I can see what the most popular apps are that are being downloaded. And if I know what I want, I can easily search for something, in this case a backgammon game and instantly find it. I can tap on it, get some screenshots, get a write up on it. And if I'm interested in using it, this this one happens to be free. I just tap up there and I tap the install button and the app is wirelessly downloaded to the iPhone using the cell network or Wi-Fi. It's that simple to put the app right on the phone.

Now, we've also built a section into iTunes where you can peruse all the apps as well. And you can download them right to your computer, a PC or a Mac, and sideload them right into your iPhone as well. But we think most people are probably going to just use their iPhone and do it over the air right to the iPhone.

So, this is pretty cool. But it goes even further. If you've downloaded an app and the developer has updated that app, the App Store will automatically tell you that there is an update available. And if you're interested, you just tap on the App Store, takes you to the update section, shows you the app that's been updated. You can see exactly what's been updated. If you like it, tap the update button and your app will be replaced by the updated version again over the air all automatically.

So we think this is pretty cool. And uh, the App Store is going to be the exclusive way to distribute iPhone applications directly to every iPhone user. Now, developers are going to ask, well, this is great, but what's the deal, right? What's the business deal? We think we've got a great business deal for our developers. First of all, the developer picks the price. Pick whatever price you want to sell your app at. When we sell the app through the App Store, the developer gets 70% of the revenues right off the top. We keep 30 to pay for running the App Store.

There are no credit card fees for the developer. We take care of all that. There are no hosting fees for us hosting the app. We take care of all that. There's no marketing fees. The developer gets 70% of the revenues and it's paid monthly. This is the best deal going to distribute applications to mobile platforms. Now, we talk about the 70/30 revenue split, but the developer gets to pick the price and you know what price a lot of developers are going to pick? Free, right? So when a developer wants to distribute their app for free, there is no charge for free apps at all. There's no charge to the user and there's no charge to the developer. We're going to pay for everything to get those apps out there for free. The developer and us have the same exact interest, which is to get as many apps out in front of as many iPhone users as possible. Now, will there be limitations? Of course. There are going to be some apps that we're not going to distribute. Porn, malicious apps, apps that invade your privacy. So there will be some apps that we're going to say no to, but again, we have exactly the same interest as the vast majority of our developers, which is to get a ton of apps out there for the iPhone and we think we've invented an incredibly great way to do it, which is the App Store. It's going to reach every single iPhone user.

That's not possible today. Developers don't, most developers don't have those kinds of resources. Even the big developers would have a hard time getting their app in front of every iPhone user.

Well, we're going to solve that problem for every developer, big to small. And the way we're going to do it is what we call the App Store. This is an application we've written to deliver apps to the iPhone. And we're going to put it on every single iPhone with the next release of the software.

And so our developers are going to be able to reach every iPhone user through the App Store. This is the way we're going to distribute apps to the iPhone. So let's take a look inside the App Store. Uh, it's got the five buttons across the bottom. So we have a featured section, which is the ones we're featuring. Just added, staff favorites. We've got categories here. If you want to find a game, if you want to find a business application, you want to find an application about finances, an example, easy to find stuff and browse the different categories.

Of course, we've got our top lists, our top downloads, top 50 in this case, where I can see what the most popular apps are that are being downloaded. And if I know what I want, I can easily search for something, in this case a backgammon game and instantly find it. I can tap on it, get some screenshots, get a write up on it. And if I'm interested in using it, this this one happens to be free. I just tap up there and I tap the install button and the app is wirelessly downloaded to the iPhone using the cell network or Wi-Fi. It's that simple to put the app right on the phone.

Now, we've also built a section into iTunes where you can peruse all the apps as well. And you can download them right to your computer, a PC or a Mac, and sideload them right into your iPhone as well. But we think most people are probably going to just use their iPhone and do it over the air right to the iPhone.

So, this is pretty cool. But it goes even further. If you've downloaded an app and the developer has updated that app, the App Store will automatically tell you that there is an update available. And if you're interested, you just tap on the App Store, takes you to the update section, shows you the app that's been updated. You can see exactly what's been updated. If you like it, tap the update button and your app will be replaced by the updated version again over the air all automatically.

So we think this is pretty cool. And uh, the App Store is going to be the exclusive way to distribute iPhone applications directly to every iPhone user. Now, developers are going to ask, well, this is great, but what's the deal, right? What's the business deal? We think we've got a great business deal for our developers. First of all, the developer picks the price. Pick whatever price you want to sell your app at. When we sell the app through the App Store, the developer gets 70% of the revenues right off the top. We keep 30 to pay for running the App Store.

There are no credit card fees for the developer. We take care of all that. There are no hosting fees for us hosting the app. We take care of all that. There's no marketing fees. The developer gets 70% of the revenues and it's paid monthly. This is the best deal going to distribute applications to mobile platforms. Now, we talk about the 70/30 revenue split, but the developer gets to pick the price and you know what price a lot of developers are going to pick? Free, right? So when a developer wants to distribute their app for free, there is no charge for free apps at all. There's no charge to the user and there's no charge to the developer. We're going to pay for everything to get those apps out there for free. The developer and us have the same exact interest, which is to get as many apps out in front of as many iPhone users as possible. Now, will there be limitations? Of course. There are going to be some apps that we're not going to distribute. Porn, malicious apps, apps that invade your privacy. So there will be some apps that we're going to say no to, but again, we have exactly the same interest as the vast majority of our developers, which is to get a ton of apps out there for the iPhone and we think we've invented an incredibly great way to do it, which is the App Store. It's going to reach every single iPhone user.

documents.content:
Thank you.
Thank you very much.
Thank you.
Thank you for the very warm welcome.
My name is Steve Jobs and I'm the CEO.
First off today, thank you for such a warm welcome in Paris.
We are really glad to be here.
So first today I want to give you a brief update on some recent things we've introduced and then I want to get into the heart of the presentation.
So for the update to start with, first of all, I just wanted to make sure you knew about the new 17-inch iMac.
Uh it's got a 17-inch display on it that is extraordinary.
Uh it's the same viewing area as a 19-inch cathode ray tube display.
It's huge and it's landscape.
It has 1440 by 900 pixels, which is 64% more than the 15-inch iMac.
It's like nothing else on the market.
So rather than seeing this, you can see this.
It's really something.
And it's powered graphically by an Nvidia GeForce 4 MX graphics chip.
So it's really, really fast graphics and it has a super drive so that you can burn your own DVDs that play in almost any DVD player built in.
Extraordinary product.
If you haven't seen one, please go to the booth today and see one.
Uh and we sell them in Europe for 21.99.
That's before taxes.
Uh different governments add different tax rates.
But uh this is what we sell them for before taxes.
And I would suggest you take a look at one.
It's it's just a wonderful, wonderful computer.
In addition, we introduced the eMac recently and it sells for 11.99, but we just introduced a second model that has a super drive.
This is the lowest cost way to burn DVDs in the entire marketplace.
And so you can make your own DVDs in this eMac and it sells for 16.99.
And we're constantly trying to drive the price of the super drive uh lower and lower because burning DVDs is so wonderful.
So the new eMac.
Next is the iPod.
The iPod for us has been a giant hit and we have three models of the iPod now, the 5 gigabyte, the 10 gigabyte, and the 20 gigabyte iPod.
And so you can have 1,000, 2,000, or up to 4,000 songs uh in your pocket on an iPod.
And these are the prices we sell them at.
These include uh I think French VAT.
So uh again, lower and lower prices on the iPods.
The uh two top models come with a carrying case and a remote control and the software is new in them as well.
Uh we've included the ability to browse your music by some new ways.
So we have artists, albums, and songs from before, but now we also have genres and composers.
And so for genres, you can browse your music by classical or country or jazz.
And if you like classical music, you can browse it by composers instead of just performers, uh which is a really wonderful way to find your music.
In addition, the iPods also store contacts, uh and they now store your calendar data too and we'll talk more about that later.
So the new iPods are pretty wonderful and they're hitting the shelves now.
Uh we also introduced an iPod for Windows.
Uh we felt like our our uh friends on the Windows side of the world were being left out and and uh we wanted to send them some iPods to get them familiar with Apple so that someday they can see that maybe our products are are better than the ones on the Windows side.
And we chose Music Match as the jukebox to work with.
Music Match uh it's not iTunes, but uh it's the best one on the Windows side.
And so uh that's the new iPods that we have.
And lastly, uh we introduced some new Power Macintosh recently, the the fastest Macs ever made.
And uh they use Xserve technology, which is this technology that we use in our servers.
That's very, very fast.
It's dual processor.
The processors each have very large L3 caches.
Very fast architecture, very fast IO uh through the disc drives, etc.
And uh this Xserve architecture is a first for the Power Max.
Uh and the keyword is dual.
Everything about the Power Max is dual.
So we have dual optical drives for the first time.
You can have two optical drives.
They all come with dual display cards, so you can drive up to uh you can drive two displays all the way up to dual uh 23-inch cinema displays off one Power Mac like this.
And of course, they have dual processors.
Uh and the three models are dual 867, dual 1 GHz, and dual 1.25 and uh and these are the prices and they're really, really fast machines.
So this is what we have uh that is new in the systems area and all of it is at the booth.
You can you can go see it.
But what I want to spend the rest of my time talking about is software.
Uh often we focus on the hardware and Apple does make the best hardware in our industry, but we also make the best software and software really is the soul of the machine.
So I want to spend the rest of the time starting with Jaguar and talking about our operating system and our uh application software.
So Jaguar is the latest release of Mac OS 10 and I think it's fair to say that after uh after three releases of Mac OS 10, 10.0, 10.1, and now Jaguar, Mac OS 10.2, Mac OS 10 has finally arrived.
It's phenomenal.
And uh if you're not running Jaguar, I'd strongly suggest you go out immediately and buy a copy because it's it's like it's it's not it's it's the best thing we've ever done in software and I would I would go check it out.
So Jaguar has over 150 major new features to it and I'd like to show you a bunch of them today.
Now, we're Unix based.
Mac OS 10 is based on Unix, industrial strength Unix.
And you may not know it, but Apple has become the number one Unix supplier in the world, bigger than Linux, bigger than Solaris, bigger than anything.
Strange, huh?
But true.
And uh we've improved our Unix quite a bit in uh in Mac OS 10.2.
We've added FreeBSD 4.4, new compiler with GCC3, and a bunch of technical stuff that you can you can learn about on the website and I won't cover here.
But uh the Unix is now uh even better than it was and I think we have uh uh arguably one of the best Unixes in the world now.
Very secure, very fast, uh very powerful.
Funny enough, we've also added more support for working in a Windows environment because a lot of our customers connect their Macs into Windows networks with Windows servers.
And we've added SMB browsing and active directory support.
So you can now go plug a Mac right into a Windows network and it just works and it's really great.
We've also added VPN support.
So if you're on the road and want to access your email, uh you can do that as well.
So a lot better Windows support.
We've also improved support for running old Mac OS 9 apps in classic.
This is the environment in Mac OS 10 that will run old Mac OS 9 applications.
And it runs them surprisingly fast.
In some cases, faster than natively on OS 9 itself.
Now, we've all had to launch classic and it used to take a long time 18 months ago.
It's now really fast.
In Jaguar, it launches classic twice as fast as before.
So it launches on our new Power Max as an example in 8 to 10 seconds.
It's very, very fast.
We have better compatibility.
We have the ability to use USB peripherals now.
You can share you can use the same internet settings in 10 and in classic, so you don't have to set them up again.
And if you use Apple Talk, your portable will wake up much faster.
All these things have been improved in classic and it's quite good now under Jaguar.
So now let's get into some of the core features.
We have a new finder in Jaguar.
It's multi-threaded.
It has spring-loaded folders, which was the number one request that we got for the finder.
It has integrated search built right into the finder.
And let me show you some of this stuff now.
I'd like to invite Ken Bereskin, uh director of Mac OS 10 product marketing up on stage and Ken.

Why don't you give us a demo of the finder?

Okay.
So that's the finder.
Next up is universal access.
We don't want anyone to get left behind in Mac OS 10.
And so we've added a ton of new technology to help people uh that need a little bit of assistance to get full benefit out of Mac OS 10.
We've got zooming, we've got a screen reader, we've got full keyboard access and visual notification.
So Ken, can you give us a brief demo of uh universal access?

Thank you, Ken.
So again, we can use the underlying technologies in Mac OS 10, in this case quartz graphics to do to go way beyond where we've ever been before in some of these areas.
Another foundation technology in Mac OS 10 is QuickTime.
QuickTime 6 ships inside of Mac OS 10.
Now, in our industry, our industry is based on open standards as you know and here are some of them.
Uh TCP IP for networking.
Almost every network you use now is based on this open standard TCP IP.
If we didn't have this, it would be a tower of Babel and we wouldn't we wouldn't have the internet today.
Uh HTML is a standard that made the worldwide web possible.
Uh MP3 ushered in the digital music age and is still the most popular digital music format by far.
Again, an open standard.
And MPEG 2 is a video compression standard that's in every DVD player and on every DVD and made the DVD possible.
The next one of these big open standards is called MPEG 4.
It's brought to us by the same people that did MPEG 2 that's inside our DVD players and made that possible.
And MPEG 4 allows us to stream video over the internet with an open standard.
It provides the highest quality out there and yet provides for very low bandwidth streaming and everybody is jumping on this standard except for Microsoft who is proposing their own proprietary standard which isn't as good.
And uh so we'll see which one wins in the marketplace, but if history is any indication, the open standards will win.
The open standard for audio is called AAC.
It's the finest quality audio codec available.
The finest one ever invented to our knowledge and we're using that as well.
That is the MPEG 4 audio standard.
In addition to that, we've added instant on streaming.
We're the first folks to ship instant on streaming and that's built into QuickTime as well.
I'd like to invite Frank Casanova, our director of QuickTime marketing up to give us a demo of QuickTime 6.
Frank, welcome.

Right? All sorts of things you can do with smart playlists. So, iTunes, we have, I'm pleased to report, we have distributed 16 million copies of iTunes. So, this is our digital hub strategy and it's working. Thanks to these great applications that we've written. And we can talk to all the coolest devices out there, but we've recently added a few more. And the ones we've added are the cell phone and officially the Palm. We've also said, we have this great portable device in the iPod and we can do even more with it. You remember that we can view contacts and calendars on our iPods too. And so these three devices are the targets for a new application we've written called iSync. So synchronize data to these devices. The purpose of iSync is to synchronize our digital lives. What do we mean by that? Well, we've got a great address book which has all the information of our contacts in it, and we've now got iCal which has our calendars in it. And that's great when we're on our Mac. But what about when we're not? We want to synchronize the information in the address book and in iCal with our iPods, our cell phones, and our Palms. All automatically. The most important of these though is the cell phone, right? Because that's the most popular. And there's a new generation of cell phones that are coming out now. Of course, they're GPRS based, you know that. You're the leaders in this in Europe, of course. They've got color screens on them. They've got organizers built into them with address books and calendars. They use the SyncML standard to make it easier to sync with them. And a lot of them have Bluetooth, so we don't even need cables. We can sync with them over Bluetooth. And we're it's exactly what we're doing. Now, why do you want to sync with your phone? What's so exciting about syncing with your phone? Well, I'll give you a few reasons. For any of you who've used a Palm, you know all this, but for those of you who haven't. Number one, you get to enter your data on a nice big display and a nice full-size keyboard instead of this little tiny phone. And it's much nicer. You can enter a few hundred numbers, it's a lot nicer. But it's more important than just convenience. If you lose your phone, you don't lose your life. If your contacts are only on your phone and you lose it, it's not good. And so, if you lose your phone, your life is still on your Mac. And, similar to that, when you buy a new phone, you don't spend hours putting in the data. You just sync it up with your Mac and you load the hundreds of contacts that you have in seconds. So, those are three good reasons why you want to sync with your phone. You want to start looking at the phone as a peripheral to your Mac. It's a whole new way of thinking about it and very productive. So, these three devices, that's what iSync is targeting. iSync is a very simple app in appearance, very easy to use. You can set what you want to sync, like in the iPod, you want all your contacts or just certain address books. Do you want all your calendars or maybe just your work calendar? For your phone, the same thing, right? And then when you push sync all, this is all you do. It syncs up every device. All of them together, all at once. So, let me show you what this is like. Let's go do a demo of iSync. Okay. So, again, iSync is using Bluetooth. Bluetooth has really arrived here. And, uh, let me take a look at the configuration panels for the phone. So, here we go. I can turn on synchronization for the phone. I can synchronize all my contacts or just some of my address books. I can decide to not synchronize contacts that don't have a phone number, or I can synchronize them all, so I have everybody's email address even if they don't have a phone number. And I can pick all my calendars or again just the selected calendars here. But I'll pick them all. And, uh, for the iPod, similar thing. Pick the contacts, pick the calendars. I can decide to automatically synchronize it whenever the iPod is connected. And, uh, now, what one of the things I'm going to do here is, uh, I've got a new phone right here, and my phone does not have, uh, any addresses in it. So, let me get the I've got the picture in picture up there. Uh, let me move this to where you can see it. And I will go to this phone and, uh, let's see. I've got, uh, I think this will show me that it has no numbers in it. Is that right? Yep. Okay. And, uh, I will push this, keep me back there. So, there's no numbers in this phone. And now I will go show you, uh, in my address book, that I have lots of contacts in my address book here. Lots of different things here. And I want to sync this stuff into this brand new phone that I just got. So, what do I do? What I do is I simply go over here and push sync now. And if everything works right, over Bluetooth, it is finding this phone. It has set the phone into synchronization mode. It is synchronizing with the phone and the iPod. In this case, it's putting numbers onto my new phone, but if I had entered new numbers on my phone, it would be syncing them also back to my Mac. So, it's bidirectional sync between the phone and the Mac. This will take about 20 or 30 seconds. The software in the phones is not so fast. Okay, there we go. And now I should be able to go over here and, uh, let's see. To get the address book, I think what I do is I think I just go like that. And as you can see, I've got all my numbers here. And let me go ahead and call Avi here. Boom. Well, hold on. Avi Tevanian, there we go. And I think I should be able to push this and I should call Avi who's out there in the audience. We'll wait till it works. There he goes. Okay. So, now, what about, um, iPod? We synced iPod as well. And let me go show you, uh, what that's like. Let's get the iPod up here. This is my iPod. I'll wake it up from sleep here. And, uh, oh, can we adjust that, please? Maybe we have a little too much light on it. But, uh, we can go into extras here in our iPod. And as you can see, we have contacts, calendars, clock and game here. And we can go into contacts. And sure enough, like there's all of Avi's contacts here. We can just, uh, get contacts for Ken Bereskin here, again. That's what contacts look like. They look about 10 times better than this, but this is the best we can do right now with this projection here. And, uh, we also have calendars that have been synced. And so here's all my calendars. And I'll just pick all of them right now. And this is what they look like. And it shows me what days I have dates events on. I can just go back and say, well, today, this is what my calendar looks like. And I can pick any one of these events and get more details on it. And so this is what my calendar looks like. And it turns out the scroll wheel on the iPod is just perfect because I can go to October here, November, December, or easily go back. There we go. To today. Boom. All on my iPod, all synced with iSync. So, iSync, what it's about is Mac to mobile. And, uh, most importantly, the phone. Because that's what we all have. We've added that to the digital hub and we've written this incredible application called iSync. Now, iSync also runs on Mac OS 10 version 10.2 Jaguar. So you need Jaguar to run iSync. And we are going to put out a beta release late this month so we can begin the testing process. It's looking very good. And it's going to be a free download at apple.com, both the beta release and the final release. So please take a look, uh, towards the end of this month. So look at what we've got here. We've got the new mail application. We've got address book. We've got iChat. We've got iCal and now we have iSync. There's never been anything like this to help you organize and manage your life and communicate with your colleagues, friends, and family. So iSync we think is going to be a really big deal and it's the start of something amazing. So the digital hub, we've added the phone, the Palm, and we've enhanced, uh, the iPod. And we've done that through these remarkable applications that we have written at Apple. iPhoto, iMovie, iTunes, iDVD, and now iSync. And with the remarkable batch of applications that come with Mac OS 10, the new address book, the new mail, new iChat, new Sherlock 3, new iCal. These are just 10 of the things that ship now in the Mac OS 10 universe. And there's nothing like this on PCs at all. And this is this is the maturing of the vision that we put in place two years ago, which was our digital hub strategy. And all of the applications are now mostly out there. They're some are on their second and third revisions. They're being used by millions of people throughout the world. And you have my promise that we're going to keep working hard to make them even better and to continue to add wonderful new capabilities to the Mac. So thank you very, very much for coming today. Please go see our booth and, uh, we'll be talking to you soon. Thanks.
