# MWSF 2006

**Source**: /Volumes/NvME-Satechi/steve-jobs.ai/Database_Steve_Jobs/2000s/MWSF 2006.mp4

**Transcribed**: 2025-12-31 11:47

---

## Part 1

[Music]

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: Good morning and welcome to Macworld. We've got a lot of great stuff for you today.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: So, I want to start off with a retail update. Tell you how we did in Apple retail stores. You know, we've got 135 Apple retail stores now. And these are just the best place to buy not only a Mac and an iPod, but one of the best buying experiences for any product in the world. And I am really pleased to announce that last quarter we had 26 million visitors during the holiday quarter in our retail stores. I mean, think about it. This is more people than live in any state in our union but California. You know, if you're in New Hampshire, it's no big deal, but if you live in New York, I mean, everybody in New York visited an Apple store by number, you know, it's it's incredible. So, that was pretty amazing. What was also amazing was that our retail stores had their first billion dollar quarter. Over a billion dollars of revenues last quarter. So, really fantastic. And I want to congratulate them all. They worked so hard and uh they did a really terrific job. Now, uh we've got a great chief financial officer, Peter Oppenheimer, and Peter told me that if I wanted to release uh this figure, I also had to release the overall sales for Apple because he didn't want anybody making the wrong assumptions and and uh and and getting the wrong data for the quarter. So, uh we're going to do something we've never done before here at a Macworld. Uh I get to tell you uh what our revenues were for last quarter. It was Apple's uh a record for Apple, the highest revenues we've ever had in a quarter. Last quarter we sold around $5.7 billion.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: So, this is uh one for the record books. So, there's a lot for these ginger mint gingerbread men to be uh dancing about. Everybody's pretty happy. So, that's a retail update. And uh now what I'd like to do is talk about our efforts in music. We went into the holiday quarter with the best lineup of music players on the planet. Uh the new iPod Nano and the fifth generation iPod. These are the best music players in the world and of course the fifth generation iPod also plays video, music videos and now television shows as well. And we sold 4 and a half million iPods a year ago in the holiday quarter 2004. And what a lot of folks have been asking us and speculating on is how many did we sell last quarter? Holiday quarter 2005 and some of the estimates were getting pretty astronomical. 8 million, 9 million, 10 million. Uh and I'm really pleased to announce today uh that last quarter we sold 14 million iPods.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: That is over 100 every minute 24/7 throughout the whole quarter. And it's still it still wasn't enough. So uh more iPods are on their way for those people that uh didn't have a chance to get one last quarter. And so that brings the total number of iPods sold to around 42 million. Uh you can see the slope of this curve is going up again. And of those 42 million, 32 million of them were sold in 2005, in calendar year 2005. 32 million iPods. Okay. Now, I'd like to give you an update on iTunes. We have sold on iTunes. We've crossed over 850 million songs. We are well on our way to hitting that billion song mark in the next few months. And we are selling songs at the rate now of 3 million per day. We've seen a really nice growth in iTunes sales. And that is over a billion songs a year run rate. Well over. So, we've seen some really great growth throughout the last year in iTunes as well. And our market share continues to be very strong. 83%.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: Yeah, I'm showing off some new keynote features here too. Couldn't help myself. So, we're really, really happy uh with how iTunes is doing. And as you know, one of the newest things in iTunes and of course on iPod are television shows and the content that we've been adding has just been spectacular. And we started selling TV shows only about 90 days ago. I'm very pleased to report uh that since we launched on October 12th, we have sold over 8 million videos. We are really happy with this. Now, last week last week for the first time we added some sports. And in partnership with ABC and ESPN, we put up the bowl games and it was really fantastic. Here's a little sampling.

**[Speaker 2]**: Hello everybody and welcome to Pasadena, California. Night of the 2006 Rose Bowl game presented by City. I'm Keith Jackson and in the unprecedented partnership between ABC Sports and Apple iTunes, you're about to see a bowl blast. The 15 minute condensed version of the National Championship game between the top ranked USC Trojans and the number two Texas Longhorns. All the key moments from this contest right at your fingertips in the iTunes video store. And it's available for all four BCS games. So, sit back, relax and enjoy this special ABC Sports presentation.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: So, uh ABC and ESPN did a phenomenal job on these 15 minute highlights and they they went to number one. The Rose Bowl is the number one video now on iTunes. So they've been extremely popular. And today we're putting up some other great new content from Saturday Night Live. This is this is some stuff that I've personally wanted to see from day one.

[Music]

**[Speaker 3]**: Good morning dear. How was your sleep face?

**[Speaker 4]**: Sufficient.

[Music]

**[Steve Jobs]**: All the great stuff here. All the great stuff, the best of stuff and all the great skits that you remember. You're going to be able to buy on iTunes starting today. This great Saturday Night Live content on iTunes. We're also introducing a new accessory for your iPod today, which is a remote control that's also an FM tuner. And it's a little thing that clips on your clothing anywhere you'd like. It's a great remote control but also includes an FM tuner. And so you can plug this into your Nano. You can plug this in to your fifth generation iPod. And when you do, uh a radio menu item will show up in the top menu and when you select it, boom, you get screens like this. You can set your presets. It's really nice. And uh it's going to be priced at $49 and it goes on sale today. Uh and last, I want to give you an update on Chrysler for those of you that missed it at the Detroit Auto Show. Uh Chrysler is the first of the big three American auto companies to announce major iPod integration support for their cars this year. Uh over 3 million Chrysler, Dodge and Jeep models are going to offer optional iPod integration this year. And when you add that to all the other cars that are doing the same thing, in 2006 over 40% of the cars sold in the US will offer iPod integration. I think that's phenomenal. Over 40%.

**[Steve Jobs]**: So, that's an update on what we're doing in music and the last thing I've got is a new ad I wanted to show you, a new iPod ad. You know, uh in our October event, uh we were so lucky to have Winton Marsalis come and play for us. Uh and he really blew us all away. And after that, we asked ourselves, wouldn't it be great to do an ad with Winton and his music? And we've done one and it'll start running soon and I'd like to premiere it for you right now. So let's go ahead and run it.

[Music]

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: So, that's what we're up to in music. 14 million iPods. But it's Macworld. So we're going to spend the rest of the day talking about the Mac.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: Now, I'm going to start off with a very important application we introduced a few months ago called Aperture. Aperture is for digital photographers. We see Aperture as being the tool for digital photographers in the same way that Final Cut Pro is for digital filmmakers. And uh it's an incredible tool designed hand in hand with digital photographers for digital photographers. When we launched the product, we created a video for it and I'd like to just show you some excerpts from that video now to give you a feel for the product. So let's go ahead and run that.

**[Speaker 5]**: In the beginning, one of the reservations I had with digital was the capture mode. Slow as molasses that delay. They fixed that. The size of the files, they fixed that. And then for me the longest period stretch now has been the software for post-production. I think Aperture is a quantum leap in the direction of where we all thought we could be. You know, initially I thought maybe the application was designed strictly for professional photographers, while it may have been, it is user-friendly enough that I think the amateur is going to love this program and what it will do for them. When I used to show my proofs was to just hand them off to the client and they would take them home and then bring them back later. Now with Aperture, what I could do is set up the 230 in screens and they can sit and relive their wedding. The way I used to deal with the proofs and lay it out for an album or a design is I would lay them out on a coffee table and I would look at them and move them around and say, okay, maybe these two work well together. The feature that Aperture has is that you can lay this out on the screen like if it were an album already. The speed that Aperture handled all these raw files. It was incredible. I've never seen anything do that before. Yes, finally, someone thought the way I'm thinking about post-production. What amazed me about Aperture is first of all, I can edit now and I'm really excited to do it because it's faster. I can loop things. I can stack them. I can put them in categories. It just blew me away. It really did. I mean Aperture just blew me away. I can bring it in, pick my selects, organize them in any way. I can keyword them. I can make a contact sheet into a PDF. You can upload them to a web gallery very quickly. Touch of a button and it's on the web. Just runs you from beginning to end flawlessly. I like to shoot in bursts. And sort of like rapid little 1 2 3 4 5 pictures. Just take a thumbnail, put them in different order and all of a sudden they're reordered in the stack. On average, a college football game would give you maybe a thousand images. The bad news is raw files take so long to work with. And now you can modify it, you can do anything you want with it and it's instantaneous. It's unbelievable. I suspect that I'm going to stop shooting JPEGs. I can take a picture and do a white balance on it, have the original thing side by side, change some color saturation and then choose the one that has the adjustments that look the best. And that's really the beauty of all this. I mean it's not just replicating something that you've done for years on a light table. It's the fact that you're replicating what you've done on a light table and moved it into the 22nd century. Stanley Kubrick would be jealous.

**[Steve Jobs]**: So, we think this is going to be a really important product and if you haven't seen it, I'd suggest you check it out. Another thing I now want to talk about is widgets. When we introduced Mac OS 10 Tiger this last spring, we introduced the concept of widgets and it's been growing ever since. There are now tons of widgets. Uh, the price today is $130, mainly because we did the fundamental things that were necessary to focus on the customer and focus on having a highly successful business.

**[Speaker 5]**: At, at Chrysler, uh, we had to take, uh, nearly $4 billion out of the cost structure to get Chrysler fully competitive, uh, particularly with the Japanese.

**[Speaker 10]**: I've seen this at DuPont, I've seen it at IBM, I've seen it at City Corp. The success starts to generate additional success.

**[Speaker 4]**: Well, the confidence has to start with a clear vision. What are we trying to accomplish? What are we trying to do? You take that vision down to a strategy. It has to, people have to look at it and say, yes, they can do that.

**[Speaker 7]**: When a company elect the energy, you can't do anything to the company. So I think with Steve and the new board members, first thing we, we need to do is inject tremendous new energy, new thoughts.

**[Speaker 8]**: Apple has very strong positions in two market segments. Uh, first education and secondly, uh, creative content.

**[Speaker 10]**: What other computer system has 20 to 25 million loyal, enthusiastic, uh, committed users? Just building on that base, recapturing, uh, their dedication and strength because we're bringing out great products.

**[Speaker 8]**: Whenever you have a strong position in a market segment, you can capitalize on that.

**[Speaker 6]**: You know, Apple's the only lifestyle brand in the computer industry. It's the only company that people feel passionate about. You know, my company Oracle, it's a huge company. IBM's a huge company. Microsoft's a huge company. But no one has incredible emotions associated with our companies. Only Apple is really a lifestyle brand.

**[Speaker 8]**: And companies can spend billions of dollars to build a brand. Apple does not have to do that. It's already been done.

**[Speaker 9]**: The important thing is to, uh, to build products that are wonderful. And, uh, or as Steve would say, insanely great.

**[Speaker 1]**: Be great and it's time to build really insanely great products.

**[Speaker 10]**: The biggest thing you can do is go out and buy a Mac.

**[Speaker 5]**: Do I use a Mac? Absolutely. I use a Mac. I have three of them in my home.

**[Speaker 2]**: I've been using a Mac since 1984 and I'm not about to stop.

**[Speaker 7]**: I probably own every single machine that Apple has ever produced and I can tell you, no one can change me in terms of personally what machine I will use. It's got to be a Mac.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: So, as you can see, this is a pretty diverse group of people, a lot of deep industry expertise who come together to say, hey, this world's a lot better place with a healthy Apple computer in it. Okay, next, market focus. Yeah, I can't get anyone to tell me the definitive market share number for Apple, but it's around 7% from what I can gather. And the question is, where is Apple relevant? Where is Apple still, uh, the dominant player? Which market segments? And there are two. The first one, I call creative content. It's publishing, design, pre-press, etc. It's creative professionals using computers. And what's interesting is Apple is still the dominant market leader for creative professionals. By far. It's like 80% of the computers used in advertising and graphic arts, design, pre-press, all Macintoshes. And 64% is the best number I could find. 64% of all internet websites are created using a Mac. It's amazing.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: But, but we haven't been doing a good enough job here.


---

## Part 2

**[Steve Jobs]**: As an example, there is something like 10 to 15% of Mac sales, which can be traced directly back to people using Adobe Photoshop as their power app, right?
When was the last time you saw Adobe and Apple co-marketing Photoshop?
You know, when was the last time we went to Adobe and said, how do we make a computer that will run Photoshop faster?
These things haven't been as cohesive as they should have been, and I think we're going to start proactively focusing much more on how we do these things.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: The the second market is is one that's very close to my heart is education.
Uh, Apple
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Steve Jobs]**: Apple put the first computers in education.
Uh, Apple did it again with the Macintosh.
And uh Apple is still uh the dominant leader in education.
Now, I'm going to ask you a question.
Who is the largest education company in the world?
Who's the largest education company in the world?

**[Audience]**: Apple!
**[Steve Jobs]**: Yeah, the answer is Apple.
Apple is the single largest education supplier in the world.
Okay, education supplier to education in the world.
Single largest education company in the world.
Now, I've asked 100 people at Apple this and only two have thought of Apple.
It's incredible the position Apple still has in education.
60% of all computers in education are Apples.
64% of computers teachers use are Apples.
It's a two to two and a half billion dollar business for Apple every year.
What an incredible foundation to build off of.
What an incredible legacy to build off of.
And so, you're going to see Apple proactively focusing much more on these two markets where it is very relevant.
And both of these markets are growing over at 20% a year.
Now, Apple share is shrinking in these markets slowly, but I think you're going to see that stabilize and turn around and you're going to see Apple grow with these markets because it's going to do a much better job of focusing where its relevance is and where its legacies lie.

**[Steve Jobs]**: Next, core assets.
As you know, Apple's greatest core asset is you all.
It's the group of 20 to 25 million active users that believe that Apple products and Macintosh is still the best in the world.
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Steve Jobs]**: I don't think we've been doing a good enough job uh taking care of you.
Have you called the I mean, I've called the support lines myself.
I've gotten very acquainted with the hold signal.
And uh so I think we're going to see some changes there soon.
And I apologize for for anything in the past.
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Steve Jobs]**: But what I want to do right now is get a little more analytical.
And I want to say sort of from a a a an more analytical standpoint, what are Apple's core assets?
And there's two of them that I've been able to uncover.
The first one is the brand itself.
And the second is the Mac OS.
Now, the brand, if you asked, you know, what are the five greatest brands in the world?
If you asked, you went out and you asked professionals this question, you know, I think Nike would be on everybody's list.
Coca-Cola would be on everybody's list.
Disney would be on everybody's list and Apple would be on everybody's list.
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Steve Jobs]**: We have we have one of the world's greatest brands and we haven't paid much attention to it in the last several years and I think you're going to see that start to change.
And now I want to focus on the Mac OS.
The Mac OS is an incredibly core asset to Apple.
And we've been walking all over it.
I mean, most people think that we're about to abandon the Mac OS.
Most people think that, you know, Macintosh OS 8, which we just released was code named Tempo as you know, right?
So we just released Tempo.
Most people think our next release next year, which is code name Allegro will come out, but then our next release will be Requiem.
And it's crazy.
It's absolutely crazy.
The Mac OS is still the best thing in the world.
It is still the best thing in the world.
There are over 20 million active users, the number is a little closer to 25 million.
There are thousands of developers and there's a billion and a half dollar software industry built around this thing.
This is one of the core assets of the company.
And we are going to invest a lot more in it because we think it is an incredible asset and it has yet to really be fully exploited.
Apple is about the Mac OS.
We're going to be doing other things because we're creative people.
But at the core, Apple is about the Mac OS and all of the the fears that I've heard of people that we're abandoning it are absolutely not true.
Our latest release, Mac OS 8, I've got some really good news for you.
We released this thing two weeks ago and we have already sold 1.2 million copies.
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Steve Jobs]**: That's four times greater than what our forecast was.
So we're scrambling to ship everything and if you uh if it takes a little bit to get yours, please uh I apologize for that, but we are scrambling and this number is going up.
I mean, there's it shows no sign of abating.
So things are going very well with uh OS 8.
Now, I'd like to talk about meaningful partners.
Apple lives in an ecosystem and it needs help from other partners.
It needs to help other partners.
And relationships that uh that are destructive don't help anybody in this industry as it is today.
So, during the last several weeks, we have looked at some of the relationships and uh one has stood out uh as a relationship that uh hasn't been going so well, but had the potential, I think, to be great for both companies.
And I'd like to uh announce one of our first partnerships today, a very, very meaningful one.
And that is one with Microsoft.
**[Audience]**: [Mixed reactions]
**[Steve Jobs]**: I'd like to take you through this.
Um, the discussions actually began uh because there were some uh patent disputes.
And uh rather than uh I know.
**[Audience]**: [Laughter]
**[Steve Jobs]**: Rather than uh repeating history, I'm extremely proud of both companies that they have resolved these differences in a very, very professional way.
And this has led, I think, to uh an overall relationship that we're announcing today that's got several parts to it and we're extremely excited about.
First part of it is a patent settlement and cross license.
Uh the two companies have reached a full cross license for all patents uh that exist and for patents that are filed within the next five years and uh it has been a uh a very serious patent settlement.
The second part of this is Microsoft is committing to release Microsoft Office on Macintosh for the next five years.
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Steve Jobs]**: They are um they are going to release the same number of uh of major releases as they release on Windows during that time.
Their first release uh uh is going they're they're going to target to have it out uh near the end of the year.
It might slip a few months into next year, but they're working real hard on it and it looks very, very good.
Next, we have taken a look uh at browsers out there and Apple has decided
**[Audience]**: [Boos]
**[Steve Jobs]**: Apple has decided to make Internet Explorer its default browser on the Macintosh.
**[Audience]**: [Boos]
**[Steve Jobs]**: Since we believe in choice, uh
**[Audience]**: [Laughter]
**[Steve Jobs]**: Since we believe in choice, we're going to be shipping other internet browsers as well on the Macintosh and the user can of course change their default should they choose to.
But uh we believe that Internet Explorer is a really good browser and uh we think it's going to make a fine default browser.
Java, we are going to be collaborating with Microsoft on Java uh to ensure that uh we can get the best from each other and ensure that uh there's compatibility between our virtual machines and uh we think that uh that will serve everybody's interests.
And lastly, Microsoft is making an investment in Apple.
Microsoft is buying $150 million worth of Apple stock at market price.
It is non-voting shares and they've agreed
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Steve Jobs]**: And they've agreed not to sell them for at least three years.
So, what this means is is that Microsoft is going to be part of the game with us as we restore this company back to health, have a vested interest in that stock price going up.
We're going to be working together on Microsoft Office, on Internet Explorer, on Java and I think that uh it's going to lead to uh a very healthy relationship.
So, it's a package announcement today.
We're very, very happy about it.
We're very, very excited about it.
And I happen to have a special guest with me today uh via satellite down link and uh if we could uh get him up on the stage right now.

**[Steve Jobs]**: Some of the most exciting work that I've done in my career has been the work that I've done uh with Steve on the Macintosh.
Uh whether it's the first introduction uh or doing products like Mac Excel.
Uh these have been major milestones.
And it's very exciting to renew our commitment uh to the Macintosh.
We have over 8 million customers uh using Microsoft software on the Macintosh.
Um we make it very easy for people use Macintosh uh to take their uh their documents and work with all kinds of machines.
Uh we're very excited about the new release we're building.
This is called Mac Office 98.
Uh we do expect to get it out by the end of this year and we've got some uh some real exciting features.
Uh it's a product that's going to require no setup.
It's going to be an easy transition from people in the past.
Uh and I think it's going to really uh set a new benchmark for doing a good job with performance and exploiting unique Mac features.
Uh in many ways it's more advanced than what we've done on the Windows platform.
Uh we're also excited about uh Internet Explorer and we've got a a very dedicated team that's down in California that works on that product uh and the code is really specially developed for the Macintosh.
It's not just a port of what we've done in the Windows environment.
And so we're pleased to be uh supporting Apple.
Uh we think Apple makes a a huge contribution to the computer industry.
Um we think it's going to be a lot of fun helping out and uh we look forward to the feedback from all of you as we move forward doing uh more Macintosh software.
Thanks.
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Steve Jobs]**: Thank you, Bill.
You know, where we are right now is we're shepherding some of the greatest assets in the computer industry.
And if we want to move forward and see Apple healthy and prospering again, we have to let go of a few things here.
We have to let go of this notion that for Apple to win, Microsoft has to lose.
Okay?
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Steve Jobs]**: We have to embrace the notion that for Apple to win, Apple has to do a really good job.
And if other and if if others are going to help us, that's great because we need all the help we can get.
And if we screw up and we don't do a good job, it's not somebody else's fault, it's our fault.
So, I think that's a very important perspective.
I think if we want Microsoft Office on the Mac, we better treat the company that puts it out with a little bit of gratitude.
We'd like their software.
So, the era the era of of setting this up as a as a competition between Apple and Microsoft is over as far as I'm concerned.
This is about getting Apple healthy and this is about Apple being able to make incredibly great contributions to the industry to get healthy and prosper again.
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Steve Jobs]**: The last thing the last perspective I'd like to leave with you on this is you know, sometimes points of view can really make you look at things differently.
When you hear a new point of view, like for me, when I was looking at the statistics and it it it it uh hit me that Apple is the largest education company in the world.
That was like a bolt of lightning.
That's huge.
What an incredible base to build off of.
Another bolt of lightning is that Apple plus Microsoft equals 100% of the desktop computer market.
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Steve Jobs]**: And so, whatever Apple and Microsoft agree to do, it's a standard.
And I think that you'll be seeing us work with Microsoft more because they're the only other player in the desktop industry.
And I think you'll be seeing Microsoft want to work with Apple more because Apple is the only other player in the desktop industry.
So, I hope we have even more cooperation in the future because the industry wants it.
Lastly, I want to just talk a little about about Apple and the brand and uh and what it means, I think, to a lot of us.
You know, I think you always had to be a little different to buy an Apple computer.
Uh when we shipped uh the Apple 2, you had to think different about computers.
I mean, computers were these things you saw in movies, they occupied giant rooms.
Uh they weren't these things you had on your desktop.
You had to think differently because there wasn't any software at the beginning.
You had to think differently when a first computer arrived at a school where there had never been one before and it was an Apple 2.
I think you had to think really differently when you bought a Mac.
It was a totally different computer, worked in a totally different way, used a totally different part of your brain and it opened up a computer world for a lot of people who thought differently.
You were buying a computer with an installed base of one.
You had to think differently to do that.
And I think you still have to think differently to buy an Apple computer.
Uh and I think the people that do buy them do think differently and they are the creative spirits in this world.
They are the people that are not just out to get a job done, they're out to change the world and they're out to change the world using whatever great tools they can get.
And we make tools for those kinds of people.
So, hopefully what you've seen here today are some beginning steps that give you some confidence that we too are going to think differently and serve the people that have been buying our products since the beginning because a lot of times people think they're crazy, but in that craziness we see genius and those are the people we're making tools for.
Thank you very much.
**[Audience]**: [Applause]

documents.title: Macworld New York 2002
documents.speaker: Steve Jobs
documents.content:
Welcome to Macworld New York. We are uh really thrilled to be here. We got some great stuff this morning too. It's going to be a long show but a good show. So let me start off with our Switchers campaign, which you just saw some fun fun ads of. Uh we our research shows us that there are a lot of people that use Windows that want to switch to a Mac, but they're a little concerned about this or that. And we thought, how can we best get them to take the next step? And the best way we thought of was to have people just like them who had switched tell them about the experience and what it was like. And that's what the Switchers campaign is all about. These are real people uh telling their story. How successful has it been so far? Well, the stuff we know, we set up a website uh and in uh a little over a month since June 10th, we've had 1.7 million unique visitors to that website. And since we can tell whether they come in on a PC or a Mac, I'm pleased to report to you that 60% of those or about a million of them are running Windows.

Another thing we're seeing is we're seeing products start to come out like this product from a company called Detto, which they're announcing at the show today called Move to Mac. It's got software that runs on your PC that sucks all the files out, all your preferences and all your files and helps you burn actually they have a USB cable in the box. You hook it up to your Mac and you run some software on your Mac and it takes those files off your PC and puts them all in the appropriate places on the Mac for I think it's $59. So there's some products like this coming out too.

The response we've had to this campaign has been off the charts and you're going to see a lot more of it because we think there's a lot more switchers out there. Now, one of the places we're really seeing this very viscerally is our retail stores. We're seeing people walk into the stores with the Switcher ads under their arms saying, tell me more. And as you know, we have 31 stores now. I'm really pleased to report that in these 31 stores, we're seeing over 100,000 visitors a week. We had 130,000 last week. Now, to put that in perspective, this Macworld is the largest computer show on the East Coast. And yet, in our 31 stores today, we're seeing two Macworlds worth of visitors every week. That's 100 Macworlds every year. 5 million visitors a year. And some of them are buying more than one computer.

We're seeing small business customers, education customers come into the store. This one in particular is buying 25 iBooks. It's the best buying experience that we know of in the world. We're opening our 32nd store tomorrow.

Apple Soho. And we we are so proud to be in New York City. This is our first store in New York City. And um it's at the corner of Prince and Green Street in Soho. This is the subway stop in case you might want to go go there. We've been in construction for a while, big barricade up in the front. And uh it's a perfect building for us. It's in 100-year-old building that's an old post office. And it's uh New York post office. Matter of fact, the post office is still in the back fourth of the building and we're in the front three fourths of the building. And it's called Station A. 100 years ago, they were thinking about us. Station A. And when you walk in this beautiful old building, it's pretty wonderful on the inside. I'd suggest you go check it out. Beautiful skylight to get some natural light in the store, all of our products displayed. And to get you upstairs, we we built this really beautiful staircase all out of glass. It's an engineering marvel in itself. And we have a genius, we have two genius bars upstairs, 40 feet of genius bars. It's been the most popular thing in our stores. We have more software titles than we've ever had before. We have the best and biggest kids section we've ever had before. So it's worth going to check out. It opens tomorrow at 8:00 a.m. If you really want to get in, you might want to get there a little early. Apple Soho. Okay.

So let's get into the technology. I want to start with Mac OS 10. There have been some questions raised about how many people are actually using Mac OS 10 lately. Well, let's talk about it. How many active users do we have? We got a lot. We've got, we've grown from under a half a million active users a year ago to two and a half million active users today. This is a very accurate number. We have several ways to triangulate this and they all point to two and a half million active users. But let's add on the next two quarters of this year because we think over the next two quarters, we're going to double that to 5 million active users by the end of this year. As you know, in January, we switched all the new Macs we ship out of Apple to boot up in Mac OS 10. And we just finished some research that answers the question, what percentage of those people who've bought new Macs in the last six months are choosing to keep Mac OS 10 as their boot OS? And the answer across all our product lines, 77% on average. And so we are very confident that we are going to hit 5 million active users by the end of the year. We are right on top of our predictions on these numbers. And that represents 20% of our installed base going from 0 to 20% in 24 months. That is the fastest OS transition we know of in history. Faster than anything Apple has done, faster than anything Microsoft has done. And so we're pretty proud of that and we think the Mac OS transition is going well.

And of course, at this stage, it's being driven by applications and we're seeing some great news there too. We've gone from under 500 applications 15 months ago to 3,500 applications today, native in Mac OS 10. And there's some new ones too being announced at the show. Alias Wavefront is announcing Maya 4.5 here at the show on Mac first. Now, why are they announcing it at Macworld? Why would they announce Maya a whole new release of Maya at Macworld? Because Maya on the Mac has gone from 0% of their business when they announced it 9 months ago to 25% of their business today in 9 months. How many software developers would like to grow their software business by 25% in 9 months these days? I think a lot. Another developer, Blizzard came out with a wonderful product, Warcraft. Warcraft came out about two weeks ago simultaneously on Mac OS 10 and Windows. And this is exactly what we're trying to see with games and we're starting to really see the game momentum pick up on the Mac OS 10 operating platform. Adobe introducing a new release of elements and this is pretty cool because as you know in iPhoto, you can set it so when you double click on a picture, it opens up any application. You can set it to open up elements and then you can do things like color correction and really cool things in elements, but they've put something in elements where when you're done, it'll send it right back to iPhoto. So you can round trip through elements from iPhoto to elements right back to iPhoto. It's really nice. And last one I want to highlight today is Real Networks. We've all wanted the Real Player on Mac OS 10 and it's my pleasure to introduce Rob Glaser, the chairman and CEO of Real Networks. Give us some good news.

Welcome Rob.

Thanks.

Well, there's a lot of great real content out there on the net and now we're all going to be able to watch it on Mac OS 10. So thanks Rob. So, Mac OS 10, 10.1, it's been an incredibly successful release. So what's next? This.

This is Jaguar, the next release of Mac OS 10. We're officially announcing it today, version 10.2.

This is what it's going to look like.

It's the most beautiful CD we've ever made. Pixar rendered the fur by the way.

Mac OS 10 Jaguar has over 150 major new features in it. And uh let let me go through a few of them. First of all, it's Unix based as you know. What you may not know is that Apple has become the number one supplier of Unix in the world. Bigger than Sun, bigger than Linux, bigger than anyone. But we don't want to rest on that. We think we have one of the best versions of Unix out there. Jaguar makes it even better with a whole bunch of cool new Unix things. We're not going to go into them today, but things like FreeBSD 4.4, IPV6, LDAP open directory structures, etc. So we think we've got the best, most advanced version of Unix out there and we are now number one. We're also doing work for Windows. We we have a lot of customers that coexist in mixed environments and we want to be an even better client on a Windows network. So we've added SMB browsing, active directory support and VPN support if you want to VPN into your Windows networks.

We've got major enhancements to the Finder. First of all, it's multithreaded, so it's much, much faster. Second of all, number one request, spring loaded folders. And something that's going to prove incredibly useful, integrated search. So I'd like to now ask Phil Schiller, our senior vice president of worldwide product marketing to come on up. Phil's going to help me with the demos today. Phil, show us the new Finder.

Thanks Phil. The next thing we've done in Jaguar is to add a lot in universal access so we don't leave anybody behind on Mac OS 10. We've added some really cool things using the quartz graphics of zooming, a screen reader, full keyboard access and visual notification. We don't have time to go through those things today, but you can see them in the booth right after the keynote. Next up is QuickTime 6. QuickTime 6 is built into Jaguar. Now, we released QuickTime 6 on Monday of this week, right? A day and a half ago, Monday afternoon. In a day and a half, we've had over 1 million downloads of QuickTime 6. QuickTime 6 is the first MPEG4 solution uh out there and the demand looks to be very high. Now what's this all about MPEG4? Well, our industry has benefited enormously by some standards that we all use. TCPIP in communications, HTML for the internet and the web, MP3 ushered in the digital audio revolution and MPEG2, which is the video that's used on every DVD player and on every DVD disc that's bringing us this sensational quality. And these standards are really important. They bind our industry together. The next big one is brought to us by the same people that did MPEG2 that we use in our DVD players and it's called MPEG4. It is the best digital video out there and the world is jumping on it. We're not going to have these islands of proprietary video anymore. Everybody's going to jump on the MPEG4 bandwagon except for Microsoft probably. But we are jumping on it with both feet. Now, for the video in MPEG4, they've adopted the best audio in the world, the best audio codec in the world, better than what we've got, better than Windows Media audio, better than anything and it's called AAC. It was invented by the folks at Dolby and it's part of the MPEG4.


---

## Part 2

standard. And we've embraced both of those in QuickTime 6, and we've added instant on streaming. So Phil, let's see a demo of QuickTime 6 if you will.
Thanks Steve. Uh we have a live stream actually going on the internet right now if you don't know where people are watching on QuickTime. So hello in Iceland. Um they are uh there's there's actually about, you know, around 50,000 people that come to the show here. There's just as many people right now watching on the internet in a QuickTime stream, over 50,000. And with that, half are watching using the standard QuickTime we've had to date. And for the first time today, half are also trying out the brand new QuickTime 6 streaming in MPEG-4. This has never been done before in the industry. So a very big event for MPEG-4. So now let me show you off some of these great features of QuickTime 6 using MPEG content. There's both video and audio. I want to do some side by side taste tests for you. First, let's look at audio. I'm going to open up an audio file, a music song, and this song is recorded that I've just opened in straight off the CD. No no extra compression applied. It takes 1.3 megabytes a second to play this and it's um in in the AIFF format for those people who know about those things. I'm going to open up the same song again now using that brand new AAC codec that Steve mentioned. And it's recorded at a tenth the data rate. It's a tenth the size. And what I'm going to do is I'm going to play them at the same time and tab back and forth between them and so you can hear one and then the other at the same time and you can judge for yourself what they sound like. You can tell which one is playing at any time by the little lights in the in the Mac OS 10 window. When the window is lit up, you know, that's the one you're listening to. So the top one is uncompressed CD music. The bottom one is AAC audio. So let's start them together.

So that's back and forth, AAC and uh raw uncompressed audio. And I don't know about you, but I can't tell the difference and this stereo is a lot nicer than what I have in my home.

So that's QuickTime 6 in every copy of Sherlock and on the web today. Sherlock. Jaguar. Next up, Sherlock 3. We've completely rewritten Sherlock to evolve Sherlock's channels into internet services. Now what are internet services? We're hearing a lot about this. Normally our interface to the internet is a browser. We go onto the internet with a browser and we click and click and click and click and try to get what we want. And yet on the other end of that internet is a server. And if we wrote more intelligent clients, we could get what we wanted in a much more intelligent way. And so most of the work on internet services is business to business stuff. So, 90s music where the play count, I played it at least 20 times and I've rated it four or five stars. And take all that music and pick 50 songs by random and put them in this playlist. Isn't that cool? I can make a playlist that says, I want a gigabyte of songs that I've never listened to at all in a playlist so I can put it on my iPod and listen to it on the train. Right? Stuff like that. Smart playlists. So, let me go ahead and give you a demo of this. It's sweet.

**[Steve Jobs]**: Let's get out of mail here. iChat. Launch iTunes 3. All righty. So, this is iTunes 3. Looks the same, just as easy to use. And uh you know, I can pick any song. Play it. Same as always. Now, let me just go let me find a song uh here. Let me just uh drag let me find one that's got a play count of zero here. Okay. It's got a play count of zero and I'm going to drag the song to the end so we don't have to listen to it. And when I'm finished listening to the song, you'll watch this play count automatically increase to one as it goes to play the next song. I can also rate this song. I can say what is it, you know, how many stars do I want on it? Zero to five. Let's say we'll put four stars on the song and now I've rated it four stars. I can sort my songs by rating and uh look at the ones that I think are the best. I can sort them by play count or anything I want. Very, very simple. So, now let me go and make a smart playlist. I'm going to make a playlist here, smart playlist. And I'm going to say uh I love Bob Dylan. So, I'm going to say artist contains Dylan. I can put as many artists in there as I want. But I like Bob Dylan. This is now a playlist of every Dylan song I have. And if I add new ones, they will automatically join this playlist. I can go say, well, this is great, but I want to enhance that playlist a little bit. Uh I want to limit it to uh 10 songs of selected at random. And so now I've got 10 songs selected at random. As a matter of fact, if I get rid of one, if I say I don't like that one, it'll immediately put another one in because it's got to have 10 songs selected at random. Just keep replacing it. Okay. I can um I can even go and I can say, fine, take this playlist and I'll switch over to advanced. It'll preserve everything I've typed in and say, okay, I want another one where it says um my rating uh is uh let's say is greater than three stars. So, I want four and five star Dylan songs selected at random and uh that's what I'm going to get. So, let me go show you another one. I can go into 60s music here. And uh this is all my 60s music. I've got a hard day's night here which is not in here uh right now. And I can just drag a hard day's night to my library and what you will see is you will see that immediately getting added to my 1960s music smart playlist because hard day's night is from the 1960s. And again, I'm going to make one last smart playlist for you here. I'm going to say um I want to make a smart playlist. I'll go into advanced where I say, I want to limit it to uh 500 and rather than songs, I've got gigabytes, megabytes, hours, minutes, whatever I want. 500 megabytes of songs um where my um actually I've got to do this in advance. I am in advance, sorry. 500 megabytes of songs where no. Got to do it up here, I'm afraid. Play count is zero and 500 megabytes selected at random. And this will give me 500 megabyte playlist with songs I have never listened to and I'm going to listen to those on my iPod. Boom. There it is. That's how easy it is to create smart playlists. It's very, very simple. And that is a preview of iTunes 3.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: So, super easy to use just like always. You can rate your songs, you have automatic play counts. There's a whole bunch of other new fields as well. But the biggest thing is smart playlists. This is going to really, I think, change the way we listen to music. We have audible.com support. Really wonderful product. Only runs on Mac OS 10. It's a free download at apple.com starting today.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: So, that's iTunes 3. Now, what would iTunes be without iPod? So, let's talk about iPod. iPod has been a giant hit for us. And we're going to make it even better today. We've got the 5 gigabyte iPod, 1,000 songs in your pocket, sells for $399. As of today, that's $299. We want to bring it down so even more people can afford it.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: The 10 gigabyte iPod, 2,000 songs in your pocket, 4.99. As of today, it is 3.99. But for the 10 gigabyte iPod, there's even more because we have made it even thinner. This is the five. We've made it about 10% thinner, which matters a lot when you're carrying something like this around in your pocket. And we have gone to a totally new solid state scroll wheel. As you know, for those of you that have an iPod, the scroll wheel is one of the coolest features of the iPod. It lets you navigate around super fast and super easy. We've actually gone to a no moving part solid state one that feels like glass. It is so cool. And that's on every 10 gigabyte iPod. And we have also added a little door to protect your fire wire, which we got a lot of requests for that. We've also added a remote. Just plug it in, you can plug in any headphones into this. Volume, play pause, next previous right on the remote, very simple. And we're also adding a case. We've got a lot of requests for this too. So, a case with a belt clip, you just drop your iPod in it and with the remote, it's really, really nice. And all this comes bundled with the new 10 gigabyte iPod. But we didn't stop there because today we're introducing a 20 gigabyte iPod. 4,000 songs in your pocket, includes the case, includes the remote, the solid state scroll wheel, etc. 4.99. So, now we've got three iPod models. We've got a 5 gigabyte at 2.99, a 10 gigabyte at 3.99 and a 20 gigabyte at 4.99. 1,000, 2,000 or 4,000 songs in your pocket. We also have some new software on them that's even better. We've added some really great features in the software. In addition to being able to browse your music by artist, album or song, we've added genre and composer. Our classical customers said, I want to find Bach, not the performer. And so we've added composer and I think that's it's quite a bit better. Play counts. Your play counts will automatically get downloaded into your iPod and the play count additions from your iPod will get then uploaded back to iTunes to the then current play counts so that every time you play something on the iPod, it's recorded in play counts on your iTunes as well. We download smart playlists into the iPod. iPod has sound check, so play all the songs back at the same volume if you want and it supports audible.com with round trip bookmarking. So, you can listen to something on iTunes, stop, when you pick up on your iPod, you pick up right where you left off, you stop, you sync back to iTunes, you pick up right where you left off on your iPod back on iTunes. So, we've got a new menu structure for the iPod as well. So, let me show this to you in a demo. This is our iPod here. And of course, we have playlists just like always. So, we can go look at our music by playlists. But we have this new menu called browse. And this is how you can browse your music. You can browse it by artist. You get a list of all your artists here. You can browse it by album. You get a list of all your albums here. You can browse it by songs, of course, alphabetical list of songs. But the two new ones are genres. So, we've got all the different genres of music that you can browse your your your music by, including spoken word here. And composers. So, you can browse them by composers, whatever you'd like. You know, going to a composer, pick a song, etc. Very, very simple.


---

## Part 5

**[Steve Jobs]**: So, that's browse. But we've added something new to iPod called Extras. Let's go find out what's in it. Well, contacts. We've seen contacts before and we can have our contacts in our iPod. So I can say, you know, let's say Fred Anderson here, and here's all of Fred's contacts. Here's Avi. Here's Avi's contacts here. Right on my iPod. So if I need a list of contacts with me, I don't have to take any other device. But here's something new. Calendars. You can have a calendar on your iPod. As a matter of fact, you can have as many calendars as you want from iCal. And so you can drag down any iCal standard calendars. Let's take a look at them all. And here's what it looks like and the scroll wheel comes in really handy here because look at this.
**[Audience]**: [Laughter]
**[Steve Jobs]**: I can just scroll through the months. Let me go back to today. Boom. And I can go into today and see all the things I've got to do. If I want to better look at any of them, I can just go right in here and take a look. So we've got calendars in iPod now along with contacts. And of course, we have a clock because when you have a calendar, you need to know what day it is. And so we've added a clock in here. And we've made the game very accessible. So if you want to play the game, you don't have to look for it anymore. And so this is the new iPod software and it's really, really nice. I'd encourage you to look at it.
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Steve Jobs]**: Genres, composers, contacts, calendars. We've got three iPods starting now at $2.99. These will be in the stores in early August. Boxes look like this. And in addition to this, we're going to sell the accessories for existing iPod owners for $39 each. So if you want to buy a case or you want to buy a pair of headphones and the remote, $39 you can pick them up. So the new iPod, three different models. But there's one more little thing. Charles Haddad of Business Week recently speculated, what if the iPod did work with PCs?
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Steve Jobs]**: Could it become a Trojan horse that steals inside Fortress Windows and wins over diehard PC fans? In other words, could it show them how good it could really be? And we think yes. And so today we are introducing iPods for Windows.
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Steve Jobs]**: And we partnered with one of the most popular music players on Windows, Music Match to do it. And we've worked with them and made the iPod so it will auto sync with their Music Match software. And yes, it's not iTunes, but it's better than anything on the Windows side. So we have auto syncing. We're going to sell the same three models at the same prices for Windows. We even include a six-pin to four-pin firewire connector for Windows machines because they generally that's what they have. These Windows models will be in the stores in late August because we want to take care of the Mac customers first. And this is the new iPod line.
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Steve Jobs]**: Okay. Now we're going to do something really fun. I want to introduce what I think is a landmark groundbreaking app. And I think this app is going to change a lot of things. We're going to look back on this app as the the beginning of something pretty cool and pretty new. Now that app is called iSync. The purpose of iSync is to synchronize your digital life. Now we've got the best address book in the world now. We've got the best calendar in the world now. And when you're on your Mac, life is going to be great. But what about when you're not on your Mac? What you want to do is take these things with you. So you have this information at your fingertips even when you're not on your Mac, God forbid. So what, what is the most popular device in the world? It's the cell phone. And there is a new generation of cell phones now that's a lot different. These are not your father's cell phones anymore. They are GPRS, so they are always on for data. They've got color screens on them. They've got organizers built into them. They've got address books and calendars in them just waiting for data. They work off an open standard called SyncML and we've joined this group. It's a good standard. And they've got Bluetooth built in them. So this is a whole new generation of cell phones and they synchronize. And we think this is so cool that we want to add it to the digital hub. This is the coolest device since the digital camera that we added in January. So we're going to make some room for it and we are going to add this new generation of cell phones to our digital hub. Now while we're at it, we might as well pick up the Palm.
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Steve Jobs]**: And and you saw calendars and contacts on the iPod. Wouldn't it be cool if they auto synced every time you plugged in your iPod the same way your music does? So let's add the iPod here too. We got three devices now that we want to sync calendars and address books to. But the most popular of these of course is the phone. And some people go, well, I don't get it. Why do I want to sync my phone with my computer? Well, because you get to enter data on a big display and a full-size keyboard. If you ever try to enter 100 numbers into this tiny little phone, you go crazy. This way you get to do it like you enter most of your data. But even more so, have you ever lost a phone?
**[Audience]**: [Laughter]
**[Steve Jobs]**: Oh, you've just lost your life. All your contacts are on that thing. You are toast. Well, if you lose your phone this way, you don't lose your life because all your data is safely on your computer and you've still got it. And the third thing is we go buy a new phone, rather than taking hours to enter in the data, you just sync it up and you load the data in seconds. So these are three of the many reasons why you want to sync your phone with your computer.
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Steve Jobs]**: So we want to sync all three of these devices and that's exactly what iSync does. This is iSync and what it does is it shows you all the devices that are connected. Firewire for the iPod, USB for the Palm, wireless Bluetooth for your cell phones, whatever, however they're connected, they show up. And you can examine each one. You can set iPod, I want to synchronize all contacts. You can just choose certain groups, synchronize all calendars and automatically synchronize whenever it's connected. Boom, that's how you set it up. The phone, same thing. Which contacts, which calendars and you know, some of the memories in the phones aren't that big. You can decide how far in the future you want your calendar to go. Boom. And then when you want to sync, you can sync all of them, any one individually or all of them together just by pushing one button, boom, they're all syncing. Takes less than a minute and they're synced. And it's really, really cool and I'd like to show you now. Okay. So I've got iSync up here and again, the first thing I'd like to say is, you know, Bluetooth has arrived. Um and we are now detecting phones with Bluetooth automatically putting them up here in iSync. And I can go through and configure things as I said. I can choose, you know, certain contacts to synchronize or all of them, certain calendars or just some of them. And I can say, yeah, sync to my iPod whenever I plug it in. And I can do the same thing with the phone, same sort of thing and how far ahead I want to go with my calendar. And what I've got over here, let's get the phone up picture in picture. Let's go ahead and get that phone up. Okay. So I've got a phone right here and this is a brand new phone. I've turned on the Bluetooth so the Bluetooth has been recognized, but as you see, the phone book is empty on this phone, right? And it asks me, do I want to load numbers in from a SIM card? I don't have a SIM card anyway. So I'm going to say no, I don't. And this phone is running on the Singular network. Singular is got about 30% of the country now including New York City and all of the West Coast running on GPRS. It's fantastic. And so what I'm going to do is just sync with the phone. And I'm going to put all of my contacts from my address book into the phone. So all I do, what do I do? I just push this button. And now, whoops. Boom. I am syncing with the phone and you can see it sync right there. Transferring my whole address book over. Calendars. Boom. Done. And now what I'm going to do is I'm going to see if this worked. I'm going to go down to my address book and I'm going to let's say pick Avi here and I'm going to push a button and let's go see if that calls Avi. I've got Avi down with a microphone on his cell phone here. Hopefully it's going to ring. Is that your, is that your beep? Well, that's Avi's beep. He's a little strange, but
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Steve Jobs]**: Great. So, this is iSync. And we think it's the beginning of something very, very big. What we call it is Mac to Mobile, right? You want to get your Mac seamlessly syncing bidirectionally with all of your mobile devices and that's what we're doing. And again, this is the beginning of something really big with a new era of cell phones. And we think the cell phone joining the digital hub, syncing with the Mac is going to be something really, really good. One of the companies that's in the vanguard of these new phones is Sony Ericsson was formed by a joint venture between Sony and Ericsson and they're coming on very, very strong. And I'm very, very proud to have Mr. Harison, the president of Sony Ericsson here today and I'd like to welcome him to Mac World for the first time.
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Speaker 2]**: Thank you.
**[Speaker 2]**: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Uh and thank you very much for Steve for inviting me to this exciting Mac World here today. Uh you remember that when we first talk about the Apple's extending its digital hub strategy to include mobile phones, I was immediately convinced that this is wonderful uh opportunities. It is wonderful for me to see the best mobile phone seamlessly connecting to the uh applications on the Macintosh. Today, I believe Apple can proudly say it is a leader in easy to use connectivity between the personal computer and and mobile phones. Our products complement each other extremely well. It is also great to have Singular, one one of my biggest customer, backing this with a new high speed network. The first Sony Ericsson branded product T68i is one of the most powerful mobile phone in the market today. In addition to the application you have just seen in the demo Steve made, uh with the extra screen and the camera attachment, it was the first world complete GSM solutions for taking and sending photos, pictures instantly to any anywhere, anybody in the world. The top priority of Sony Ericsson and Apple is to make sure our product work together as smoothly as possible with minimal setup and very easy to use applications. Both company understand the open technology standards are essential to make this happen. We are delighted that Apple has adopted the Bluetooth and the SyncML standards. Sony Ericsson is reading the development of both technologies and has introduced several products supporting them. Today, many more manufacturers across a whole range of industries are releasing Bluetooth products. In the PC industry, Apple has once again taken the lead by embedding Bluetooth support in its operating system. As you can see, I am very much excited about the cooperation between Apple, Sony Ericsson and Singular. Today, we have reached an important milestone. The dream of easy easy wireless connectivity between personal computer, mobile phones and networks is now reality. This is a result of three companies sharing the vision and the passion to deliver. The demonstrations that you have seen today are just first example of what we will be able to do. As form become even more advanced, the range of applications and their impact will be even more impressive. This is the only the beginning of fascinating journey. Watch this space. Thank you very much for Steve your commitment and thank you very much for your attention. Thank you.
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Steve Jobs]**: You know, a year from now, every phone is going to have these capabilities, but Sony Ericsson really is in the lead right now and they make some great stuff. And Harison is right. We're working so well with them and we're just at the beginning. We want to do things like be able to sync up certain iPhoto albums with your phone so that you have your pictures on your phone that you want etcetera etcetera. It's just the beginning and it's very, very exciting. The third part of this equation though, beyond the Mac and the phone is the network and the networks are being retooled for GPRS. And a company that's in the lead is Singular Wireless. And I'm very happy to invite Stephen Carter, the CEO of Singular Wireless up on stage at his first Mac World to say a few words.
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Speaker 3]**: Thanks Steve. Well, I guess that it's uh somewhat inevitable that a a wireless company that believes in the power of self-expression should one day come across a company that thinks different. And uh certainly, thank you Steve for the opportunity to get here today. We are on the the dawn of a new era, I think in wireless. Not not your father's wireless phones, a great expression, I think uh I'm going to maybe plagiarize that a little bit in the future. But I it really is where we are today. Wireless is not about voice anymore exclusively. And why is that? Well, one of the key things is the networks are changing. We're investing billions of dollars in a new network that's going to provide increasingly fast, always on data capability. In fact, by next year, the GPRS GPRS will be enhanced again to something called Edge, which in theory can produce 470 kilobytes per second and in actual working conditions easily 150. So we've got networks that are changing. We've got devices like this fantastic phone from Sony Ericsson, the T68, the color screen, the icons, the incredible functionality in it. So two things going for us. But there's a third thing and I call it the who gives a damn factor. And the who gives a damn factor is applications. And at Singular, we've been running a developer uh program now for a couple of years, I guess and the number of developers coming in working on applications has increased steadily. We have now nearly 5,000 uh developers enrolled. But when Steve called and talked about this particular application, we really got excited. We really started to think in terms of everybody's looking for the killer app. Now no one's found the killer app yet. I'm not sure if this is the killer app, but it comes a darn sight closer than many that we've seen before. And so we're very, very excited about this. The other thing we got very excited about was that phrase open standards because I think we're in a position now where wireline, wireless, computing, it's all coming together and it should come together. But to enable that, we have to have open standards and we applaud Apple and Sony Ericsson for embracing that concept. So as we look out now, there are so many applications that Bluetooth and the other technologies can enable. We're very excited about it. We think the the synchronization of the address book, the calendar etcetera is just one of the the keys to allowing people to change their lives in a mobile sense. And at the end of the day, I think what really uh is going to make all of this sell is the ability of all of these companies to make the complex simple. Something that we try to do at Singular. I know is at the heart of your philosophy and looking at the way that Sony Ericsson's now developing their user interfaces is definitely top of their minds. So again, I thank you for the opportunity to be here today. Thank you all and uh buy lots of GPRS phones.
**[Audience]**: [Applause]
**[Steve Jobs]**: So, we are adding the phone to the digital hub. We think this is going to be a really big deal. Now, there's one other time when you'd really love to be able to synchronize stuff.

---

## Part 6

**[Steve Jobs]**: And that is, if you have more than one computer, right? How many of us change something on our computer at work and get home and find out, Jesus, it's not there, it's on my work computer, right? I do it very frequently. Wouldn't it be great if you could synchronize your address book and your calendar between your multiple computers? Well, this is another thing that we're going to be adding to .Mac. We're going to add .Mac to iSync. And so if you're a member of .Mac, you're going to be able to sync your computer to our internet servers. And do it hourly, do it every 15 minutes, do it daily. And so you sync your computer before you leave work, you sync your home computer when you get home, and everything you did all day is on your machine at home. You have multiple machines and they're frequently syncing with this, they're going to stay in sync. And this is going to be added for .Mac members as well. So all you do is push one button and sync everything in your life, including your multiple computers for your address books and your calendars, and who knows what else down the road. So that's iSync, work and home computer synchronized. So Mac to mobile.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: iSync, iSync runs on top of Jaguar. It's going to be available in September. It is going to be a free download at apple.com, and I hope all of you have a chance to try it out.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: So, digital hub. We've added the phone, we've added the palm. Got a great story here, and the thing that really makes this story great, of course, is the applications that we've written behind this. These are all written at Apple. And there's some amazing applications like iTunes 3, blow away. You've got to try this. iPhoto, best digital photography app in the world. iMovie, best consumer video editing application in the world. iDVD, the finest way to make DVDs in the world. iSync, a totally breakthrough application that is going to open a whole new door of applications for us. And then applications like iCal, the best calendar that we've ever seen on a personal computer. Address book, the best database and application for managing contacts we've ever seen. Mail with junk mail filtering that is the first real breakthrough we've seen in that area. iChat, the best instant messaging on any personal computer, and Sherlock 3, the beginning of internet services for the rest of us. All of these applications are bundled or free. And there is nothing like them on the Windows side of the fence. And that's why we think that this is going to grow and have even more force as we move forward with these amazing new applications. So thank you.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: But there was, wait a minute, there is one more thing I forgot about. That's the iMac. I wanted to talk about the iMac for just a minute. The iMac has been really great for us. I think customers just love them with the flat screen, the super crisp flat screen displays, the really fast G4 processors, and the super drives. You can burn your own DVDs that play in consumer DVD players. And its design is just stunning where you can move the display anywhere you want. And the feedback we've gotten on this has been fantastic. Walt Mossberg, not an easy journalist to please, said, "The new flat panel iMac is the best consumer desktop PC on the market and costs less than a Windows PC with the same specs." He said that last month. So we're really happy with the iMac. I've got some fun data to share with you. We sell three models. The high-end one has a super drive in it. Burn your own DVDs, as I said. I'm really pleased to report that the percentage of all the Macs sold with a super drive, 50%. Customers want the super drive. It is the most requested thing we've got in the iMac line in terms of get me one with a super drive, which is showing up in the sales stats. And that model sells for $18.99. As of today, we're lowering the price back down to $17.99, so we can try to reach even more people with it. But this doesn't address the number one request we've gotten for the iMac. The number one request is for a larger display.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: And the iMac's got a fantastic 15-inch display, but today we are introducing a model with a 17-inch landscape display. Let's go ahead and take a look at it. It is gorgeous. It's really beautiful. It's giant. And again, you can move it anywhere you like, even when it's twirling. We've got a 17-inch display on this. That 17-inch LCD has the same viewing area as a 19-inch CRT right on your desktop, adjustable to any angle right in front of you. It's incredible. And it's got 1440 by 900 pixels, which is 64% more pixels than the 15-inch iMac. Now, keep in mind that a cinema display is only 1600 by 1024. This is most of a cinema display right here on this iMac, adjustable at any angle. And of course, it's in a cinematic aspect ratio, which our customers have come to love. It's really wonderful what you can see with this wider screen. We've also increased the graphics to Nvidia GeForce 4.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: So it's got really fast graphics on it. And so a 17-inch LCD, 800 MHz G4, quarter gigabyte of memory, 80 gigabytes of disk, Nvidia GeForce 4MX and a super drive, $19.99.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: We will have these in the store two weeks from now. I urge you to check them out. They are truly remarkable. So this is what I had for you today. And in ending, I would just like to do two things. One, I would like to thank everybody in our software groups, both Avi's group and Cena's groups for these incredible operating system and applications that we're seeing. These guys have worked really, really hard over the last year, and I'd like to give them a round of applause.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: And secondly, I'd like to thank all the thank all the folks in John Rubinstein's hardware group, Tim Cook's operations group for the new hardware, the new iPods, and the new iMacs you're seeing here today. Again, they've been working around the clock, too. So thank you guys.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: We find ourselves in very challenging times across our whole economy and in particular in our industry. Our competitors are laying off thousands of people, and there is certainly cause for despair if you believe that the personal computer basically is something to do spreadsheets and word processors on and is an HTML terminal to the internet. And if that's all you think it is, then there is cause to for despair. But that's not what we think. We think different. We believe that the personal computer is undergoing a rapid evolution to be the center of our digital lives, and we have never been more excited about this stuff. And we are investing, and we are going to innovate our way through this downturn like the products you've seen here today and more coming. And when this thing turns around, we're going to be in a great place. So we're going to invest our way through this because we see the brightest future ever for the personal computer lies ahead. Thank you very much.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Music]**: If my words did glow with the gold of sunshine and my tunes were played on the harp of a star, would you lend my voice come through the music? Would you hold it near as it were your own? It's a handmade deal. The thoughts are broken. Perhaps they're better left unsung.

Walt Mossberg, a man of few words.

documents.content:
Thank you. Thanks. Well, good, good morning, everyone. And I can tell you how personally excited I am to be the one to deliver Macworld 2009's keynote to you. And I can tell you how much I appreciate you all showing up and bringing your energy and enthusiasm to this keynote. Uh, so from the bottom of my heart, thank you so much. Um,

It is, it is an incredibly exciting time at Apple. There is so much going on across all of our businesses, all around the world. And you can feel it in so many ways, but probably nowhere better than in all these incredible stores that Ron and his team has opened around the world. Here's, here's our store last year we opened in Beijing, China. Incredibly beautiful place.

Here's Munich, Germany. We opened it to crowds and crowds of people in Europe. And this one, and this photo is just unbelievable. This is Sydney, Australia.

A beautiful city, has a beautiful Apple store. But just look at the crowds of people lining up in that store. And, and I don't know about you, when I look at this photo, and I look at that big, gorgeous, glowing Apple up in front of it, and I think, what other company's logo could be there in, in, could you could ever imagine in that photo? And I can't. I can't think of one company in the world that could have a store that beautiful, such incredible customers coming, bringing all their energy and love to, to visit with our stores and talk to the sales consultant and get help with the geniuses and do one-on-one training. I couldn't imagine any other company delivering something like that. Each and every week, now 3.4 million customers visit an Apple store around the world. That's unbelievable, unbelievable. And, I'm sorry, I have to make the comparison. That's 100 Macworlds each and every week going on around the world in our Apple stores. So it's no wonder, no wonder that these, the, what's happening with these stores is, it's just so important to us. And they do it because they're such a great place to shop, but they're, they also come because they want to get their hands on and touch and try out an iPhone, an iPod Touch, and yes, the Mac. The Mac has had a resurgence and excitement and interest with customers bigger than we've ever had before. And I tell you, that means so much to us because it is an important part of our business. So today, what I'm going to talk to you about is all about the Mac. I think that's appropriate at Macworld that we talk about the Mac.

Last fiscal year, we had the biggest year in the history of the company in Mac sales. We sold 9.7 million Macs. We're so proud of that. Everyone worked so hard and we did it by growing over twice as fast as the rest of the industry. And that's because we have the best product line we've ever had for the Mac. Up and down the line, amazing, great, beautiful products. The hardware, the Leopard, Mac OS 10 operating system, all the amazing applications, it's just tremendous. Well, if you want to hear some new things today, and I assume some people want to hear a few new things today.

Well, I've got three new things to tell you about. And I'm really excited to be the one to tell you about each one of these things because they're really special. First, number one, an entire new version of iLife. iLife '09.

Now, hopefully a lot of you know that iLife has become one of the reasons people buy a Mac today. Because we all use these incredible applications. They're so helpful, they're so useful and fun. iPhoto, iMovie, GarageBand, iWeb, iDVD. There's nothing like it on any other computer platform. And as much as some people up north might think that they have some things that are pretty good, there's nothing as good as iLife on a personal computer. So what's new in iLife '09? First up, a brand new version of iPhoto, iPhoto '09. Last year, we introduced an idea to a technology in iPhoto called Events. So not only could you see the thousands of photo in photo of your photos in iPhoto, you could look at them by events. And that took thousands of photos and made it down to a manageable couple hundred events because they're based on time, a birthday party you attend, a vacation you go on. It's turned out to be incredibly useful. Customers use it, love it. It's just a natural intuitive way to use all your photos. Well, this year with iPhoto '09, we're adding two events another way for you to manage your photos called Faces. It's really powerful.
