documents.content:
Good morning.

Thank you.

It's an important day.

Thanks.

Uh, welcome to our World, Worldwide Developers Conference 2005.

Today's an important day.

We've got some great stuff for you today.

But I want to start off, uh, with uh, just some stats on the conference.

Uh, there's over 3800 attendees today here.

Uh, this may be the largest developers conference in Apple's history.

I'm not sure, but I know it's the largest in the last decade.

So welcome.

There are developers here from over 45 countries, including China and India.

And uh, we've got some great stuff for you.

Over 110 lab sessions, and of those 39 are hands-on, where you're sitting there at machines during the labs.

Uh, 95 presentation sessions, and uh, over 500 Apple engineers are going to be on site this week to help you.

So, we have um, we have our Apple uh, uh, design awards, and uh, this year we've gotten more entries than ever before, over 400 entries, and it just shows the vibrancy of uh, of the developer community out there.

It's fantastic.

But the number that blows my mind, uh, for Apple developer connection members, we have now crossed a half a million members.

Isn't that amazing?

So, the developer community at Apple is thriving.

Uh, I'd like to give you a quick update on retail next.

Um, Apple retail, we've got 109 stores now around the world.

We are seeing over a million visitors per week.

A million visitors per week.

And over the last 12 months, uh, the retail stores and the online store have sold over a half a billion dollars worth of your products.

So, they're doing really well for us.

We've um, we've opened a lot of stores like this in malls.

Uh, we've also opened some what are called flagship stores.

Uh, this one being in London.

I don't know if you've been to the London store, but it's hopping.

It's a phenomenal store.

I was there about two weeks ago on a Tuesday afternoon.

There were over 250 customers in the store.

Tuesday afternoon at 2:00.

So it it was amazing.

Now, our retail group is constantly trying to find the best real estate to locate stores.

And they made a video to show at a real estate convention, and I saw it and I I nabbed it because I wanted to show it to you.

So could we run that video now?

[Music playing]

So that's a little update on Apple retail.

We think it's the best buying experience in the world for personal computers.

Now, I'd like to give you an update on the iPod and our music efforts.

Uh, you know, the iPod is really uh, entered popular culture in America.

You know that when you're lucky enough to get on the cover of the New York.

So we were thrilled with that.

And uh, that's reflected in in iPod sales.

Uh, this is the cumulative iPod sold, and at the end of last quarter, at the end of March, we'd sold about 16 million iPods.

And that's also reflected in the iPod's market share of all types of MP3 players, including flash and hard drive, everything, 76% market share.

So we're thrilled with that.

Now, as you know, iTunes goes with the iPod, and we just recently crossed 430 million songs sold and downloaded in iTunes.

We're thrilled with this, and that is again reflected in iTunes' market share.

We've gotten a lot of competition over the last nine months, and what's happened?

Our market share has gone up.

It's now 82% in the month of May.

And we recently announced something new for iTunes and iPod, and it's called podcasting.

Uh, as you know, the podcasting phenomenon is exploding right now.

And uh, podcasting, of course, is a concatenation of iPod and broadcasting.

And what is podcasting?

You know, it's been described a lot of different ways.

Um, one way has been uh, TiVo for radio.

You can download radio shows and listen to them on your computer or put them on your iPod anytime you want.

So it's just like television programs on TiVo, and that's true.

Another way it's been described is Wayne's World for radio.

Um, which means that anyone, uh, without much capital investment can make a podcast, put it on a server and get a worldwide audience for their radio show, and that's true too.

Um, we see it as the hottest thing going in radio, hotter than anything else in radio.

And as you know, what podcasting is, is that you can not only download radio shows and listen to them, you can subscribe to them.

So that every time there's a new episode, it automatically gets downloaded to your computer.

You can listen to it there, or it automatically gets synced to your iPod the next time you dock your iPod.

So it's very, very exciting.

And um, there are over 8,000 podcasts now, and this is growing really, really fast.

So that's pretty exciting.

Now, it's not just amateurs doing these things though.

These 8,000 are not all amateurs, but the pros have realized that this is huge.

And here's just a list of some of the companies doing podcasts now.

All the major radio broadcasters, the network broadcasters, major magazines, major newspapers, even major companies like Disney and Proctor and Gamble and Ford and General Motors.

So it's pretty exciting.

And so what we're doing is we're going to make this even easier because you're not going to have to go download other applications and get all sorts of stuff together to make this happen.

We're going to build it right into iTunes and iPod.

So you can subscribe to any podcast, and we're going to uh, to make it really easy.

And so right into iTunes, very simple.

But one of the most important things is how do you find these podcasts?

You want people typing URLs into iTunes?

Well, they could do that, but we're also going to build right into the iTunes music store an iPod or a podcast directory.

So that we're going to list thousands of podcasts and you'll be able to click on them, download them for free, and uh, subscribe to them right in iTunes.

So I'd just like to give you a quick peek of what this is going to look like.

Let me bring up iTunes here.

And I'm going to go to the uh, podcast homepage.

And this is the podcast directory.

And uh, we're going to list again thousands of podcasts.

Let's just go ahead and listen to one.

Uh, we can go to one here.

This is Adam Curry.

He's one of the inventors of podcasting, and you could listen to his uh,

So you could listen to an episode here, but it's much more interesting to subscribe to the podcast.

And we've now subscribed to Adam Curry's podcast.

It's flipped us up to this podcast thing right in the source list.

It's downloaded the most recent one.

If I want to download another one, I can just push a button and go download uh, one of the older episodes, and I can listen to an episode.

Okay.

Uh, so, let me give you another one.

Uh, Adam's great.

This is um, this is KCRW.

Uh, this is a show called The Treatment.

They're a public radio station in LA.

So let me go ahead and subscribe to the treatment.

And again, uh, here's another one.

I can close this one if I want to.

And let's go listen to the treatment.

So you get the idea.

These are really cool.

Some are amateur and some are pro.

Uh, one more I want to just highlight.

Uh, we're going to do one ourselves because we have new music Tuesdays when we put new music on the iTunes music store.

So we decided to do a podcast.

This is just a a test, but uh, you can subscribe to that.

And um, you know, get uh,

[Music playing]

And the nice thing about this one is as we scrub along, you'll see that the artwork changes too.

Right?

And you can go to different chapters in this thing.

You can go right to different chapters.

So, very, very simple.

And we think it's going to basically take podcasting mainstream to where anyone can do it and uh, really easy to find these podcasts, really easy to listen to them.

So we're very excited about this.

I think it's going to be one more way in which iPod and the iTunes digital music community are really at the forefront of this stuff, bringing the innovation into the marketplace.

Now, I'd like to give you uh, a little update on Mac.

Mac is doing really well right now.

Let me start off with just some figures.

If we look at growth rates, these are year-over-year unit growth rates for the last five quarters, ending in March.

Uh, and if we look at the PC market, uh, the growth has slowed down a little bit from just under 20% five quarters ago to just over 10% today.

This is again, year-over-year growth rates in terms of unit ship.

But let's look and see how the Mac's done in the same period.

Look at this.

Nine months ago, the Mac took off in terms of growth rates and it grew over 40%.

So last quarter, the Mac grew at over three times the rate of the rest of the industry, and we're pretty excited about that.

The most important thing, of course, happening in the Mac is Mac OS 10 Tiger.

I hope all of you are using it.

We shipped it recently.

I'm sure you're all using spotlight, dashboard.

We've shipped H264 based QuickTime 7.

And as a matter of fact, today we're previewing QuickTime 7 on Windows, so you'll be able to download that later on today.

So Windows users as well can get the best digital video in the world.

You know, we've shipped over a billion copies of QuickTime during its lifetime.

Over a billion copies.

And now QuickTime 7 with H264 is available on Macs and a preview released today on Windows.

You've seen the new mail with instant searching in it.

We've seen Safari with instant RSS access built right into it, and you've seen iChat AV where up to four people can do video conferencing right on the desktop with great quality.

Again, because of H264.

So Tiger, we think is the best release we've ever shipped.

And you know what?

The critics have agreed.

You know, you should the quotes, I'm sure you've seen some of them.

This is from Computer World.

Want to see what the future of personal computing looks like?

Don't wait for Microsoft to show you.

Go out and get yourself a copy of Apple's OS 10 Tiger.

It's that good.

Here's the New York Times.

Spotlight isn't just a super fast find command.

It's an enhancement that's so deep, convenient, and powerful, it threatens to reduce the 20-year-old system of nested folders to irrelevance.

Here, here.

CBSnews.com.

I remember writing an article about Lotus 123 back when the product was released during the 80s.

It may have been nearly two decades since I wrote that column, but it took spotlight less than two seconds to find it.

Business Week.

Tiger bolsters OS 10's edge as the best personal computer operating system around.

And a similar one from the Detroit Free Press.

It's the most elegant, useful, and powerful operating system I've ever used in three decades of computer ownership.

It runs circles around Windows.

And finally, Walt Mossberg, it leaves Windows XP in the dust.

So,

And I know you guys are all taking advantage of the latest greatest Tiger features in your apps and it's it's very exciting.

And I'm really pleased to report to you that this week, uh, we will deliver copies sold through retail, delivered through maintenance and shipped on the Macs since we cut over, the 2 millionth copy of Mac OS 10 Tiger.

This is the fastest, remember, it's been about six weeks since we started shipping it, and we are thrilled with this.

This is the most successful OS release ever.

And it's not just us that's been busy with Tiger.

Take a look at the the third-party stuff that's been released.

Over 400 spotlight plugins, are 40, I'm sorry, over 400 dashboard widgets and over 550 automator actions have already been posted.

And in particular, I want to focus in on these dashboard widgets.

Dashboard is one of the most exciting features of Tiger and people have done some beautiful things and I'd like to just show you a few of them now.

So let me go ahead into dashboard.

You all know dashboard.

And um, let me get a few out here.

Let me go back here.

Uh, here's a great one for Amazon.

Uh, this one doesn't just uh, take you to Amazon when you search for something, but I can search for um, let's say uh, Tiger.

And uh, it right in place goes and searches Amazon and just gives me all the stuff I might want, right?

Or iPod.

Boom.

And there's all the stuff on Amazon I might want for an iPod.

Uh, let me show you another one that's really cool.

Business Week uh, is just releasing this, I think today, but this gives me uh, up-to-date Business Week stories right here.

And so I can look and uh, you know, take a look at uh, Apple if I want to.

And there's all the stories about uh, about Apple today, and I can flip it around in the back and uh, look at top news or technology or whatever I want to do.

It's pretty cool.

So there we go.

Um, and uh, let's go on to uh, CNN has got a similar thing.

It's not as nice looking as Business Week's, but uh, does the job.

And there's all the latest CNN stories.

Um, you know, here's a cool one if you haven't seen it called countdown calendar.

So you bring up this countdown calendar and you go in the back and you fill in the date uh, that you want to count down to.

So I'm going to say 1231 2006 and I'm going to put in uh, Longhorn.

And uh, that's the days until Longhorn.

Just counts them down.

Um, here's, you know, here's a good package tracker for UPS, DHL or FedEx and uh, I was tracking a package earlier, so I can just go track a package here.

And there's my FedEx package.

Um, you know, here's a fun one, Rabbit Radio.

Uh, this finds your local uh, NPR station.

Isn't that great?

And you can just listen to it.

And you can even listen to it when dashboard's off.

Nothing is great as NPR.

Um, here's uh, let me go find another one here.

Let's see uh, here's a fun one for uh, sports enthusiasts, which is baseball scores, just sitting there scrolling.

Uh, TV tracker, I'm sure you've seen, goes and finds all the TV shows that you might want.

This is a favorite of mine, uh, Wikipedia.

Uh, for those of you who don't don't know, this is an open source encyclopedia where everybody contributes to it.

It has now become uh, one of the most robust and certainly accurate encyclopedias in the world because you've got experts from all over the world contributing to it and uh, we just look up Tiger here and uh, you can get the lowdown on uh, all kinds of tigers.

So that's Wikipedia, which is great.

And lastly, I just wanted to show you uh, Yahoo just released an updated one on their traffic and I can put uh, San Francisco, California here.

Uh, and uh, there is the traffic updates for San Francisco.

So these are just

---

## Part 2

just a few of the over 400 uh dashboard widgets that uh are available now uh on uh Tiger that you can go get.

And we just released a new site uh on the OS 10 tab of apple.com which makes it much easier to find these things.

So go check them out, they're pretty amazing.

So, OS 10 Tiger.

Now, what percent does this represent of all Mac OS users?

These 2 million copies that we've delivered so far.

They represent already 16% of the entire Mac OS 10 user base.

Panther is about half, uh about a quarter is Jaguar and about 10% are the laggards on early versions of 10.

And after six weeks, this is phenomenal.

Now, where do we expect to be when we meet again here next year?

This time next year, we expect that Tiger is going to be half of the OS 10 user base.

So we're really thrilled about that.

And if we take a look at what we've done over the last five years, we've released five major versions of OS 10 over the last five years.

In that time frame, of course, Microsoft released XP.

And looking forward, looking forward, what do we see?

Well, the next release, I'm very pleased to announce that the next release of OS 10 is going to be called Leopard.

And uh we're not going to be focusing on it at this conference today, but uh we certainly will in the future.

And uh we intend to release Leopard at the end of 2006 or early 2007 right around the time when Microsoft is expected to release Longhorn.

So that's what the future looks like and uh we look forward to telling you about Leopard.

So that's what's up for Mac OS 10 Tiger.

Now, let's go to a big topic.

Transitions.

Let's talk about transitions.

The Mac in its history has had two major transitions so far, right?

The first one, 68k to Power PC.

And that transition happened about 10 years ago in the mid 90s.

I wasn't here then, but the team then did a great job from everything I hear.

And the Power PC, the Power PC set Apple up for the next decade.

It was a good move.

The second major transition though has been even bigger.

And that's the transition from OS 9 to OS 10 that we just finished a few years ago, the early part of this decade.

This was a brain transplant.

And even though these operating systems vary in name only by one, they are worlds apart in their technology.

OS 10 is the most advanced operating system on the planet and it has set Apple up for the next 20 years.

Today, it's time to begin a third transition.

We want to constantly be making the best computers for you and the rest of our users.

And so it's time for a third transition and yes, it's true.

We are going to begin the transition from the Power PC to Intel processors and we are going to begin it for you now and for our customers next year.

Now, why are we going to do this?

Right?

Didn't we just get through going from OS 9 to OS 10?

Isn't the business great right now?

Why do we want another transition?

Because we want to be making the best computers for our customer looking forward.

Now, I stood up here two years ago in front of you and I promised you this.

And we haven't been able to deliver that to you yet.

I think a lot of you would like a G5 in your PowerBook and we haven't been able to deliver that to you yet.

But these aren't even the most important reasons.

The most important reasons are that as we look ahead, though we have great products right now and we've got some great Power PC products still yet to come, as we look ahead, we can envision some amazing products we want to build for you and we don't know how to build them with the future Power PC roadmap.

And that's why we're going to do this.

When we look at Intel, they've got great performance, yes, but they've got something else that's very important to us.

Just as important as performance is power consumption.

And the way we look at it is performance per watt.

For one watt of power, how much performance do you get?

And when we look at the future roadmaps projected out mid 2006 and beyond, what we see is the Power PC gives us sort of 15 units of performance per watt.

But the Intel roadmap in the future gives us 70.

And so this tells us what we have to do.

Now, this is not going to be a transition that happens overnight.

It's going to happen over a period of a few years.

Again, we've got great products right now and we've got some great Power PC products in the pipeline yet to to be introduced.

But starting next year, we will begin introducing Macs with Intel processors in them and over time this transition will occur.

I invited him here because I wanted you to hear directly from him uh what he thinks about all this. **[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Paul Otellini]**: Well, I suspect there's a whole bunch of you that never thought you'd see that uh logo on this stage. Uh I was one of them for a while. I'm not anymore, obviously. We are uh so excited at Intel to be to be have given the opportunity to work with Apple to bring you some really great products. I I thought I would try to explain how we got here today and I would do it in the context of telling you a story and the story is really about Apple and Intel and I call it the Silicon Valley story. And it goes back a ways. In fact, it goes back almost four decades. Intel was founded in 1968 by Gordon Moore and Bob Noyce. Bob was the co-inventor of the integrated circuit. We started out building memories. First product was an SRAM. We invented the DRAM and a few years later, we invented the world's first microprocessor, the 4004. And we were in Mountain View. Well, sort of uh eight years later, five miles away in Cupertino, Apple was founded. And you can see the picture of Steve and Waz there. Uh you can also see on the right hand side a picture of Steve **[Audience]**: [Applause] and Bob Noyce on the right hand side having dinner. Uh I asked Steve last night as an aside, was that the last time you wore a tie? And he said, no, it's the last time I wore a mustache though. But what you may not know is that our connection between Intel and Apple started around the same time. Bob and Andy Grove actually were early investors in Apple Apple Computer. And in fact, Anne Bowers was Bob Noyce's wife and she was Apple's first VP of HR. So there were some early signs of genetic connection. It didn't quite work out the way we had hoped. And in fact, Apple started in 1976 with a chip from MOS Technology. Well, our microprocessor business in the PCs came quite after that. In 1981, IBM chose the 8088 to go in their first PC. And things went along for quite some time. And as Steve has pointed out in 1993, two events happened. Well, Apple switched from the 68k to the Power PC and Intel launched the Pentium processor and started ramping it in earnest. And for the next couple of years, competition really heated up quite a bit. It got pretty intense. It got so intense that in 1996, Apple **[Audience]**: [Laughter] They they set fire to our bunny person. And I know some of you may not be as old as this commercial, but I thought I'd let it run for you anyway in case you haven't seen it. Apple Computer would like to apologize for toasting the Pentium 2 processor in public. But the fact remains, the chip inside every new Power Macintosh G3 is up to twice as fast. **[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Paul Otellini]**: Now, now, you know, we didn't have a grudge about that. We just thought it was a not so subtle message that they thought our Apple thought our processors were too hot and they wanted us to run a lot cooler. Well, by the time we got to 2005, in fact, the processors are running a lot cooler and we are so happy that the world's most innovative computer company and the world's most innovative chip company have finally teamed up. This I thought I would give you my perspective on the partnership. I think that this brings together the skills and the opportunities and the engineering excellence of two great companies and they combine our strengths and they play on our respective strengths. Apple has a legendary capability in hardware and software engineering and design and an innovation. You all know that. What you may not be familiar with is us. Our strengths are a little bit different, but they're entirely complementary. We are all about computer architectures. We're about scale and scope and being able to deliver in high volume the world's best technology, the world's best processors and what we are most about is the relentless advancement of Moore's Law to give you better and better machines year after year. And so, after almost 30 years, Apple and Intel are together at last. And I don't think of this as a fairy tale with a happy ending. I think of this much more as a exciting and important story with a very, very happy beginning. Thank you very much. **[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: Thanks Paul. That's great. **[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: So where does that leave us? Well, Apple is strong. Apple's pretty strong right now. And the Mac is strong. We saw this. So this is great. This is a great time to start building for the future to make us even stronger. We know transitions. We've been through two of them and they've kept our platform at the forefront and we're going to continue to be bold and begin a third transition today as far as the developers are concerned to make the best machines that we know how to make in the future. This transition isn't going to happen overnight. Again, we're making awesome machines right now. We got a lot of great Power PC products in the pipeline. But we are also working to design some Intel-based Macs and when we're here next year, we plan to have them in the marketplace and there will be a transition over the next two years. We're getting ready. We've done a lot of work as you've seen today. OS 10 is running fantastic on Intel processors. Xcode 2.1 in your hands today. Rosetta for our customers for those apps that are not universal on day one. We've already made a big investment in this and we're fairly far along. It's time for you to get ready too now. And what do you have to do to get ready? One thing. Create universal binaries of your apps. We've got a lot of stuff going on at the conference to help you today. Over 90 of the 95 presentations that we've got here today include content about universal versions. 100 developer systems in seven labs and the labs are open every night till at least 9:00. I think tomorrow night they're open till midnight. So go see if you can beat Tao and his team on Mathematica. 500 Apple engineers on site. So if you brought your source code, go for it. And when we meet again here next year, we will have Macs with Intel processors.

---

## Part 4

**[Steve Jobs]**: entering the market.

**[Steve Jobs]**: I suspect a lot of you will be shipping universal binaries.

**[Steve Jobs]**: And we will be very excited to keep pushing the frontiers and tell you about Leopard when we meet again here next year.

**[Steve Jobs]**: Because more than even the processor, more than even the hardware innovations that we bring to the market,

**[Steve Jobs]**: the soul of a Mac is its operating system and we're not standing still.

**[Steve Jobs]**: So I'll see you all here next year and uh I look forward to a lot of universal binaries.

**[Steve Jobs]**: Thank you very much.
**[Audience]**: [Applause]

And uh we've got a new tab feature uh that's in all versions of Safari 3 where I've got tabs here and LA Times and I can drag tabs around, right? Which is kind of nice. Uh the other thing I can do is I can just drag them off and put them in their own window, which is kind of nice. Uh but what I really want to show you actually is I want to show you uh the Ibench speed test shootout. And uh so to do that, um let's see. I'm going to go back in here and I've got the Ibench shootout. And uh this is going to run through the Ibench scripts three times just so you can see it because if it runs through it once, it's pretty fast. Safari on the left, IE7 on the right. So here we go. And three, two, one, let's start the tests. And it just loads a ton of websites. Again, Safari on the left, IE7 on the right. 6.64 seconds for Safari on Windows. 13.56 seconds for IE7 on Windows. There you have it.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: So, Safari is the fastest browser on Windows. Again, as you can see, you can run these tests yourself. Anyone can and verify this. But how are we going to distribute this? I mean, we don't really talk to these customers, do we? You know, there are 500,000 downloads of Firefox a day. What are we going to do? Well, it turns out there's over a million downloads of iTunes a day. As a matter of fact, there have been over a half a billion downloads of iTunes to Windows machines. Over half a billion. And so we know how to reach these customers and we're going to do exactly that. So there are three different versions of Safari 3, one that runs on Leopard, one that runs on XP and Vista. And we are releasing them to you today as a public beta on Leopard. It's in your developer preview. We are also releasing today a public beta that runs on both Windows, Windows and Tiger. Since nobody outside of the developer conference gets Leopard, we're going to release it on Tiger and on Windows today. It's a free beta. Apple.com/safari. You can go get it today. And who knows, maybe we can grow our Safari share in the future. We're going to go try. So that's Safari on Windows. We hope you like it.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: So there you have it. Leopard, Safari on Windows. But I do have one last thing that I want to talk about. And that of course is the iPhone.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: The iPhone ships on June 29th. That is just 18 days from today. I believe it's 6:00 p.m. in the evening they will go on sale. June 29th, 18 days from today. Now, what about developers?

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: What about developers? We have been trying to come up with a solution to expand the capabilities of iPhone by letting developers write great apps for it and yet keep the iPhone reliable and secure. And we've come up with a very sweet solution.

**[Steve Jobs]**: And let me tell you about it. So, we've got an innovative new way to create applications for mobile devices. Really innovative. And it's all based on the fact that iPhone has the full Safari inside it. The full Safari engine is inside of iPhone. And it gives us tremendous capability, more than has ever been in a mobile device to this date. And so you can write amazing web 2.0 and Ajax apps that look exactly and behave exactly like apps on the iPhone. And these apps can integrate perfectly with iPhone services. They can make a call. They can send an email. They can look up a location on Google Maps. After you write them, you have instant distribution. You don't have to worry about distribution. Just put them on your internet server. And they're really easy to update. Just change the code on your own server rather than having to go through this really complex update process. And they're secure with the same kind of security you'd use for transactions with Amazon or a bank. And they run securely on the iPhone so that they don't compromise its reliability or security. And guess what? There's no SDK that you need. You've got everything you need. If you know how to write apps using the most modern web standards to write amazing apps for the iPhone today. You can go live on June 29th. And we'd like to show you an example of the kind of apps that you can write starting today. So I'd like to bring up Scott Forstall, our VP of iPhone software who's going to show us one of those apps.

**[Speaker 1]**: Okay. Not only am I going to show you how you can build great applications for iPhone using web technologies, but also how your applications running on the iPhone can take advantage of all the built-in native services as well. So let's get going. Here is uh an iPhone and we have it tethered up here so you can get the video out there. I push the button to wake it up. Again, we have this great touchscreen, slide across, we are unlocked. This is the home screen. So all of your applications are going to run right here in the Safari application. Now, as Steve said, this is the exact same Safari engine that we have running on iPhone as we have running on both the Mac OS 10 and now Windows. So you know, I can do things like double tap to zoom in, double tap to zoom out. All the standard web pages out there just work on the phone. But what's really exciting is you can build custom applications for the phone that have the look and feel of the phone. So we actually built one of these. It's Apple directory. Our IS team decided they wanted to have a custom application for iPhone to get into our corporate uh address book database. Now this database is backed by an Ldap database, but they wanted to build something which looked and felt natural on the phone and that's what they've done. It actually took less than one person month to do this. It used all web standards, nothing special and it's under 600 lines of code to do the whole thing. Let me tap here on Apple directory. You see we automatically slide up the keyboard. I'll go ahead and search for let's say John if I can type here today. That's why shake on stage. Uh so here's John. Now you see it did the lookup into into the Ldap database, brings back this website which looks exactly like the built-in applications. You get the scrolling, you see, it's all touch interface, scrolling. Let me go ahead and choose someone. Say John Keith here. And again, it goes, it brings that card back. Here is the card running in this web application. Now as I said, you get the same look and feel, the same behavior as you do for the built-in applications. So let me show you that to you. If I hit the home button here, here's our home screen. Let me go into our native contacts application, right? So again, it's all the same scrolling, same uh columns and everything. If I tap on Tim Cook, here's what Tim Cook's card looks like in the native built-in contact application. If I hit this home button, take you back to this app. This is a web application, it looks the same. So that's great. But the next thing I said is we can actually take advantage of the built-in services of iPhone from these web applications made for phone. So, if I tap here on the phone number, it automatically goes and calls the person. So you can have, you can call right from your web application. Another one here, it has an email address. If I tap on that, it slides up the built-in mail service. So this is the built-in compose window comes up. You can type something here, compose a message right from your application. Let me say uh what if I was interested in seeing the floor plan of uh John Keith. So I can tap on here. Again, goes back, does a standard web query, comes back with an image. This could be a PDF, it could be a JPEG, could be a TIFF, almost any image type. Uh I can even take and I can watch I can two pinch, zoom it up. So it's a multi-touch display, move it around, zoom it up just like that. There's his office. I can double tap and zoom back down. I'm going to go back to his card.


---

## Part 5

**[Steve Jobs]**: I can even, here, tap on his address. This address takes me directly to the built-in Google Maps application. You can see where the office is. You can double-tap to zoom in, move over a little bit. I can actually switch to satellite mode. I want to see exactly what the office is going to look like when I get there. Zoom way in there. Boom. Integrated right in with your custom apps built for iPhone. I can go back to the app. I can go back to the manager. Tap on the manager. It's walking the LDAP tree back on the server. You can see, you know, here's Kathy Ames, the manager. Here's all the direct reports. It's absolutely incredible. So, when we were looking for a developer story for iPhone, we realized by building in all of the latest web standards, the entire engine from Safari right into here with all of Web 2.0, and then tying it with the services that we've built in to the phone, you can build fantastic applications for iPhone. And I I tell you, I can't wait to run all the apps that you're going to end up building. Thank you very much.

**[Audience]**: [Applause]

**[Steve Jobs]**: Thank you.

**[Speaker 2]**: You know, there are whole companies building their applications this way. Salesforce.com, Google comes to mind as well. And this is a very modern way to build applications. We think it's going to be awesome on the iPhone. So, developers, we think we've got a very sweet story for you. You can begin building your iPhone apps today. You can get your hands on an iPhone, do your final testing and have them out early in July. You can run your applications on Safari on your Mac in the meantime because it's the same browser. It's the same engine underneath them. So, we're very excited about this. June 29th, 18 days from now. So, we've seen this morning, Leopard, Safari for Windows, and now an awesome way to write apps for iPhone. And that's what today's about. We have an awesome week planned for you here at WWDC. Again, 159 sessions on everything you've heard about this morning and more. 94 hands-on labs and 1200 Apple engineers on site. So, enjoy the week and I hope you love the kinds of things we're working on and providing you. Thank you very much. Take care.

documents.title: Xserve introduction 2002
documents.speaker: Steve Jobs
documents.content:
Good morning.

I'm Steve Jobs and I'd like to thank you all for coming.

Um, we've got a really interesting morning plan, uh, because we're going to introduce our first real server.

And we wanted to take you through it.

We've got a few presentations, uh, I'm going to do an overview.

We got a presentation on the software and remote management.

Uh, we got a presentation on sales, support and service.

We got a few partners and customers and then we'll do a Q&A.

We had three hours down on the agenda.

I'm hoping we only take about two.

So, um, get you out of here a little after 11:00 and then we've got some stuff set up in the piano bar across the hall here where you can go get your hands on some of the stuff yourself.

So, let's get going.

This calendar year Apple has already introduced a stream of innovation.

Uh, just since January, we introduced uh, the new iMac, which has been a really big hit for us.

It's selling very well and I think it's one of the best products we've ever made.

We also introduced a um, desktop for our education customers, the eMac.

And this has been received very well by our customers.

We're in the first quarter of selling it and we expect to do very well this quarter.

The reaction so far also has been very strong from our education customers.

We also introduced an upgraded PowerBook that's got a dramatically better display on it and the industry's first DVI connector on a portable.

So you can connect to new projectors with DVI connectors on them, but also you can connect to our displays.

So this PowerBook can drive a Cinema HD display and has all the graphics and video memory inside it to be able to do that and so you can triple your pixels when you get that get to your desk and plug in one connector all digitally.

And last week, we introduced an amazing, or we previewed, excuse me, an amazing new product, Mac OS 10 Jaguar, the next release of Mac OS 10.

We had our most successful developer conference last year in the company's history, which is saying a lot given the travel and budget restrictions this year.

Uh, as you may know, the number of registered Apple developers has doubled in the last 12 months and all of the new developers are principally Unix and Java developers and we are so excited to have people coming to our developer conference that wouldn't even talk to us before our Unix based Mac OS 10.

Uh, Jaguar, which we previewed, which will be available late this summer, has a ton of new features in it.

Some major enhancements to mail, a whole new address book, Inkwell, which is probably the best handwriting recognition out there, uh, which came from, you know what?

Uh, and universal access so that we, we don't leave anybody behind.

Um, a new finder, something incredible called Quartz Extreme, which is taking our whole Quartz graphics pipeline and putting it through our graphics hardware so that it is uh, amazing what you can do now or what you will be able to do with Quartz Extreme.

A technology called Rendezvous, which allows multiple computers and devices, let's say in a home or in a business, to automatically find each other.

It's dynamic discovery over IP networks with zero configuration.

It's really, really cool and our developers loved it.

Uh, two of the biggest things we introduced was, was QuickTime 6, which is a whole new version of QuickTime based on MPEG 4.

This is the best MPEG 4 streaming video solution around and it's going to be bundled in uh, the next release of Mac OS 10 coming out late this summer.

And instant messaging coming to the Mac, integrated right into the operating system, uh, in an application called iChat.

It's totally compatible with AOL's AIM instant messaging network.

And it's the first time AOL's sort of let another company into the tent officially.

And all of this stuff, of course, runs on Mac OS 10, which is Unix, true Unix under the hood.

And as a matter of fact, we are now the largest supplier of Unix in the world.

Isn't that incredible?

I'll say that again.

Apple is now the largest Unix supplier in the world.

It's hard to believe.

And uh, that's why all these Unix developers now are coming to Apple and Mac OS 10.

So that was Jaguar.

So we've seen, uh, already, we're, we're only in our fifth month.

We've seen a tremendous stream of innovation so far this year, continuing what we've done for the last 18 months to try to uh, innovate our way through this uh, this economic period.

So we're going to add another piece of innovation today coming from Apple, which is a server and we call it Xserve.

Uh, Xserve is a new server from Apple.

Now, when you think about servers, you think about the enterprise, right?

And when you think about the enterprise and Apple, you're more likely to think about this than than anything else.

But it's not really true.

Uh, though, though we are not on every desktop in every Fortune 500 corporation, we are in most Fortune 500 corporations.

And uh, they have departments that use Macs.

Uh, AOL Time Warner uses a lot of Macs.

Their magazines every week are put out on Macs.

Uh, companies like Disney, companies like in biotech, like Genentech, uh, usually half or more of their computers are Macs.

So there are a lot of Macs in a lot of Fortune 500 corporations.

But uh, Xserve is really designed not only for business, but also for education because we have a large presence there as well.

So, if there's one word uh, that I would say describes our entrance into the server market, it is um, humble.

We know we have a lot to learn.

And uh, this is our first offering.

Uh, we've listened to our customers a lot and we think we got a pretty hot product, but we know that for everything we know, there's 10 things we don't know.

So we're approaching this uh, we're approaching this very humbly.

So Xserve, what is it?

It's a 1U server solution designed from the ground up.

It's been customer driven and our customers have told us they want to do the following things.

They want to do file and print service, obviously.

They want to do web and email service.

They want to um, do database on their server.

They want to do QuickTime streaming.

This is a way to, and they want to stream, you know, hundreds of streams.

Boom.

And uh, they want to do computational service.

Uh, as an example, our uh, customers in biotech want to run probably the most popular program in biotech, they run dozens of times a day called Blast.

And they want a uh, a computa, one or a cluster of servers to run this very fast.

So, what did they want to see in a server?

Well, the first thing they want from Apple is a dedicated server platform.

They don't want to use a uh, uh, a Power Mac G4 as a server.

They want a dedicated server platform.

Uh, they want it to be rack mounted.

It's the most efficient uh, way to do it.

That's how they do it now and they want to see that from Apple.

Uh, they want a lot of storage flexibility.

Some customers need a little storage, some customers need a lot of storage and they want the flexibility to design the storage that they need.

They want serviceability.

Uh, they know that these things uh, need to be very reliable, but sometimes do need to be serviced and they want great serviceability on this.

And of course, they have to be able to manage these things remotely.

So they want great remote management.

So we're, I'm going to go through all these things and tell you what we've done with Xserve.

To start with, Xserve is a dedicated server platform.

So let, let me take you through the architecture.

First, we start off with a 1 GHz G4 processor, which has 256k of internal level two cache running at the processor speed.

This is a very, very fast chip.

Um, faster than than most chips that chip in servers today.

And to this we add an external 2 megabyte cache, which is DDR SRAM.

Very, very fast cache for a gigabyte per second throughput to the processor.

So it's got a level two internal cache and a level three external cache.

To that, we add a mirror, a second processor with its own cache.

So we've got dual 1 GHz G4s, each with their own level two cache, each with a large level three cache.

Okay.

To that, we add a system controller.

Now, this system controller is a custom ASIC that we've done and it provides exceptional throughput.

Uh, way more than than than most of the other stuff on the market.

And it's got built in it, uh, gigabit Ethernet and it's got FireWire and as we'll see a whole bunch of other things built right in it in a single chip.

Next, we add onto that up to 2 gigabytes of DDR SRAM.

This is the first time DDR SD RAM, excuse me, has been used in a 1U server that we know of.

First time.

266 MHz double the rate of the memory in every other server that we've been able to find.

It's also the first Apple DDR SD RAM system that we will have shipped.

Then we add a PCI slot with a second gigabit Ethernet to it.

So this server is going to come standard with two gigabit Ethernet ports.

These are ports that are 10, 100 and gigabit Ethernet full auto detection.

Next, we add an IO channel out of the system controller and we add quad ATA 100 drives.

These are all on independent controllers, all have independent channels in through the system controller.

A CD ROM and two 64 bit 66 MHz PCI slots for expansion.

We also have three FireWire ports, two USB ports, a serial console port and all of those other kinds of things as well.

Now, this is going to be the first mainstream server to use ATA drives.

Most of the other ones use scuzzy drives.

We're going with ATA drives because it turns out they're just as fast as scuzzy drives now and they offer some real benefits in terms of larger capacities.

This is the fastest Mac architecture we've ever built.

Again, featuring dual GHz G4s, 266 MHz DDR SD RAM, quad independent ATA drives, dual gigabit Ethernet ports and two 64 bit 66 MHz PCI ports.

So this is a dedicated server platform, fastest architecture we've ever built.

Next, rack mounted.

This is Xserve.

This is what it looks like.

Let me show you actually, I've got one here.

Got a few here actually.

This is Xserve.

Here's five of them and here's one of them.

This is the back of the product.

This is the top.

Let me slide it out.

That's what it looks like.

We've got our four ATA 100 drives right there in the front.

We've got our CD ROM.

We've got fans right here.

Power supply.

Dual G4 processors.

2 gigabytes of DDR SD RAM and our three PCI slots.

One for the second gigabit Ethernet and two for expansion.

So that's what it looks like inside.

Now, you can put these in a rack of course and you can just start stacking them up in a rack.

And if you fill this rack, what you'll get is 84 processors, storage of up to 20 terabytes in a 42U rack.

So, rack mounted.

Yes.

Storage flexibility.

We are shipping with 60 gigabyte and 120 gigabyte ATA 100 drives.

Now, we support four drive bays and so if you put 120 gigabytes in each of those, you get 480 gigabytes in a 1U rack mount server.

So, up to 480 gigabytes online with quad ATA 100 drives, that's 400 megabytes per second throughput off the drives, which is huge.

It's also very important when you're doing file service, when you're doing QuickTime streaming, etcetera.

Your disk bandwidth is very, very important.

We've got striping and mirroring.

We've got smart drive monitoring.

We are actually monitoring these drives to look at their error rates, to look at their, their all the statistics about the drive so we can do predictive failure on them, which we'll talk about in a little bit.

And we've got a CD ROM built in for of course software install and restore.

These drives are hot pluggable.

We've designed a really nice carriage where you can unplug them.

And so just, you know, boom, boom, boom, boom.

Really easy.

Take one out.

Just that's it.

Very simple.

And they are hot pluggable.

That's it.

So, 480 gigabytes of storage, hot pluggable, four drives, I think we've delivered storage flexibility.

Next, serviceability.

You can service an Xserve in seconds.

Of course, you can service the drives like we just saw.

But in terms of the units themselves, they literally just slide out.

There's nothing extra to buy.

The rack mount guides are supplied as part of Xserve.

There's no top to take off.

So you can just literally slide the thing part of the way out or all the way out.

There's no nothing to take off to get at the guts and to service almost every component in seconds.

So, we also have hardware monitoring where we try to alert you to what needs service in some cases ahead of time.

So, what are we monitoring with hardware?

The drive status and pre fail, which is part of that smart disk technology.

We're monitoring the temperature of both the processor and the enclosure.

We're monitoring that the fans are working and what their RPMs are.

We're monitoring the power supply voltages and we're monitoring that the network connections are established.

And you will see more about this a little later.

It's really impressive what we can do with this.

We also have built in security since this is so easy to open up.

Uh, we have an enclosure security lock that keeps it from being opened.

We have an intrusion alert that lets you know if it's been opened and we have a software lock so that you can lock down FireWire, USB and the CD ROM from letting anyone in.

So we've tried to think of the type of security that people want in a modern day server.

So, this is Xserve.

You can service anything in seconds.

We think we've built in state of the art hardware monitoring and security and have a very strong serviceability story.

So pricing and availability.

Pricing on Xserve starts at $29.99.

There are two standard models.

One comes with one 1 GHz G4, the other comes with dual GHz G4 processors.

One quarter gigabyte of DDR memory, the other with a half a gigabyte of DDR memory.

Both come with 60 gig drives as standard.

One for $29.99, one for $39.99.

But most people aren't going to buy these standard configurations.

They're going to configure one exactly like they want.

You can go to our website and do that.

Select the server page, select one of our standard models or customize it any way you want.

Thousands and thousands of configurations.

Now, how does this compare to the competition?

What does it look like out there?

Well, we picked a few different things to compare to.

Here's Xserve.

We're going to take the dual processor model.

We're going to take our competitors and configure them as close as we can to Xserve.

So here's a Dell Power Edge 1650 with dual processors.

Uh, configured it's about $4277.

An IBM eServer X3300 for 5186.

And a Sun, this is the closest Sun we could get.

The low end Suns are not competitive and it's uh, it's almost $20,000.

So, three of these are 1U servers.

The Sun is a 4U server.

1U servers.

And uh, as I mentioned, they have dual processors in them, dual 1 GHz G4 in Xserve.

Uh, the other two, uh, the middle two use Pentium 3s.

They can't put a Pentium 4 in because they can't get the heat out in a 1U server.

So they use Pentium 3s at 1.4 GHz and the Sun uh, uses a dual 900 MHz Ultra Sparc 3s.

Now, if we look at level, they all have uh, level two caches built in.

If we look at level three caches though, which really can speed up performance, the Xserve again has 4 megabytes of level three cache, 2 megabytes on each processor.

Uh, and the Sun has 8 megabytes of level three cache, but the Dell and the IBM have no level three cache and it's not even possible to add it.

So this does affect performance.

In terms of memory, uh, we've loaded uh, the Dell and the IBM up to get to 512 megabytes.

The Sun, the lowest you can buy it with is 2 gigabytes, which is great.

Um, but if you notice, the Xserve is the only one that uses 266 MHz DDR memory.

The rest of them are at 133 MHz uh, SD RAM.

And that makes a difference in performance, double the bandwidth to memory.

On the disc drive front, uh, we've loaded them up to get as close as we can to Xserve with its 60 gigabytes.

We've got 73 gigabytes uh, on the middle two and about the same on the Sun.

If you notice again, everyone else uses scuzzy drives.

We think there is an absolute trend to ATA drives now that they've gotten as fast as scuzzy drives and uh, are less expensive and uh, larger capacity.

But if you look at the total capacity of each of these servers, we've got four bays in the Xserve for 480 gigabytes of storage.

But look at the two middle ones, 219 gigabytes max on the Dell with three bays and 144 gigabytes uh, on both the IBM and the Sun.

So all three of these servers have a lot less storage capacity than and flexibility than Xserve does.

Ethernet, uh, again, uh, uh, Xserve and Dell come standard with dual gigabit Ethernet.

We've loaded the IBM up.

Uh, you can't get dual gigabit Ethernet on the Sun, but we've, we've ordered the optional uh, single gigabit Ethernet included in that price.

So again, the prices for these things are um, as I've mentioned.

But these prices are um, for Linux on the middle two servers.

Mac OS 10 server on Xserve of course, Linux on the middle two and Solaris of course on the Sun.

But what if you want to run Windows on the middle two?

---

## Part 2

You're in for a shock. Because to buy a Windows license on the middle two for just five users, which is not too useful in an enterprise, $799 additional dollars. Most people are going to have to buy the 25 user license, which cost $3,295 from Dell or IBM. And when you add that price, as you see Xserve and Sun come with unlimited user licenses bundled in, if you add that to um to the price, look at what you get. Look at the hidden cost of actually running these as Windows servers with just 25 concurrent user license. Look at what they cost compared to Xserve with an unlimited user license at $39.99.

So, again, two standard models, single and dual processor, and you can configure anything you want on the website. We are taking orders beginning today. So after this meeting, you can all go order your server. And uh we will be shipping these next month. So um we're very close to shipping you your Xserve.

Now, again, let's run through um what our customers asked for. Dedicated server platform. We're giving them a great one, we think. Certainly rack mounted. Storage flexibility. With 480 gigabytes. You can service it in seconds with intrusion alerts and hardware monitoring. And remote management. For remote management, I'm going to go uh back to our agenda here. We're going to go to the second topic on our agenda, the software and remote management. And I'm going to turn it over to Phil Schiller. But before I do, I forgot to do one thing, which I want to do, which is just uh pull one of these guys out so you can see how easy this is.

That's all there is to it. To get to every part in the server. So, take a look at one of these after the presentation and see for yourself how easy it is. Phil?

So now, thank you Phil.
Now we get to how are we going to service, support and sell these servers.
And you might think, wow, Apple's Apple's never done this before.
Apple doesn't do anything close to this before, but you might be wrong.
So here to tell us about that is Tim Cook.
Tim is our executive vice president who runs operations, sales and support and uh how are we going to service and support and sell these things, Tim?
Thank you Steve.
Good morning.
So I'd like to talk about both support and sales.
You've heard a lot about the product features and I'd like to first start by saying that we fully recognize that server support is really, really hard.
And so as Steve indicated earlier, we've entered into this very humbly.
We discovered two things as we began to look at this and why it's really, really hard.
And the first is that the applications running on servers are generally mission critical.
They're things that must happen.
So for me that might be taking orders, hopefully many of them, fulfilling orders, shipping orders, invoicing customers, things you can't stop.
Also, there's a fundamental lack of integration among most of the solutions on the market today.
And this has a this has a consequence that's really awful for customers, which is they have more issues and maybe even worse than that, when they have an issue, the timely response really isn't there.
So with that kind of backdrop, we went out and asked our customers, what do you want?
And when when we asked that, we got back seven simple kind of things.
Maybe not simple to deliver, but fairly simple to understand.
The very first was they really don't want support.
They want products to work.
Now this this is a fairly simple thing maybe to understand.
But so we looked at how do we provide this?
And as it turns out for those of you that are using Macs today, you may not know but but you've seen the results of, we have very robust quality assurance processes in Apple.
And it's because we control the whole of the solution.
Our reliability testing and engineering is enormous before we bring a product to market.
And maybe more importantly than both of those, our customers that are operating in mixed environments tell us that the Mac is better.
And that's the ultimate test.
The second thing they told us was that they want really expert technical support.
Really expert.
